<sig>B 2</sig>

## GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN

I. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was a God. <note>original: ⲟⲩⲛⲟⲩⲧⲉ ⲡⲉ ⲡϣⲁϫⲉ. In Coptic, the use of the indefinite article ("a") here is a notable grammatical feature that scholars often discuss regarding the nature of the Word (Logos) in relation to the Father.</note> ² This one in the beginning was with <note>original: ϩⲁⲧⲙ̄, meaning "beside" or "at the side of."</note> God. ³ All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being. That which came into being ⁴ in him is the life, and the life is the light of mankind. ⁵ And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not grasp it. <note>The Coptic word for "grasp" or "apprehend" can mean both to understand and to overcome.</note> 1. ⁶ There was a man who had been sent from God, his name being John. ⁷ This one came for a witness, that he should bear witness—

---

**Notes on Textual Variations**

**Verse 3:** "that which became" is omitted in the Bohairic <note>The dialect of Northern Egypt.</note> manuscript G₂.

**Verse 3–4 Connection:** "that which became in him"] <note>This refers to a famous ancient debate about where to place the period: "without him nothing became. That which became in him was life" versus "without him nothing became that which became. In him was life."</note> This specific phrasing (joining "that which became" to "in him") is found in the Sahidic manuscript 1ᵉᵖ and others (109, 28¹, 48¹), as well as in the Greek manuscripts C* D G*, several Old Latin versions, the Syriac, Armenian, and various early Christian writers like the Naassenes, Valentinians, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and Eusebius. 
<note>original: ὁ γέγονεν. ἐν αὐτῷ. The alternative punctuation "that which became. In him [was life]" is found in the Greek manuscripts Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Vaticanus (B), and Codex Delta (Δ).</note>

**Verse 4:** "in him"] Found in Sahidic manuscripts 109, 13¹, 28¹, 48¹. The Armenian version reads "by him."
"is" (1st occurrence)] Found in Sahidic manuscript "c" and others, matching Greek manuscripts ℵ and D, Old Latin, and various Church Fathers. Other sources (including Codex Vaticanus) use "was."
"and"] Found in 1ᵉᵖ, 13¹, 28¹, and the Armenian; the Ethiopic reads "but."
"is" (2nd occurrence)] Found in "c," 109, 28¹, and 48¹; other sources use "was."
"of the men/mankind"] Found in 1ᵉᵖ, 109, and 13¹; omitted in the original hand of Codex Vaticanus (B*).

**Verse 5:** "and" (1st occurrence)] Found in "c" and others; omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts; the Ethiopic reads "but."
"is enlightening"] Found in "c" and 109, matching major Greek manuscripts; manuscript 1ᵉᵖ and the Syriac read "was enlightening."
"the darkness"] The Sahidic definite article "the" is missing in manuscript 13¹.
"apprehended it"] The Coptic uses a masculine pronoun here. The Bohairic version adds "could not apprehend it," while the Ethiopic reads "findeth it not."

**Verse 6:** "There was" (literally: "he became")] Found in Sahidic "c" and others; the Ethiopic adds "and."
"from"] Found in "c" and 41, matching the Greek word *para* (beside/from).
"God"] Found in "c" and 41; the Greek manuscript D* reads "the Lord."

# JOHN I 36-39

...standing, and two of his *disciples*. $^{36}$ And when he <note>John the Baptist</note> had looked at Jesus walking, he said, "Behold the *Christ*, <note>original: ⲡⲉⲭⲣⲓⲥⲧⲟⲥ; The Coptic Sahidic version includes "the Christ" here, whereas most Greek manuscripts simply say "the Lamb of God."</note> the lamb of God." $^{37}$ His two *disciples* heard him speaking, and they followed Jesus. $^{38}$ But when Jesus had turned, he saw them following him: he said to them, "What are you seeking?" They said to him, "Rabbi" <note>original: ϩⲣⲁⲃⲃⲉⲓ; a Coptic transliteration of the Hebrew/Aramaic term for teacher</note>, which is usually interpreted as "Master" <note>original: ⲡⲉϣⲁⲩⲟⲩⲁϩⲙⲉϥ; literally 'that which they usually repeat' or 'translate'</note>, "Where are you dwelling?" $^{39}$ He said to them, "Come and see": they came therefore, they saw where he was dwelling, and they stayed with him on that day; it was <note>The text cuts off here, likely leading into the mention of the hour.</note>

### Critical Apparatus: Textual Variations
<note>This section compares different ancient manuscript versions of these verses. Key: ℵ is Codex Sinaiticus, A is Codex Alexandrinus, B is Codex Vaticanus, Bo is the Bohairic Coptic dialect, Syr is Syriac, and OL/Vg are Latin versions.</note>

**saw**] Supported by manuscript groups (c), (20), 109, Bohairic (F), and Ethiopic. The Greek <note>original: και θεασαμενος; 'and having seen'</note> is found in ℵ, A, B, and others. The Bohairic (ΓP), Christian Palestinian Syriac, and Armenian add "and he saw." The Sinaitic Syriac omits "he saw them following."

**him** <note>original: ⲛ̄ⲥⲱϥ; 'after him'</note>] Supported by (c), 109, Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (C), Old Latin (a, b, e, f, ff, l, q), Vulgate, Bohairic, various Syriac versions, Armenian, and Ethiopic. It is omitted in ℵ, A, and B.

**said he** <note>original: ⲡⲉϫ.</note>] Found in (c), 20, 109, Christian Palestinian Syriac, and Armenian. Some versions (Bohairic, other Syriac, Ethiopic) add "and" before "said."

**to them** (1st occurrence)] Found in (20) and 109. Omitted in the original hand of ℵ.

**said they** <note>original: ⲡⲉϫ.</note>] Found in (c), 20, 100, 109, and most Syriac and Armenian versions. The Greek <note>original: οι δε ειπαν; 'but they said'</note> is in ℵ, A, B, and others. The Ethiopic says "and they say."

**Rabbi** <note>original: ϩⲣ.] ϩⲣⲁⲃⲃⲉⲓ</note>] Found in 20, 100, 109, ℵ, and B. Codex Alexandrinus (A), Bohairic, Harklean Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic use the spelling **Rabbi**. The Curetonian/Sinaitic Syriac uses **Rabban**.

**that-interpreted** <note>original: ⲡⲉϣⲁⲩⲟⲩⲁϩⲙⲉϥ</note>] Found in (c) and 100. Variants of "which is interpreted" <note>original: ο ερμηνευεται</note> are in Greek manuscripts 1, 118, 209, and the Ethiopic/Old Latin. Other Greek manuscripts (ℵ, A, B) use variations meaning "which is said, being interpreted." It is omitted in several Syriac versions. The Armenian says "which being interpreted is called."

**art thou dwelling** <note>original: ⲉⲕⲟⲧⲏⲣ</note>] Found in (c), 20, 100, and 109. This matches the Greek <note>original: μενεις; 'you remain/stay'</note> in ℵ, A, B, and others, as well as Bohairic, Harklean Syriac, and Ethiopic. The Sinaitic Syriac simply says "are you." The Armenian reads "are the dwellings yours."

**39** **said he**] Found in (c), 20, 100, 109, ℵ, A, B, etc. The Bohairic and Ethiopic add "but" or "and."

**and see** <note>original: ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲩ</note>] Found in 75, 109, and Greek manuscripts <note>original: και ιδετε</note> including ℵ and A, as well as Latin, Bohairic, and Armenian. However, (c), 20, 57, 100, and Codex Vaticanus (B) read **and ye will see** <note>original: ⲁⲩⲱ ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲛⲁⲛⲁⲩ</note>, matching several Syriac versions and Origen.

**therefore** <note>original: ⲥⲉ</note>] Found in (c), 20, 100, 109, and major Greek manuscripts (ℵ, A, B). Some Syriac and Latin versions use "and" or omit it entirely.

**they saw** <note>original: ⲁⲩⲛⲁⲩ</note>] Found in 20, 91, 100, 109. Most other manuscripts (ℵ, A, B, etc.) add "and" before "they saw."

**he is dwelling** <note>original: ⲉϥⲟⲩⲏⲣ</note>] Found in (c), 20, 91, 100. Matches the Greek <note>original: μενει</note>. Some Bohairic, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions use slightly different verbs for "staying" or "dwelling."

**they abode** <note>original: ⲁⲩⲱ.; ⲁⲩⲱϫⲡ</note>] Found in (c), 20, 91, 100, 109. Matches the Greek <note>original: εμειναν</note>. The Sinaitic Syriac says "they were [with him]."

### Critical Apparatus: Textual Variations
<note>This section lists how different ancient manuscripts of the Bible vary in their wording for these specific verses.</note>

**the hour** <note>original: ⲡⲛⲁⲩ</note>] Supported by manuscripts 91, ℵ, A, B, and others, including the Old Latin (q), Ethiopic, and the writings of Epiphanius and Cyril. Some versions add "but" <note>original: ⲇⲉ</note>, while others add "for it was" <note>original: ⲅⲁⲣ / erat enim</note> in manuscripts p, Old Latin (bf), and Armenian.
**tenth** <note>original: ⲛ̄ϫⲡⲓⲛⲧⲉ</note>] Found in manuscripts c, p, 20, 91, 109, and the Bohairic and Ethiopic versions. Some Greek manuscripts (ℵ, A, B) prefix this with "about" <note>original: ⲱⲥ; hōs</note>. The Ethiopic version reads "until the tenth hour."

$^{40}$ **Andrew** <note>original: ⲁⲛⲇⲣⲉⲁⲥ</note>] Supported by ℵ, B, Old Latin, and Bohairic. Some manuscripts (A, Ⲗ) add "but." The Ethiopic says "and one is Andrew." The Syriac versions vary, with one noting "and one of these disciples of John, Andrew his name was..." 
**Peter** <note>original: ⲡⲉⲧⲣⲟⲥ</note>] Found in most, but the Syriac (c) and Armenian use "Stone" or "Kepha."
**was one** <note>original: ⲛⲉ ⲟⲩⲁ ⲡⲉ</note>] Found in 57 and 109. The Greek uses "one was."
**the two** <note>original: ⲡⲉⲥⲛⲁⲩ</note>] Found in 20. Some Greek manuscripts use "two of..." or just "two."
**and** <note>original: ⲁⲩⲱ</note>] Omitted in some Bohairic versions.
**him** <note>original: ⲛ̄ⲥⲱϥ</note>] Supported by ℵ, A, B, and the Syriac and Armenian versions.

$^{41}$ **this** <note>original: ⲡⲁⲓ</note>] Manuscript 57. The Bohairic replaces this with "Andrew." The Syriac says "this [man] saw Simon his brother." The Ethiopic says "and first he found."
**his brother Simon** <note>original: ⲡⲉϥⲥⲟⲛ ⲥⲓⲙⲱⲛ</note>] Found in 57 and Bohairic. The Syriac (s) adds "his brother that day."
**first** <note>original: ⲛ̄ϣⲟⲣⲡ̄</note>] Most Greek manuscripts use "first" <note>original: proton</note>, while others use a slightly different grammatical form <note>original: protos</note>. Some Old Latin versions use "in the morning" <note>original: mane</note>.
**to him** <note>original: ⲛⲁϥ</note>] The Syriac (s) adds "my brother."
**Messiah** <note>original: ⲙⲉⲥⲥⲓⲁⲥ</note>] Found in 57 and Greek manuscripts ℵ, A, B.

# THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN

### Chapter 1: 40-43

->THE DISCIPLES OF JESUS<-

...at the tenth hour <note>Approximately 4:00 PM; the Jewish day was calculated from sunrise (6:00 AM).</note>. $^{40}$ Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who heard John <note>John the Baptist</note> and followed him. $^{41}$ This man first found his brother Simon and said to him, "We have found the Messiah," which is usually interpreted as "the Christ" <note>original: ⲡⲉⲭ̅ⲥ̅ (Christos); both titles mean "the Anointed One," with Messiah coming from Hebrew and Christ from Greek.</note>. $^{42}$ He brought him to Jesus. But Jesus, when he had looked upon him, said, "You are Simon the son of John; you shall be called Cephas," which is usually interpreted as "Peter" <note>original: ⲡⲉⲧⲣⲟⲥ; "Cephas" is the Aramaic word for rock, and "Peter" is the Greek translation.</note>. $^{43}$ On the next day, he <note>Jesus</note> wished to go out to Galilee, and he found <note>The text likely continues with the finding of Philip on the next page.</note>

---

### Critical Apparatus: Textual Variations
<note>This section compares different ancient versions of the New Testament to show where the wording varies between the Sahidic Coptic and other traditions.</note>

**Verse 41**
**Messias** <note>original: ⲙⲉⲥⲓⲁⲥ</note>] This reading is supported by manuscripts 75, 91, 109, the Bohairic Coptic, the Philoxenian Syriac, and the Armenian version. It is omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac.
**that which is interpreted** <note>original: ⲡⲉϣ.</note>] Present in manuscript c, 109, the Harklean Syriac, and the Armenian; omitted in several other Syriac versions.
**the Christ** <note>original: ⲡⲉⲭ̅ⲥ̅</note>] Supported by manuscript 57, 109, and the Bohairic and Armenian versions. However, it is omitted in the major Greek Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), and Vaticanus (B), as well as in the writings of Origen, Epiphanius, and Cyril. The Sinaitic Syriac uses the term *meshīkko* <note>Syriac for "Anointed One"</note>.

**Verse 42**
**he brought him** <note>original: ⲁϥⲓⲧⲧϥ̅</note>] Supported by manuscript c and Greek Codices Sinaiticus and L. Other variations include "but this one was" (Greek G and I), "and this one" (Bohairic and Ethiopic), or "and he led him and came" (Syriac).
**Jesus (1st mention)**] The Sinaitic Syriac replaces the name with "our Lord."
**but Jesus...** <note>original: ⲓ̅ⲥ̅ ⲇⲉ</note>] This specific phrasing is found in manuscripts 57 and 91, and several Latin and Syriac versions. Manuscript 75 reads "Jesus therefore," while major Greek codices (ℵ, A, B) omit the word "but."
**said he** <note>original: ⲡⲉϫ.</note>] Manuscripts p, 57, 75, and the Syriac and Ethiopic versions add "to him" <note>original: ⲛⲁϥ</note>.
**the son** <note>original: ⲡϣ.</note>] Most manuscripts include the definite article "the."
**of John** <note>original: ⲓ̅ⲱ̅ⲁ̅ⲛ̅ⲛ̅ⲏⲥ</note>] The Sahidic reading "John" matches the oldest Greek Codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. However, other versions (Codex Alexandrinus, the Vulgate, and some Syriac/Bohairic) read "Jona" or "Iona."
**Cephas** <note>original: ⲕⲏⲫⲁⲥ</note>] Variations in spelling occur across Bohairic and Armenian versions (e.g., Kepha, Gephas).
**interpreted as Peter** <note>original: ⲡⲉϣ.-ⲡⲉⲧ.</note>] Omitted in the Old Syriac. One Syriac version specifies "which is interpreted in Greek as Petros."

**Verse 43**
**on the morrow** <note>literally: "on his morrow"</note>] This Sahidic form is supported by the major Greek codices. The Bohairic version adds "again" <note>original: ⲟⲛ</note>.
**wished** <note>original: ⲁϥⲟⲩⲱϣ</note>] Supported by most ancient versions. Some Greek manuscripts add "Jesus" as the explicit subject. Manuscript 99 and certain Bohairic versions change the tense to the present ("he wisheth") or a participle ("having wished").
**and** <note>original: ⲁⲩⲱ</note>] Omitted in some Bohairic and Armenian manuscripts. The Ethiopic adds the name "Jesus."
**said he** <note>original: ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ</note>] Found in manuscript 43 and some Bohairic manuscripts; major Greek and Syriac versions prefix this with "and."

### Critical Apparatus: Textual Variations
<note>This section details how this Coptic manuscript differs from other ancient versions of the New Testament, such as the Greek codices or other Coptic dialects.</note>

**Verse 43**
**Jesus** <note>original: ⲓⲥ̅</note>] Supported by manuscript 43 and others, manuscript 99 (corrected), Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Vaticanus, and others; also the Old Latin (a, b, c, f, ff, l, q), the Vulgate, the Bohairic Coptic, the Syriac (Jerusalem and Harklean), the Armenian, and the writings of Epiphanius and Cyril. The Sinaitic Syriac reads "our Lord." It is omitted in manuscript 99 (original hand), codices F, H, M, Γ, and others, Old Latin (e), and by Ambrose, Fulgentius, the Bohairic (A, C, G2, H, L), the Curetonian Syriac, the Ethiopic, and Chrysostom.

**Verse 44**
**Now** <note>original: ⲇⲉ (de)</note>] Supported by manuscript 43 and others, the corrected Sinaiticus, Bohairic, and the Palestinian and Harklean Syriac. Omitted in the original Sinaiticus. The Armenian reads "and."
**from Bethsaida** <note>original: ⲟⲩⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̅ ⲃⲏⲇⲥⲁⲓⲇⲁ; literally: "one out of B."</note>] Found in manuscript 43 and others. Greek codices use "from (apo) B." The Bohairic reads "a native of B." The Sinaitic Syriac reads "his kin was from B." 
**Bethsaida** <note>original: ⲃⲏⲇⲥⲁⲓⲇⲁ</note>] Manuscript 75 and some Old Latin manuscripts spell this "Betsaida."
**the city** <note>original: ⲧⲡⲟⲗⲓⲥ</note>] Found in manuscript 43 and others. Omitted in the original Sinaiticus and some Old Latin and Vulgate versions.
**Peter** <note>original: ⲡⲉⲧⲣⲟⲥ</note>] The Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions read "Simon."

**Verse 45**
**Philip** <note>original: ⲫⲓⲗⲓⲡⲡⲟⲥ</note>] The Curetonian Syriac and Ethiopic add "and."
**said he** <note>original: ⲡⲉϫⲁϥ</note>] Several Greek codices and other versions prefix this with "and."
**and** <note>original: ⲁⲩⲱ</note>] Manuscript 75 uses "with" <note>original: ⲙⲛ̅</note>.
**the prophets** <note>original: ⲛⲉⲡⲣⲟⲫⲏⲧⲏⲥ</note>] Supported by most Greek and Syriac witnesses.

**Verse 48**
**know** <note>original: ⲥⲟⲟⲩⲛ̅</note>] Manuscript 43 uses a shorter spelling.
**Before** <note>original: ⲉⲙⲡⲁⲧⲉ</note>] Manuscripts 99, 109, and 91 add "that" <note>original: ϫⲉ</note> before this word.
**fig tree** <note>original: ⲕⲛ̅ⲧⲉ</note>] Spelled differently in manuscripts 75 and 133.

### Critical Apparatus: Textual Variations
<note>This section lists differences between ancient versions of the text. Scholars use these notes to determine the most original wording. Abbreviations like ℵ, A, and B refer to major Greek codices; Bo refers to the Bohairic Coptic dialect; OL refers to Old Latin versions.</note>

**son]** Supported by manuscript p and others, Codex Alexandrinus and others, Chrysostom; but the Greek word for "the" <note>original: του</note> is omitted by Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and minuscule 33, as well as Epiphanius and Cyril.

**Nazareth <note>original: ⲛⲁⲍⲁⲣⲉⲑ</note>]** Spelling found in p and others, Codex E and others, Old Latin (manuscripts b, c, f, l, q), the Vulgate, Bohairic, and Armenian; whereas "Nazaret" <note>original: ναζαρετ</note> is found in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, L, X and others, Old Latin (a), Origen, Epiphanius, Chrysostom, and Cyril; variants include "-rath" <note>original: -ραθ</note> in Codex Delta and Pi², and "Nazara" in Old Latin (e).

**⁴⁶ Said]** Found in p and others, Codex Sinaiticus, minuscule 71, Old Latin (a, b, e), and Bohairic (manuscripts Lq 18) and Syriac (g, s); but preceded by "and" <note>original: και</note> in Codex Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and others, Old Latin (c, ff, g₁, q), the Vulgate, Bohairic, Syriac (j, h), and Ethiopic, as well as Epiphanius. 

**to him (first occurrence)]** Found in manuscript 43 and others; omitted in Bohairic (manuscript M).

**a good (thing)]** Found in 43 and others; "something good" <note>original: τι αγ.</note> in the corrected Codex Sinaiticus and others; "good thing" <note>original: αγ. τι</note> in the original Codex Sinaiticus.

**to be]** Found in 43 and others, Syriac (g, h), and Armenian; "come" in Bohairic (L); "come forth" in Syriac (s) and Ethiopic.

**out]** Found in 43 and others; omitted in manuscript 57.

**Nazareth]** Found in 43 and others, Codex Gamma and others; "Nazaret" <note>original: ναζαρετ</note> in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, L, X, Delta and others, and Old Latin (a) and others.

**and see]** Found in manuscript c and others, and "and behold" <note>original: και ιδε</note> in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus and others, Syriac (h), and Armenian; "and thou wilt see" in Syriac (g, s) and Armenian.

**⁴⁷ saw-and]** Found in manuscripts (c?), 43, 57, 133, the corrected Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus and others, Old Latin (c, f, q), Vulgate, and Syriac (g, h); "and" is omitted in 75, 91, 99, 109, the original Codex Sinaiticus (124), Old Latin (a, e, ff, l), Bohairic (F₁* Q), Armenian, Ethiopic, and (Epiphanius); "but seeing" <note>original: ιδων δε</note> in 124, Old Latin (a, b, ff), Epiphanius; "but he saw" <note>original: ⲁϥⲛⲁⲩ ⲇⲉ</note> in Bohairic; "but Jesus when he saw" <note>original: ihs autem ut vidit</note> in (c); "but Jesus saw" <note>original: ⲓⲏⲥ ⲇⲉ ⲁϥⲛ.</note> in Bohairic (T); "and saw" in Syriac (g, h, s); "when he saw" in Armenian; and "and when he saw" in Ethiopic.

**concerning him]** Found in (c) and others, and 133; "concerning Nathanael" <note>original: περι του ναθ.</note> in the original Codex Sinaiticus; omitted in Old Latin (e).

**Israelite]** Found in (c), 57, 75, 99, Alexandrinus, and the second correction of Vaticanus; "an Israelite" <note>original: ⲉⲓⲥⲣ.</note> in 43, 109; "Israelite" <note>original: ⲥⲣⲁⲏⲗⲓⲧⲏⲥ</note> in 91, 133; variant spelling in Codex Sinaiticus and original Vaticanus.

**⁴⁸ said]** Found in 43 and others, and 75; preceded by "and" in Bohairic (G, M, T, S) and Ethiopic.

**answered-he]** Found in (c?), 43, 57, and Bohairic (several manuscripts); "Jesus answered saying" <note>original: ⲁ ⲓⲥ ⲟⲩⲱϣⲃ ⲉϥⲭⲱ</note> in 91 and others; "Jesus answered and said" <note>original: απεκριθη ⲓⲥ και ειπεν</note> in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus and others, Bohairic, Syriac (h), Armenian, and Ethiopic; "but Jesus answered and said" in Bohairic (T); "Jesus said to him" in Syriac (g).

**within under]** Found in 43, 57, and Ethiopic; preceded by "you being" <note>original: ⲉⲕⲉ</note> in 75 and others, and Bohairic.

**⁴⁹ Nathanael...him]** Found in (p) and others, and (109); "Nathanael answered him" in Codex Vaticanus, L, 33, 249, and Old Latin (b); "and Nathanael responded" <note>original: et nat. respondit</note> in (e); "answered him" <note>original: ⲟⲩⲱϣⲃ ⲛⲁϥ</note> omitted in (c); "answered Nathanael and said."

# JOHN 2:4–9

"Woman, what do you want with me? My hour has not yet come."
$^5$ His mother said to the servants, "Whatever he says to you, do it."
$^6$ Now there were six stone <term>water jars<note>original: 'hydria', large vessels used for ritual washing</note></term> standing there according to the purification rites of the Jews, each holding two or three <term>measures<note>original: 'metrētēs', a Greek liquid measure of about 9 gallons</note></term>.

$^9$ When the master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine, and did not know where it was from (but the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast... <note>The text breaks off as he prepares to call the bridegroom.</note>

### Critical Apparatus: Notes on Variant Readings

**Manuscript Variants for Coptic Text:**

**What do you want]** Variants in manuscripts 43, 57, 75 use the spelling `ⲉⲣⲉⲟⲩⲉϣ`, while others like manuscript 91 use `ⲉⲣⲟⲩⲉϣ`. **Not yet]** Manuscript 133 reads `ⲙⲡⲉⲧⲉ` instead of `ⲙⲡⲁⲧⲉ`. **Hour]** Manuscript 109 reads `ⲟⲩⲛⲏⲟⲩ` instead of `ⲟⲩⲛⲟⲩ`. $^5$ **Whatever he [says]]** Spelling variations between manuscripts p, 43, 57, 99 and the standard text. $^6$ **There were]** Minor spelling differences in the Coptic verb "to be" across manuscripts 75, 91, 109, and 133. **Stone jars]** Abbreviated in some versions. **Holding/Being]** Variation in the verb for "containing" or "being" across multiple manuscripts. **Three]** Manuscript 57 uses a shortened form for the number three. $^7$ **Fill]** Manuscripts 75 and 91 use a slightly different verbal prefix. $^8$ **Master of the feast]** The Bohairic version and various Greek-influenced Coptic manuscripts (75, 91, 109, 133) show different spellings for this Greek loanword. $^9$ **Tasted]** Manuscripts 91 and 133 use a shorter form of the verb. **Wine]** Omitted in one fragmentary version (p). **It was]** Minor grammatical variation in manuscripts 91 and 133.

---

**Comparison with Other Ancient Versions:**

**Verse 4: They have no wine]** <note>original Greek: 'oinon ouk echousin'</note> Found in the corrected Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, and Codex Vaticanus, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Armenian versions. The original hand of Codex Sinaiticus reads "There is no wine" <note>original Greek: 'oinos ouk estin'</note>. The Syriac and Ethiopic versions read "Wine is not to them." Some Old Latin manuscripts add the word "son."

**Jesus said]** Found in most manuscripts. The Greek "He says" <note>original: 'legei'</note> is found in the earliest hand of Sinaiticus and the Bohairic Coptic. Some versions (Vulgate, Armenian, Ethiopic) add "And." **To her]** Omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts. **The woman]** <note>original Coptic: 'teshome'</note> Literally "the woman," used as a respectful address. Greek manuscripts and the Ethiopic version often include the vocative "O" <note>original: 'ō gynai'</note>.

$^5$ **Said to the servants]** Most versions agree. The Ethiopic adds the word "and." A unique Old Latin manuscript (e) expands this to: "And having called the servants to her, the mother of Jesus said to them."

$^6$ **Six]** Omitted in one Old Latin manuscript (b). **Stone]** Found in the majority of manuscripts including the major Greek Codices and Old Latin.

My hour has not yet come." $^5$ His mother said to those who draw <term>the wine<note>The Coptic text refers to the servants specifically as "those who draw," likely referring to the water or wine.</note></term>, "Whatever he says to you, do it." $^6$ But there were six <term>waterpots of stone<note>original: 'hydria', large stone jars used for Jewish ritual purification</note></term> put down there, according to the cleansing of the Jews, each receiving two or three <term>firkins<note>original: 'metrētēs', a Greek liquid measure roughly equivalent to 9 gallons or 34 liters</note></term>. $^7$ Jesus said to them, "Fill the waterpots with water," and they filled them up to their mouths. $^8$ He said to them, "Draw now, and bring to the <term>ruler of the feast<note>original: 'architriklinos', the master of ceremonies or headwaiter at a banquet</note></term>." And they brought it. $^9$ But when the ruler of the feast had tasted the water having become wine, and he did not know where it was from (but the <term>drawers<note>The servants who drew the water.</note></term>, those who filled the water, knew), the...

### Critical Apparatus: Notes on Manuscript Variations

<note>This section compares different ancient versions of the Bible, including Coptic, Greek, Latin, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Syriac, noting where they differ in word order or phrasing.</note>

**Verse 6**
**Stone waterpots]** The Armenian version adds "marble." This detail is also found in the writings of John Chrysostom and Cyril of Alexandria. Several early Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.) and the Latin Vulgate change the word order.
**Put down]** In several Coptic manuscripts (coded c, p, b1), the word for "put down" <note>original: 'kē esrai'</note> is moved after the word for "Jews." In other Greek and Latin versions, it is moved after the word "six" or "there." Some very early manuscripts omit the word entirely.
**Measures (firkins)]** <note>original: 'metrētēs'</note> Variously spelled across Coptic and Greek manuscripts.

**Verse 7**
**Said]** <note>original: 'pedje'</note> Some versions (like the Ethiopic) add "and" before Jesus's name. Certain Old Latin manuscripts read "and Jesus called them to himself" or simply "and Jesus called."
**With water]** The Ethiopic version adds "up to their mouths" here instead of at the end of the sentence.
**And they filled them]** The Bohairic Coptic version uses "but they filled them" <note>original: 'mmou de'</note>.
**Up to their mouths (to the brim)]** Various Coptic dialects use different prepositions for "up to" or "out to." Some versions use "up to the top."

**Verse 8**
**Said to them]** Various Greek and Syriac manuscripts use "he says to them" or "and he says to them." One Coptic manuscript adds "Jesus" to the sentence.
**And bring]** One Bohairic manuscript omits the "and."
**But they brought]** There is a variety of phrasing here. Some Latin versions add a explanatory note: "and they did as Jesus said to them." Others simply say "they drew and they brought."

**Verse 9**
**Whence (from where)]** Most manuscripts agree, though some use a slightly different Greek form for "where."
**The water]** Some Old Latin versions add "which was made wine" or "because wine was made from water." Others include a note: "and seeing what was done, they wondered."
**Ruler of the feast]** <note>original: 'architriklinos'</note> Some manuscripts add "but" or "and" <note>original: 'de'</note> after the title.

### Critical Apparatus: Notes on Manuscript Variations

<note>This section provides a scholarly comparison of how different ancient translations of the Bible (Coptic, Greek, Latin, Syriac, etc.) record these specific verses. Each abbreviation refers to a specific ancient manuscript or regional version.</note>

¹⁰ **said he]** Found in various Coptic fragments and the Bohairic <note>The dialect of Coptic used in Lower Egypt</note> version. Some manuscripts, including the <term>Codex Sinaiticus<note>one of the oldest surviving Greek Bibles, denoted by the symbol א</note></term>, the Codex Alexandrinus (A), the Codex Vaticanus (B), and the Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions, add "and" before "he said."
**to him]** Present in Coptic and Latin versions; omitted in the Sinaiticus and Armenian versions.
**is put/serves]** The Sahidic <note>The dialect of Coptic used in Upper Egypt, represented in the main text above</note> manuscripts vary between "is put" and "they are wont to serve."
**until now]** Some manuscripts transpose the word order. 
**and]** Omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts; the Greek text often uses "but" or "then" <note>original: 'de' or 'tote'</note>.

¹¹ **the first]** The Coptic and Latin Vulgate agree on "this first sign." Greek manuscripts like Sinaiticus use "the beginning of signs."
**and]** Included in most Sahidic fragments; omitted in some Bohairic versions.
**his glory]** Omitted in the original hand of the Sinaiticus manuscript.
**believed]** Most manuscripts add "and" before "believed."
**him]** The word order varies in the Sinaiticus manuscript; it is omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts.

¹² **after these]** Agreement between several Coptic fragments, the Old Latin versions, and the writings of the church father John Chrysostom.

<note>The following section contains technical scholarly notes (an apparatus criticus) comparing different ancient versions of the Bible, including the Coptic Sahidic and Bohairic dialects, the Greek Codex Sinaiticus (symbolized by ℵ), the Old Latin (OL), Syriac (Syr), Armenian (Arm), and Ethiopic (Eth) versions.</note>

**Verse 15**
Regarding the phrase <note>original Greek: 'ta pro[bata]', meaning 'the sheep'</note> found in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus, Old Latin manuscripts (a, e, l, q), and the Armenian version; the order of **oxen-sheep** is swapped in the Syriac version.
The word **the oxen** appears in Coptic manuscripts 32, 97, 109, and 42¹.
The Old Latin manuscript (e) adds the name **Jesus**.
Manuscript (q) adds the word **sellers**, while manuscript (e) adds the phrase **who were selling oxen and sheep**. 
The Bohairic Coptic manuscripts (D, A, E, J, O, S) show a variation in the word for **temple** <note>original: 'p-ape-s' or 'p-ape-r'</note>.
The Syriac version adds the phrase **and the changers**. 
The word **and** (the third instance in the verse) is found in Coptic manuscripts 32, 97, 109, and 42¹, but is omitted in Bohairic manuscripts (D, E, F, J).
In Bohairic manuscript (M), the word for money is <note>original: 'p-somnt', literally 'the brass' or 'copper coins' (plural)</note>, also found in manuscripts 32, 97, and 42¹.
Other Greek and Latin sources use the term <note>original: 'ta kermata', meaning 'the small coins'</note>.

**Verse 16**
**Said he**: found in Sahidic Coptic manuscripts (p), 32, 97, 42¹, and Bohairic (F, T). 
The major Greek manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus) and the Syriac and Armenian versions add the word **and** at the start of the sentence.
**Make not**: found in Sahidic Coptic 32, 97, 42¹, and Greek manuscripts ℵ and B. 
A different group of manuscripts (including the Latin Vulgate and other Greek texts) adds **and** before this command.

**Verse 17**
**Remembered**: found in Coptic manuscript 32, Greek manuscripts ℵ, B, L, T, X, and the Bohairic version. 
Other sources add the word **but** or **then**.
The Syriac version reads: **when he did these things, his disciples remembered**. 
**Will eat me** <note>original: 'pash-om-t'</note>: The Bohairic and Armenian versions use a future tense verb <note>original Greek: 'kataphagetai', meaning 'will consume'</note>. Some other versions use a past tense form meaning **has consumed**.

**Verse 18**
The Syriac version reads: **the Jews say to him**.
**The Jews**: found in Sahidic Coptic manuscripts 32, 75, 91, 97, 99, 133 and several Greek minuscules. 
Other manuscripts add the word **therefore**.
One Latin source reads **then they answered**, while another reads **and the Jews answered**.
**Said they**: found in manuscripts 32 and 75. The Bohairic manuscript (B) uses the word **saying**.
**To us**: omitted in Greek manuscript L and the Ethiopic version.

**Verse 19**
**Jesus**: The Syriac version uses the title **our Lord**.
**Overthrow**: The Bohairic manuscript (M) uses a variation meaning **I shall [raise]**.
**This**: omitted in the Syriac version.

### Critical Notes on the Text
<note>This section compares various ancient hand-copied versions of the Bible to see where they differ. Abbreviations like "ℵ A B" refer to the most famous Greek manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus), while "OL," "Syr," and "Eth" refer to Old Latin, Syriac, and Ethiopic translations.</note>

²² **therefore** <note>original Coptic: de</note>] (found in manuscript 32?) and others, including manuscript 109, and Greek manuscripts ℵ A B etc. .. **but/therefore** in manuscripts 41 and 99 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **that which he was saying** <note>original Coptic: penefjo m</note>] in manuscript 32 etc., Greek manuscripts ℵ A B etc., Old Latin, Vulgate, Bohairic Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, and the writings of Cyril of Alexandria .. some versions add **to them** <note>original Greek: autois</note> in manuscripts K and Π &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **said** <note>original Coptic: joof</note>] manuscript p etc. 109 .. some add **to them** <note>original Greek: autois</note> in manuscripts 69, 346, and others.

# III

¹ Now there was a man from the Pharisees, whose name was **Nicodemus**; he was a **ruler** of the Jews. ² This man came to him by night and said to him, "**Rabbi** <note>original: Rabbei; a title of respect for a Jewish teacher</note>, we know that you are a **teacher** who has come from God; for no one is able to perform these **signs** <note>original: maein; referring to miracles that point to a greater truth</note> that you are doing, unless God is with him." ³ Jesus answered and said to him, "**Truly, truly** <note>original: Hamēn hamēn</note>, I say to you, unless someone is born **again** <note>original: nkesop; can mean "again" or "from above"</note>, he is not able to see the **kingdom of God**." ⁴ Nicodemus said to him, "How can a man be born again after he has grown **old**?"

### Textual Variations in Coptic Manuscripts
<note>This section compares different hand-copied Coptic fragments. The numbers (26, 32, 41, etc.) refer to specific manuscript fragments held in various museums and libraries.</note>

**what was in**] written as *pe et-hm* in manuscript 32.
¹ **Now there was a man**] Recorded in manuscripts 26, 32, 41, 43, 57, 91, 99, 133, and 46¹.
**Pharisees**] Spelled with a double 's' in manuscripts 26, 91, 133, and 46¹.
**Nicodemus**] Spelled *Nikodimos* in manuscripts 133 and 46¹.
² **we know**] manuscript "p" spells this slightly differently.
**you are**] manuscripts 91 and 133 use a contracted form.
**no one is able**] variations in the negative particle used between manuscript 43/57 and manuscript 41/109.
**unless**] manuscript 46¹ uses a different spelling for "God" and manuscript 91 uses a different suffix for "with him."
³ **truly (first instance)**] manuscript "a" omits the first 'h' (*Amēn* instead of *Hamēn*).
**kingdom**] manuscripts 91, 109, and 133 use a slightly different noun form for "royalty/kingdom."
⁴ **Nicodemus**] manuscripts 91 and 109 use a variant spelling starting with "O" instead of "I".

### Comparative Analysis of Ancient Versions
<note>This section compares the Coptic text against other ancient languages to help scholars understand the history of the Bible's transmission.</note>

**the man** (first occurrence)] Found in Coptic manuscripts 26, 41, and 99; matches the major Greek manuscripts ℵ <note>Codex Sinaiticus</note>, A <note>Codex Alexandrinus</note>, and B <note>Codex Vaticanus</note>, as well as the Harclean Syriac. However, manuscripts 43 and 57 omit the definite article, matching the Greek writer Origen and the Armenian version. Manuscripts 32, 91, and 133 read "concerning him." The Sinaitic Syriac reads "the heart in man what it is."

**but there was a man**] Matches the Greek manuscripts ℵ A B. The Philoxenian Syriac adds "there," reading "but there was there one man." The Ethiopic and Armenian versions vary on the placement of "one."

**his name was**] The Coptic uses a construction meaning "his name [being]." The Sinaitic Syriac and Ethiopic versions explicitly say "his name was." The major Greek manuscripts (except the original hand of Sinaiticus) and the Armenian version say "the name to him." The Old Latin version (manuscript e) uses "who was called."

**a ruler**] Variation in manuscript 57.

### Critical Apparatus: Manuscript Variations
<note>This section compares the Coptic text with other ancient versions like the Greek (ℵ, A, B), Syriac, and Latin.</note>

**a ruler**] Found in manuscripts (c), (p), 97, and fragments. The Greek term **ruler** <note>original Greek: αρχων</note> is used in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), and Vaticanus (B), as well as the Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions. The Sinaitic Syriac reads: *and this man was a ruler*.

² **this**] Found in Coptic manuscript 26, the major Greek codices (ℵ, A, B), the Bohairic Coptic, and Armenian versions. Omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac. The Armenian also reads: *and he*.
**unto him**] Found in manuscript (p), the major Greek codices, and some Old Latin versions. Other versions read **to Jesus** <note>original Greek: προς τ. ι̅ν̅</note>. The Sinaitic Syriac reads: *to our Lord*.
**by night**] literally: *of the night*. Codex Sinaiticus and some Old Latin versions change the word order.
**said he**] manuscript (p) and Bohairic. Other Greek codices add the word **and** before "said."
**to him**] found in manuscript (p); omitted in some Bohairic fragments.
**Rabbi**] spelled **Hrabbei** in most manuscripts and major Greek codices.
**who camest**] found in manuscript 32, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Some Syriac versions read: *who wast sent* or *who wast sent to us*. Manuscript 26 reads: *who came*.
**it-possible**] manuscript (c), the major Greek codices, and the Vulgate.
**for** <note>original: gar</note>] found in manuscript 26, 109, and Codex Alexandrinus. Omitted in others. Codex Sinaiticus reads: *and no one*.
**these signs**] manuscript (c) and the major Greek codices. Manuscript 4 reads: *the signs*.
**which-doest**] found in most, but omitted in manuscript I.
**unless**] Manuscript 4 adds the word **one** here.
**being**] found in manuscript (c) and 26. Omitted in some Latin versions. The Syriac reads: *unless it is he whom God is with*.

³ **ans. Jesus**] Found in manuscript 26, the major Greek codices, and the Bohairic. Manuscript 4 reads: *Jesus answered*. Some versions (91, 97, 99) add **and**. The Sinaitic Syriac reads: *saith to him our Lord*.
**said-him**] Found in manuscript 4 and the Bohairic. Omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus. Manuscript 97 uses the word **saying**.
**another time** <note>lit. "born again"</note>] Found in (c), manuscript 4, Bohairic, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Old Latin versions use **born again** <note>original Latin: natus-denuo</note> or **reborn again** <note>original Latin: renatus-denuo</note>. The Greek codices use **from above** <note>original Greek: ανωθεν</note>.
**to see**] manuscript 4. Some manuscripts read **to enter into** the kingdom.

⁴ **said**] manuscript 4 and others.
**to him**] manuscript (p).

"Is it then possible for him to go into his mother’s womb **a second time** <note>original: nkesop; literally 'another time' or 'again'</note> and be born?" ⁵ **Jesus** <note>original: IS; a shortened sacred form (nomen sacrum) of the name Iēsous</note> answered: "**Verily, verily** <note>original: Hamēn, hamēn</note> I say to thee, unless one is born of **water** and the **Spirit** <term>pneuma; a Greek loanword used by Coptic writers for the Holy Spirit, but also meaning 'breath' or 'wind'</term>, it is not possible for him to enter into the **kingdom of God**. ⁶ That which is born from the **flesh** is **flesh**, and that which is born from the **Spirit** is **spirit**. ⁷ Do not marvel that I said to thee: It is necessary for you to be born **again** <note>original: nkesop</note>. ⁸ The **Spirit** breathes where it wills, and thou hearest its voice, but thou knowest not from where it has come and where it goes. ### Manuscript Variations and Notes
<note>This section lists how different ancient copies of the Bible vary in their wording for these verses.</note>

**is it... possible for him to go]** Found in various manuscripts including the Sahidic (α, 41, 43). Some versions (p, 26, 97) and the Bohairic <note>Bohairic was the Coptic dialect of the Nile Delta</note> use a phrasing that means "for him to enter."

**his mother]** Manuscript 46¹ and others use "the mother."

**Jesus]** Most manuscripts (α, 26, 97, 98) agree with the major Greek codices like Codex Sinaiticus (א) and Codex Alexandrinus (A). Manuscript 46¹ and the Old Latin version (f) add the phrase "said he."

**Verily, verily]** Found in nearly all sources; however, Codex Alexandrinus (A) strangely omits the second "verily."

**to thee]** Most manuscripts say "to thee" (singular), but manuscript 46¹ says "to you" (plural).

**unless they beget/one is born]** The Coptic uses a literal phrasing "unless they beget one." The Old Latin and Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> use "unless he be born again."

**again / a second time]** The Coptic term **nkesop** literally means "another time." This corresponds to the Greek term **anothen** <note>original: ανωθεν</note> which can mean "again" or "from above." The Syriac and Armenian versions emphasize "twice" or "two times," while the Old Latin uses "born anew."

**having grown old]** Manuscript 32 and 109 use a slightly different verb tense: "he became old."

**and be born]** The Coptic literally says "and they beget him," matching the Greek phrasing "and be born."

**breathes/blows]** Variations in spelling occur in manuscripts 91, 133, and 46¹.

**where it wills]** Some minor spelling variations occur in manuscripts 91 and 133.

**from where it has come]** Manuscript 41 uses a slightly different grammatical form for "from where."

<note>The following notes represent the "apparatus criticus," where scholars compare differences between ancient Coptic manuscripts of the New Testament (identified by numbers like 91, 109, 133).</note>

**who has been born]** manuscripts 32, 91, 109, 133, 46¹ use slightly different grammatical forms. ⁹ **Nicodemus answered]** manuscripts 26, 32, 41, 43, 57, 91, 109, 133 vary in punctuation and phrasing. **Nicodemus]** spelled "Nikode" in manuscript 133. ¹⁰ **Are you...]** manuscript 91 uses a different form of "you." ¹¹ **what we...]** manuscript 109 repeats the phrase "what we" three times. **testify]** manuscript 109 uses a different spelling for "testify." **our testimony]** manuscripts 91 and 133 omit a possessive marker. ¹² **earthly things]** manuscript 133 omits the word "of." **believe]** some manuscripts (4, 26, 41, 43, 57) use a future tense construction. ¹³ **unless]** manuscript 98 uses a different spelling <note>original: eimēti</note>. ¹⁴ **the serpent]** slight spelling variations between manuscripts 4, 26, 41, and 109. ¹⁵ **in him]** manuscript 4 uses "up into" and manuscript 98 uses a slightly different preposition.

---

<note>This section compares the Coptic text with other ancient versions like Greek, Latin (OL), Syriac (Syr), and Ethiopic (Eth).</note>

**out of the spirit]** <note>original Coptic: ebol hm p-pneuma</note> corresponds to the Greek: "out of the water and the spirit" <note>original Greek: ek tou hydatos kai tou pneumatos</note> found in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Old Latin versions, and the Syriac. Hilary adds the word "holy." ⁹ **Nicodemus answered]** manuscripts 26, 32, and 109 vary; some Bohairic manuscripts add "and." The Sinaitic Syriac version reads "saith to him Nicodemus." **said he]** Bohairic and other Coptic versions vary on whether they add the word "and" before this phrase. **these things]** most versions agree, though the Armenian version reads "for this," and some manuscripts (109, 133) and major Greek codices (A, B) use the plural "these."

¹¹ **truly (the second one)]** omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac. **and (the first one)]** included in manuscript 26 and others.

# JOHN IV 7–10

It was the sixth hour <note>Ancient noon.</note>. $^7$ A woman came out of Samaria to fill water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink." $^8$ For his disciples had gone to the city to buy for themselves that which they would eat. $^9$ She, the *Samaritan woman*, said to him, "How is it that you, being a *Jew*, wish to drink from me, I being a Samaritan woman?" For *Jews* are not accustomed to mingle with *Samaritans*. $^{10}$ Jesus answered and said to her, "If you had known the gift of God, and who it is who says to you..."

---

<note>The following notes represent a "critical apparatus," a scholarly record comparing different ancient manuscripts. Abbreviations like "Bo" refer to Bohairic Coptic, "Syr" to Syriac, "Arm" to Armenian, "Eth" to Ethiopic, "Vg" to the Latin Vulgate, and "ℵAB" refer to famous Greek codices like the Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus.</note>

(g 39) **for** <note>original: "ⲅⲁⲣ" (gar), a Greek loanword meaning 'for'</note>] Found in manuscripts 21, etc., 100, the Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Vaticanus (B), etc., and the Bohairic version (Bo). It is omitted in the Sahidic version (T). **but** <note>original: "ⲇⲉ" (de), meaning 'but' or 'and'</note>] Found in manuscripts 114 and 43$^1$, Bohairic, and the Syriac version (g). **and**] Found in the Curetonian Syriac (Syr cs). **had gone** <note>original: "ⲏⲥⲁⲣ ⲉⲱⲕ"</note>] Found in manuscript 21, etc., 100. Manuscript 24 adds a particle. The Greek word for "they departed" <note>original: "απηλθον"</note> is found in the Codex Regius (L). **the city** <note>original: "ⲧⲡⲟⲗⲓⲥ"</note>] Found in manuscript 21, etc. The Greek article "the" <note>original: "την"</note> is omitted in the Codex Sangallensis (Δ). **to buy** etc. <note>original: "ⲉϣⲱⲡ"</note>] Found in manuscript 43, etc., 100. Omitted in manuscript 91. **to buy bread** <note>original: "ⲉϣⲉⲡ ⲟⲉⲓⲕ"</note>] Found in manuscripts 21 and 24. **in order that they might buy food** <note>original: "ινα τροφας αγορασωσιν"</note>] Found in Greek manuscripts ℵAB, etc., and the Harklean Syriac (Syr h) and Armenian versions. **that they might buy victuals for them**] Found in the Bohairic version. **that they might buy their food**] Found in the Ethiopic version.

$^9$ **to him** <note>original: "ⲛⲁϥ"</note>] Found in manuscripts 21, 114, 43$^1$, and several Greek minuscules, as well as the Bohairic and Syriac versions. A prefix meaning **therefore** <note>original: "ⲇⲉ" (de)</note>] Found in manuscript 57, etc., and the corrected Sinaiticus (ℵ$^c$), as well as the Old Latin (OL) and Vulgate (Vg). **the Samaritan woman** <note>original: "ⲧⲉⲥϩ. ⲛ̄ⲥ."</note>] Found in manuscripts 24, 43, 114, 133, the Bohairic, and most Syriac versions. $^{10}$ **Jesus answered** <note>original: "ⲁ-ⲟⲩ."</note>] Found in manuscripts 57, 94, 115, etc. Another variation for **answered Jesus** <note>original: "ⲁϥⲟⲩ. ⲛ̄ϭⲓ"</note>] Found in manuscripts 85, 91, 109, 133, and the Sinaiticus (ℵ). **said he** <note>original: "ⲡⲉϫ."</note>] Found in manuscript 57, etc., and the Bohairic version. The Greek **and said** <note>original: "και ειπεν"</note> is found in ℵAB, etc. **to her** <note>original: "ⲛⲁⲥ"</note>] Found in manuscript 57, etc. **to thee** <note>original: "ⲛⲉ" / "ⲛⲏ" / "ⲡⲉ"</note>] Various spelling differences across manuscripts 85, 109, 91, 115, and 57. **thou** <note>original: "ⲛ̄ⲧⲟ"</note>] An emphatic form of "you."

# JOHN

...you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.
¹¹ The woman said to him, "Sir, <note>The Coptic *p-choeis* can be translated as "Lord" or "Sir," a title of respect.</note> you have no bucket <term>kados: a Greek loanword for a water jar or bucket</term> and the well is deep. Where, then, do you get this living water? ¹² Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well? He himself drank from it, as did his sons and his cattle." ¹³ Jesus answered and said to her, "Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again. ¹⁴ But whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will never thirst again forever. ¹¹ (Manuscript group 57, 85, 91, 109, 133, 43¹, etc.) **bucket**] variant spelling *-tos* in manuscript 91; the Bohairic version uses *antlēma* <note>Bohairic: a different Coptic dialect's word for bucket</note>. **the well**] variant spellings in manuscripts 57, 85, 91, 61, 43¹, 133. **deep**] variant *shakt* in manuscript 91. **you have**] variations in the grammatical prefix across manuscripts 57, 109, 133, 61, 85, 43¹, 91. **there**] omitted in manuscript 85. **from/out**] omitted in manuscripts 91, 109, 133.

<note>The following section is the critical apparatus, which tracks how different ancient copies of the Bible differ in their wording. The numbers (8, 13, 114, etc.) refer to specific Coptic manuscripts. Symbols like ℵ, A, and B refer to major Greek codices: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus.</note>

**³³** **his disciples** <note>original: "ⲛⲉϥⲙⲁⲑⲏⲧⲏⲥ" (nefmathetes)</note>] Found in manuscripts 8, 13, the Old Latin versions, the Bohairic (Northern Coptic), and Ethiopic versions. The word "his" <note>original: "αὐτοῦ" (autou)</note> is omitted in the Greek Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), and Vaticanus (B), and the Syriac versions. The phrase "the disciples" <note>original: "οἱ μαθηταὶ"</note> is moved to follow the word "therefore" <note>original: "οὖν"</note> in the Greek Codices ℵ, A, and B. The Syriac (Curetonian and Sinaitic) versions simply say "they." **to one another** <note>original: "ⲛⲉⲩⲉⲣⲏⲩ"</note>] Transposed before "the disciples" in the Greek Codex Bezae (D) and others.

**³⁴** **said** <note>original: "ⲡⲉϫⲉ"</note>] In manuscript 114; the Ethiopic version adds "and." **Jesus** <note>original: "ⲓ̅ⲥ̅"</note>] Omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac. **to them** <note>original: "ⲛⲁⲩ"</note>] Manuscript 114 and others. **of me** <note>original: "ⲧⲁⲟⲟⲓ"</note>] Various spellings in manuscripts 91, 92, and 57. Manuscript 114 reads "of the Father, he who sent me." **his work** <note>original: "ⲡⲉϥϩⲱⲃ"</note>] Found in manuscripts 109, 114, and the Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions. The Curetonian Syriac reads "the work."

**³⁵** **yet** <note>original: "ⲕⲉ" / Greek: "ετι"</note>] Found in manuscript 8, the Greek Codices ℵ, A, and B, the Vulgate, and Bohairic. Omitted in Codex Bezae (D) and others. **behold you** <note>original: "ⲉⲓⲥ-ⲏⲏⲧⲛ"</note>] Found in manuscript 109 and the Syriac versions; omitted in others. **that white** <note>original: "ϫⲉ ⲏⲁⲏ ⲁⲩ."</note>] Variations in the word order of "already white for harvest." Some versions, like the Vulgate and certain Bohairic copies, say "that they are white already for harvest" <note>original: "οτι λευκαι εισιν ηδη προς θερισμον"</note>. Others, like Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), put "already" <note>original: "ηδη"</note> at the start of the next sentence: "Already he who reaps..."

**³⁶** **he who reapeth** <note>original: "ⲡⲉⲧⲱϩⲥ"</note>] Found in manuscripts 114, 123, and the major Greek Codices. Some versions add "and" <note>original: "και"</note> before "he who reaps." The Ethiopic reads "for he also reapeth." **and** <note>original: "ⲁⲩⲱ"</note>] Omitted in some Bohairic copies. **to a life** <note>original: "ⲉⲡⲱⲛϩ"</note>] Manuscript 114 reads "of life." **that** <note>original: "ϫⲉⲕⲁⲥ"</note>] Omitted in some Syriac versions. **he who soweth** <note>original: "ⲡⲉⲧⲭⲟ"</note>] Follows the Greek and Coptic standards. **should together rejoice** <note>original: "ⲉⲩⲉⲣⲁϣⲉ ϩⲓⲟⲩⲙⲁ"</note>] The placement of "together" varies; in the Ethiopic, it is placed before "he who sows."

...a man was there, having spent thirty-eight years in his sickness. ⁶ When Jesus had seen this man lying there, and knowing that he had been in that state for a long time, he said to him, "Do you wish to be made whole?" ⁷ The sick man answered him, "Lord, I have no one <note>original: "man"</note> who, when the water is stirred up, can cast me into the pool; but while I am coming, another is accustomed to go down before me." ⁸ Jesus said to him, "Rise, take up your bed, and walk." ⁹ And immediately the man was made whole, and he took up his bed and walked; but it was the *Sabbath* <term>Sabbath: the Jewish day of rest, where carrying a bed or working was traditionally forbidden by religious law</term> on that day. ¹⁰ Therefore the *Jews* said to him who had been relieved of his pain, "It is the *Sabbath*, and..."

# JOHN 5:11-16

<page-num>69</page-num>

...it is not granted to you to take up your bed. ¹¹ He answered to them, "The one who cured me, that one is he who said to me, 'Take up your bed, and walk.'" ¹² They asked him, "Who is the man who said to you, 'Take it up, and walk'?" ¹³ But he who had ceased <note>original: "ceased," a Coptic idiom meaning his suffering had ended or he was healed</note> [from pain] did not know who it was; for Jesus had withdrawn himself, as there was a multitude in that place. ¹⁴ After these things Jesus found him in the temple, and said to him, "Behold, you were made whole; do not return to committing sin, so that something worse <note>literally: "evil"</note> than this does not happen to you." ¹⁵ The man went and showed to the *Jews* <term>Jews: here referring to the religious authorities who enforced the Sabbath laws</term> that Jesus was the one who cured me <note>Some manuscripts read "me" here, following the man's direct report, while others say "him."</note>. ¹⁶ Because of this the *Jews* were persecuting...

---

### Critical Notes on Manuscript Variations

The following notes compare different ancient versions of these verses, including Syriac (Syr), Armenian (Arm), Old Latin (OL), the Vulgate (Vg), and various Coptic dialects.

**Verse 11 and 13 Variations**
*   **is]** Found in manuscript 13; the Greek "is" (*estin*) appears in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), and Vaticanus (B). Codex Bezae (D) reads "was" (*ēn*).
*   **for]** Found in manuscript 13 and Bohairic Coptic; the Sinaitic Syriac reads "because our Lord."
*   **had withdrawn himself]** Manuscript 13 and Old Latin; some manuscripts read "he withdrew himself," while the main Greek tradition uses "slipped away" (*exeneusen*). The Syriac adds that he withdrew "into the great multitude."
*   **in that place]** Found in manuscript 13, Old Latin, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Greek manuscripts vary between "in the place" (*en tō topō*) and "in the midst" (*en tō mesō*).

**Verse 14 Variations**
*   **after these things]** Found in manuscript 13, Bohairic, and major Greek codices. The Old Latin (l) says "and afterwards," while the Ethiopic says "and then."
*   **Jesus found him]** Most versions agree; Codex Sinaiticus and the Syriac specify "our Lord finds him."
*   **him]** The original hand of Codex Sinaiticus and the Ethiopic use "the one who was healed" (*ton tetherapeumenon*) instead of just "him."
*   **said he]** Manuscript 13 and Bohairic; major Greek manuscripts prefix this with "and."
*   **behold]** Found in manuscript 13 and most versions. Some Greek manuscripts use a slightly different word for "look" (*ide*).
*   **to sin]** Manuscript 13; other manuscripts like 91 and the Greek tradition add the word "anymore."
*   **than this]** Found in manuscript 13 and the Sinaitic Syriac; the Curetonian Syriac reads "than the former." This phrase is omitted in many Greek manuscripts.
*   **happen to you]** Variants exist in the word order of the Greek (*soi ti genētai* vs. *ti soi genētai*), supported by early church fathers like Origen and Chrysostom.

**Verse 15 and 16 Variations**
*   **he went]** Manuscript 13 and Codex Vaticanus (B). Other versions say "he went away" or "he went away therefore."
*   **he showed]** Manuscript 13; Greek versions use "he announced" (*anēggeilen* or *apēggeilen*) or "he said" (*eipen*).
*   **cured me]** Manuscript 13 and the Syriac follow the man's perspective ("me"); most Greek manuscripts say "made him whole" (*poiēsas auton hygiē*).
*   **because of this]** Manuscript 91 and Bohairic; manuscript 13 and the Greek tradition add "and" to the beginning of the sentence.

# JOHN 5:16-20

<page-num>70</page-num>
<header>JOHN</header>

<term>the imperfect tense</term> the *Jews* <term>the Jews: referring to the Judean religious authorities</term> were persecuting <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: "ic̄," a sacred shorthand for Iesous</note>, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. ¹⁷ But <term>Jesus</term> answered them, "My Father is working until now, and I [too] am working." ¹⁸ Because of this, therefore, the *Jews* sought even more to kill him; because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was also saying, "God is my Father," making himself equal with God. <note>original: "ia" — This is the numeral 11, marking a new section in the manuscript</note> ¹⁹ <term>Jesus</term> answered and said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, there is no power for the Son to do anything of his own accord, unless he sees the Father doing them; for those things which he [the Father] does, these also the Son does likewise. ²⁰ For the Father loves the Son, and shows him [every] work...

---

### Textual Variations in Coptic Manuscripts

*   **persecuted]** Found in manuscript 13 and ε; manuscript 91 uses a slightly different spelling.
*   **Verse 17]** Variations found in manuscript 13, ε, and 91.
*   **Verse 18]** Variations found in manuscript 13, ε, and 91.
*   **Verse 19]** Variations found in manuscripts 13, 91, and fragments. The word for **"there is not"** varies between manuscript c and 13 versus ε and 91. The spelling of **"to do"** or **"would do"** varies across all fragments.
*   **Verse 20]** Witnessed in manuscripts c, 13, ε, 91, and fragments.

---

### Comparative Analysis of Ancient Versions

**Verse 16 — "the Jews [persecuted] Jesus"]** Most Coptic manuscripts follow this order. However, Greek manuscripts like Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and others include different Greek articles. Some versions, like the Armenian and certain Syriac texts, add the phrase "and sought to kill him" earlier in the verse.

**Verse 17 — "and I [too]"]** This reading is supported by Codex Alexandrinus (A) and the Ethiopic version. Some Syriac versions change the emphasis to "because of this also." 

**"until now"]** Most versions agree; however, some Bohairic (Northern Coptic) manuscripts read "until this hour" or "until today."

**Verse 18 — "therefore"]** Omitted in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and some Old Latin versions, but present in the Coptic and most major Greek texts.

**"to kill him"]** Most manuscripts include the word "him," though some of the earliest Greek witnesses (ℵ, A, B) omit the specific pronoun.

**"was he breaking"]** The Coptic uses a continuous tense; some versions, like the Bohairic and specific Greek texts, use a simple past tense "he broke."

### Textual Variations and Manuscript Comparisons

**but-also** <note>original Coptic: "alla-de"</note>] Found in manuscript **s** and others, and the Bohairic <note>The Coptic dialect of Lower Egypt</note>; others read "but that" <note>original Greek: "all' hoti"</note> in manuscript Λ, 13, and others, as well as Bohairic, Syriac, and the writings of John Chrysostom; whereas Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus, along with the Armenian version, read simply "but" <note>original Greek: "alla"</note>.

**was saying**] Found in manuscript **s** and ε 91; manuscript 13 reads **is saying**; the Syriac and Armenian versions read **was calling**. 

**also** <note>original Coptic: "on"</note>] Found in manuscript **s** and others; omitted in manuscript 91.

**my Father** <note>original Coptic: "pa-eiōt"</note>] Found in manuscript **s** and others, and the Syriac; however, Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus, along with Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions, read **his own Father** <note>original Greek: "patera idion"</note>.

**equalizing**] Found in manuscript **s** and others; the Armenian and Ethiopic versions add the word **and** before this.

$^{19}$ **answered**] Found in manuscript **s** and others, manuscript 33, and several Old Latin versions, Bohairic, and Armenian; whereas manuscript ε, Codex Sinaiticus, and others add **therefore** <note>original Greek: "de"</note>; the Ethiopic version prefers **and then**. 

**answered-them**] Found in manuscript **s**, others, and manuscript ε, and the Armenian; a Bohairic manuscript adds **to them** after **answered**; Codex Sinaiticus reads **Jesus then said to them**; and the Syriac reads **saith to them Jesus**.

**the [Son]** <note>original Coptic: "p-shēre"</note>] Found in manuscript **s** and others; omitted in manuscript B and some early Latin fathers like Tertullian.

**said he**] Found in manuscript **s**, others, and some Bohairic manuscripts; whereas Codex Alexandrinus and the Latin Vulgate read **and said** <note>original Greek: "kai eipen"</note>; others read **and saith** or **and was saying**.

**to them**] Found in manuscript **s** and others; omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts.

**Verily** (the second occurrence)] Found in manuscript **s** and others; omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus and the Syriac.

**the Son**] Found in manuscript **s** and others; some manuscripts (D, 13, 69) and the Syriac and Old Latin versions add **of man** <note>original Greek: "tou anthrōpou"</note>.

**anything**] Found in manuscript **s** and ε; some Greek manuscripts change the word order.

**except**] Found in manuscript **s** and others; the Syriac version phrases this as **nor anything which he saw not his Father do**.

**the-them** <note>referring to the Father doing things</note>] Found in manuscript **s** and others; manuscript D reads **doing the [things] of the Father** <note>original Greek: "poiounta ta patros"</note>.

**that**] Found in manuscript **s** and others; Codex Sinaiticus and others read **that one** <note>original Greek: "ekeinos"</note>; Origen and some Syriac versions read **the Father**.

**likewise** <note>original Greek: "homoiōs"</note>] Found in manuscript **s**, 13, ε, and Syriac and Armenian versions; one Syriac version reads **the Son also him imitateth**.

**likewise will do**] Found in manuscript **s**, 13, ε, and most major Greek codices and Church Fathers; however, Codex Sinaiticus and D read **likewise does** <note>original Greek: "poiei homoiōs"</note>.

$^{20}$ **For** <note>original Greek: "gar"</note>] Found in manuscript **s** and others; omitted in some Bohairic; the Ethiopic reads **and**.

**(is) loving**] Found in manuscript **s** and others, using the Greek word <note>original Greek: "philei"</note>; while manuscript D and Origen use a different Greek word for love <note>original Greek: "agapa"</note>.

**and** (the first occurrence)] Found in manuscript **s** and others; omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts.

**showeth to him**] Found in manuscript **s** and others; manuscript D uses a different Greek verb for **shows** <note>original Greek: "deiknuei"</note>.

<note>This section is a technical "apparatus," where the translator compares this Coptic manuscript against other ancient versions (Greek, Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic, and Armenian) to note differences in wording.</note>

**[Manuscripts B, N, Q, T, V]** **My Father** <note>original: "paeiōt"</note>] Supported by Armenian and Coptic manuscript 133. Other versions (including Greek, Syriac, and Ethiopic) simply say **the Father** <note>original: "ho patēr"</note>.

**They** <note>original: "nt-", lit. "they"</note>] Supported by Greek manuscripts Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), and Vaticanus (B), plus Syriac and Armenian. Manuscript 33 and Ethiopic omit this.

**The works... witness** <note>original: "peph-pm."</note>] Coptic manuscript 91 reads **those which bear witness** <note>original: "petermntre"</note>.

**Which I do** <note>original: "eti."</note>] Found in many Greek manuscripts (ℵ, A, B, D, L), Old Latin, Bohairic Coptic, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Some other versions (including the Vulgate and Syriac) read **which I myself do** <note>original: "ha egō poiō"</note>. One Bohairic manuscript reads **which they do** <note>original: "etoura"</note>.

**The Father** <note>original: "peiōt"</note>] Supported by ℵ, A, B, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Manuscripts 91 and 133 read **my Father** <note>original: "paeiōt"</note>.

<margin>37</margin> **And the Father** <note>original: "auw peiōt"</note>] Some Bohairic and Ethiopic manuscripts read **and my Father**. One Bohairic manuscript reads **the Father also** <note>original: "phiōt"</note>.

**He** <note>original: "ntof"</note>] Supported by manuscript A, Latin versions, Bohairic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Greek manuscripts ℵ, B, and L use the Greek word for **that one** <note>original: "ekeinos"</note>.

**He who bore witness** <note>original: "pentafer."</note>] Found in many sources (ℵ, A, B, Vulgate, Armenian). Manuscripts 91, 133, and D read **he who beareth witness** <note>original: "petermntre"</note>.

**Ever** <note>original: "eneh"</note>] Some manuscripts transpose the word order from **heard ever** to **ever heard**.

**Of his**] One Bohairic manuscript adds the word **ever** here as well.

<margin>38</margin> **Abiding in you** <note>original: "ephō. nr."</note>] Found in manuscripts A and D, Old Latin, Bohairic, and Syriac. Others (ℵ, B, L, Vulgate, Armenian) have a slightly different word order.

**Because... sent**] One Old Latin manuscript (e) has a long expansion: **for he sent his only son and this one you did not hear nor did you believe.** <note>original Latin: "misit enim unicum filium suum et hunc non audistis neque credidistis"</note>

<margin>39</margin> **Search** <note>original: "hot-ht"</note>] In Syriac and Armenian, this is written as a command (imperative). The Ethiopic version translates this as **seek that you may see**.

**The scriptures** <note>original: "ngeph."</note>] Manuscript 13 and others; some read **in the scriptures**.

### Textual Variations and Manuscript Notes
<note>The following notes compare the Coptic text with other ancient versions. Numbers like 13, 91, and 101 refer to specific Coptic manuscripts. Letters like A, B, and א refer to famous Greek codices.</note>

**Verse 2.** **signs**] In manuscript E and others. Manuscript 101 reads *the works*. **upon**] Found in 13 and 101. The Greek word <term>epi</term> (upon) is found in codices A and B, the Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Old Latin versions (*super* or *supra*). Codex Sinaiticus (א) reads <term>peri</term> (concerning/around), as do Old Latin manuscripts b, e, f, and ff.

**Verse 3.** **Jesus**] Found in 13 and others (manuscript a¹). This name is moved after the word *but* in manuscript U* (and the Syriac and Ethiopic versions). It is moved after the Greek word for **mountain** <note>original: "oros"</note> in codices א, A, and B. It is omitted in Codex Delta (Δ). The Syriac (Sinaitic) version reads *our Lord*. &emsp; **but**] Found in 91, the corrected Codex Sinaiticus (אᶜ), A, B, and the Old Latin manuscript q, as well as several Bohairic Coptic manuscripts and the writings of Chrysostom and Cyril. It is omitted in other Bohairic and Armenian versions. Manuscript 13 and others use the Greek word <term>de</term> (therefore). The original Codex Sinaiticus (א*) and Syriac versions use <term>kai</term> (and). &emsp; **up**] Found in 13 and others, codices אᶜ, A, B, several Latin versions, and the Vulgate. The original Codex Sinaiticus (א*) and Codex Bezae (D) use the Greek for *he departed*. &emsp; **he sat**] Found in 13 and others. The Bohairic, codices א, A, and B, and the Syriac versions read *and he was sitting*. &emsp; **there**] Found in 13, Codex Bezae (D), and manuscript U. It is moved earlier in the sentence in Codex אᶜ and omitted in the original Codex א* and some Syriac/Armenian versions.

**Verse 4.** **the Passover-Jews**] Found in Syriac and Armenian. Some Bohairic and Ethiopic versions read *the feast of the Passover of the Jews*. The Syriac (Sinaitic) version reads *the feast of the unleavened bread*.

**Verse 5.** **Jesus**] Found in 13, 91, and 133. The Syriac (Sinaitic) reads *our Lord*. Most major Greek codices (א, A, B, D) move the name after the word for **eyes**. &emsp; **therefore**] Found in 13, 91, and 133 and the Harklean Syriac. Omitted or replaced with *but* or *and* in other versions. &emsp; **lifted**] Found in 13, 91, and 133 and several Syriac versions. Major Greek codices use the participle <term>eparas</term> (having lifted). &emsp; **his eyes**] Found in 13 and 91. Most major Greek codices (א, A, B) omit the word *his*. &emsp; **he saw**] Found in 13 and 91. Most major Greek codices and the Bohairic read *and having seen*. &emsp; **a great multitude**] Found in 13 and 91. Codex B and others use the Greek <term>polys ochlos</term> (much multitude). &emsp; **said**] Found in 13 and 91, and the Bohairic and Syriac. Codex Bezae (D) and others read *and he says*. &emsp; **are-buy**] Found in 13 and 91. The Bohairic version expands this to: *where are we about to find bread to buy*.

<note>This section compares different versions of the Coptic text. Numbers like 13, 91, 100, and 101 refer to specific physical papyrus or parchment manuscripts studied by scholars.</note>

**may eat**] The word "may" is omitted in manuscript 13.
**testing him**] Manuscript 13 and 91. Manuscript 91 uses a slightly different spelling for "testing."
**what he was going to do**] Manuscripts 13 and 100 read "what he would do"; 91 uses a variant form of the same phrase.
**receive a**] Manuscripts 13 and 91. Manuscript 101 omits the word "receive."

### Detailed Comparative Notes
<note>This section compares the Coptic (Sahidic) text with other ancient languages such as Greek (represented by letters like A, B, and the Hebrew letter Aleph ℵ), Syriac (Syr), Latin (OL/Vg), and others.</note>

**bread**] Found in Coptic manuscripts 13 and 91. Omitted in the Syriac versions.
**these**] Found in Coptic manuscripts 13, 91, Greek Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), and Old Latin. Transposed in some Greek versions (A and B), the Bohairic Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic.
**he said**] Coptic 13 and 91. The Bohairic Coptic says "when he said it." The Syriac version says "he asked."
**testing**] Manuscript 91 and the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ*) use "for" here. Bohairic Coptic and Ethiopic also include "and."
**answered**] Found in Coptic 13, 91, 100, and major Greek codices. The Syriac version simply says "says." The Ethiopic version expands: "and Philip answered and said to him."
**to him**] Found in Coptic 13, 91, 100, and most Greek/Latin/Syriac versions. Omitted in Bohairic and some Armenian manuscripts.
**of bread**] Coptic 13 and 91. The Greek versions use "loaves."
**will-them (be enough)**] Manuscript 13, 91, and the Bohairic. Greek versions vary between "will be enough" and "is enough."
**each**] Manuscripts 13, 91, 101, and major Greek Codices (A, B, L). Codex Bezae (D) and the Syriac add "of them."
**said**] Coptic 13 and others. The Ethiopic adds the word "and" before this.
**Andrew**] Coptic 13 and others. One Syriac version adds "his name was."
**the brother**] Found in Coptic 13 and others. Omitted in some Greek minuscules (manuscript 69).
**Simon Peter**] Coptic 13, Syriac, and Ethiopic. Other Syriac versions use a shortened form.
**a young boy**] Coptic 13, 91, 101. Found in Greek Codices ℵ, B, D, L. Some versions (A) add the word "here" or "in."
**having**] Coptic 13 and 91.

### Technical Manuscript Variations
<note>This section compares the Coptic text with other ancient versions like Greek, Syriac, and Latin. Scholars use these notes to trace how the Bible was copied over centuries.</note>

**who has** <note>original Greek: 'ος εχει'</note>] Found in manuscripts ℵ, A, B, and others, including the Armenian version. The Ethiopic version reads “with whom there is.” The various Syriac versions read “on whom there is,” “and there is on him,” or “on one boy there is here.”

**about to be** <note>original Coptic: 'etnar'</note>] Manuscripts 13 and 91, and some Syriac versions. The Greek versions ℵ, A, B, and others, along with the Syriac and Armenian, simply read “is” <note>original Greek: 'εστιν'</note>.

**this multitude** <note>original Coptic: 'peie'</note>] Manuscripts 13 and 91, and Bohairic Coptic manuscripts. Other Bohairic manuscripts read “these multitudes.” The Greek versions ℵ, A, B, and others, along with Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic, read “so many” <note>original Greek: 'τοσουτους'</note> or “all these.”

$^{10}$ **Jesus said** <note>original Coptic: 'p-is'</note>] Found in Coptic manuscripts 13, 91, 100, and several Greek manuscripts like ℵ, B, and L. Also found in Old Latin, Bohairic, and Syriac versions. Other manuscripts (A, O, L) add “But” or “Therefore” to the beginning, reading “But Jesus said” or “Jesus therefore said.” The Ethiopic and some Bohairic manuscripts read “And Jesus said.” One Syriac version omits the name of Jesus entirely. Some versions add the phrase “to them.”

**let them sit down** <note>original Coptic: 'mare-pol'</note>] Manuscripts 13 and 91, and a Syriac version. Other Syriac versions read “let all the men sit down” or “go, make the men sit down by companies.”

**but/and** <note>original Greek: 'δε'</note>] Found in manuscripts 13 and 91. It is omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts but present in the Armenian and Ethiopic.

**much** <note>original Coptic: 'epash'</note>] Found in manuscripts 13 and 91. The Greek manuscript A and some Latin/Ethiopic versions reverse the word order.

**the place** <note>original Coptic: 'pima'</note>] Manuscripts 13, 91, and 100.

**the men** (the second mention)] Found in manuscripts 13 and 91. One Syriac version replaces this with a command: “He says to them, ‘Go, make the men sit down on the grass,’ thus repeating the command and omitting the number of people.”

**therefore** <note>original Greek: 'δε'</note>] Found in manuscript 13 and most major Greek manuscripts (ℵ, A, B) and the Vulgate. Manuscript 91 uses a variation. Other versions use “and” or omit the word entirely.

**about to make** <note>original Coptic: 'etnar'; literally 'about to make/be'</note>] Found in manuscripts 13 and 91. Most Greek manuscripts (ℵ, A, B) use the phrase “in number” <note>original Greek: 'τον αριθμον'</note>.

**about five [thousand]** <note>original Coptic: 'atou'</note>] Found in manuscripts 13 and 91. Greek manuscripts ℵ, A, and B use the words “about” or “as if” <note>original Greek: 'ως, ωσει'</note>. Interestingly, the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ*) mistakenly wrote “three thousand” <note>original Greek: 'τρισχιλιοι'</note>.

$^{11}$ **therefore** <note>original Greek: 'δε'</note>] Found in manuscripts 13, 91, and most major Greek versions. A few manuscripts use “and” or omit it.

**the loaves** <note>original Coptic: 'pi-oik'</note>] Found in manuscript 13 and some Bohairic versions. Some Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions read “the bread.” One Greek manuscript (D) and a Syriac version specify “five loaves.” Manuscript 91 and most major Greek versions add the word **and** <note>original Coptic: 'auw'</note> before the next phrase.

### Manuscript Variations and Comparative Notes
<note>This section identifies differences between ancient copies of the New Testament. Scholars use these "critical notes" to track how the text was transmitted or changed over time. Abbreviations like "ℵ" (Sinaiticus), "A" (Alexandrinus), and "B" (Vaticanus) refer to famous 4th and 5th-century Greek Bibles.</note>

### Comparative Textual Notes
<note>This section compares the Sahidic Coptic text with other ancient versions like Greek, Syriac, and Latin. Scholars use these notes to understand how the Bible's phrasing changed as it was copied by hand over centuries.</note>

**Verse 16: Regarding the name "Jesus"**
**Jesus** <note>Coptic abbreviation: "ⲓ̅ⲥ̅"</note>] Manuscript **c** and others place this word before **to** <note>Greek: "προς"</note> in Codex Sinaiticus <note>ℵ</note>, Codex Bezae <note>D</note>, and manuscript 80; it appears after **them** <note>Greek: "αυτους"</note> in Codex Alexandrinus <note>A</note>, the Vulgate <note>Vg</note>, and the Armenian version. It appears after the word **having come** <note>Greek: "εληληθ."</note> in Codex Vaticanus <note>B</note>. Some manuscripts add the phrase **into the boat** <note>Greek: "εις το πλ."</note>.

**Verse 18: The Rising Storm**
**but-being forth** <note>original: "ⲉⲣⲉ-ⲡⲃⲟⲗ"; describing the wind blowing</note>] Found in manuscript **c** and others. The Curetonian Syriac reads: "and the wind arose violently." The Bohairic Coptic and Sinaitic Syriac move the phrase "blowing a great wind" to the end of the sentence. **a great** <note>Coptic: "ⲟⲩⲛⲟϭ"</note>] Found in manuscript **c**, but omitted in manuscript 69. **but/therefore** <note>Coptic: "ⲇⲉ"</note>] Found in most manuscripts, including the Vulgate and Ethiopic; however, the Bohairic and some Syriac versions omit it. **rose** <note>Coptic: "ⲧⲱⲟⲩⲛ"</note>] The Philoxenian Syriac <note>Syr (g)</note> translates this as "was swelling against them."

**Verse 19: Walking on the Water**
**when-therefore** <note>original: "ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟⲩϩⲓⲛⲉ ⲇⲉ"</note>] The Curetonian Syriac reads "and they had brought the ship." **about-five** <note>original: "ⲛ̄(ⲡⲛ ⲉ)ⲁϣ."</note>] Referring to twenty-five. Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus include the word **about** <note>Greek: "ως" or "ωσει"</note>, but it is omitted in some Old Latin and Syriac copies. **stadia** <note>original: "ⲥⲧⲁⲇⲓⲟⲛ"</note>] A Greek unit of distance. Various Greek manuscripts use different grammatical cases for this word. **walking** <note>original: "ⲉϥⲙⲟⲟϣⲉ"</note>] The Bohairic Coptic adds the word "and" before this; the Sinaitic Syriac adds "coming." **the sea** <note>original: "ⲑⲁⲗⲗⲁⲥⲥⲁ"</note>] Some Syriac versions read "the water." **having approached** <note>original: "ⲉⲁϥϩ."</note>] Some Greek manuscripts use the word **being** <note>Greek: "γενομενον"</note>; the Sinaitic Syriac suggests "he was wishing to pass by." **to the ship** <note>original: "ⲉⲡϫⲟⲓ"</note>] Some Syriac versions read "to *their* ship." **they feared** <note>original: "ⲁⲩⲣϩⲟ."</note>] Most manuscripts include this; the Sinaitic Syriac says "they cried out from their fear."

**Verse 20: "It is I"**
<note>The Bohairic manuscript L omits this entire verse because of a "homeoteleuton"—a common scribal error where the eye skips from one word to a similar-looking word later in the text.</note>
**but he** <note>original: "ⲛ̄ⲧⲟϥ ⲇⲉ"</note>] Some manuscripts substitute "and" <note>Greek: "και"</note> or add the name "Jesus." **I am** <note>original: "ⲁⲛⲟⲕ ⲡⲉ"</note>] The literal Coptic for "It is I." **fear not** <note>original: "ⲙ̄ⲡⲣ̄ⲣ."</note>] Omitted in the Curetonian Syriac.

**Verse 21: Reaching the Destination**
**they-up** <note>original: "ⲛⲉⲩ-ⲧⲁⲗⲟϥ"; meaning they took him up into the boat</note>] The Sinaitic Syriac reads "and when they took him." **therefore** <note>Coptic: "ⲇⲉ"</note>] Follows the major Greek codices; other versions use "and."
