<note>The following section is a "critical apparatus," a technical record used by scholars to track how different ancient copies of the Bible differ from one another in their wording.</note>

**boat** (1st instance)] The spelling varies between different Sahidic manuscripts; some use a version ending in "ei." **boat** (2nd instance)] Similar spelling variations found in manuscripts 13 and others. ²² Variations in manuscript 13 and others. **the shore**] Manuscript **c** and the Bohairic <note>The dialect of Coptic used in northern Egypt</note> version use a slightly different prefix. **entered** (1st instance)] Manuscripts 13 and 91 use a variant form of the verb "to go up." **entered** (2nd instance)] Found in manuscripts 20, 91, and others. ²³ Variants found in manuscripts 13, 20, 91, and the fragments. **they had**] Manuscripts 20 and 26 vary the grammatical prefix. **eaten the bread**] Spelling variants for "eat" and "bread" appear in manuscript 91 and the fragments. ²⁴ Noted in various manuscripts including the P version and fragment **a**.

---

**to make-up** <note>original: "ⲉⲧⲁⲗⲟϥ"; to take him in</note>] Manuscript **c** and the Armenian version <note>Arm edd</note> suggest a word order meaning "to take him," matching the Greek reading <note>original: "αυτον λαβ."</note> found in Codex Bezae (D) and others. **and**] Omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts. **the ship was moored**] The Old Latin and Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> versions use "it happened that the boat," while the Syriac <note>A dialect of Aramaic</note> version suggests it "approached" the shore. **at the shore**] Some Greek manuscripts read "to the land" <note>original: "εις τ. γην"</note> or "upon the land" <note>original: "επι την γ."</note>, as seen in Codex Sinaiticus <note>ℵ</note> and the writings of Origen. **were-going**] Variants suggest "being about to go" or simply "they were going" <note>original: "υπηγον"</note>.

²² **on his morrow** <note>meaning the next day</note>] Most manuscripts include this; some add the word "but" <note>original: "ⲇⲉ"</note>. **who stood**] Variants include the singular "standing" <note>original: "εστηκως"</note> or "who were standing" in the Bohairic and Syriac versions. **saw**] Some manuscripts use the plural "they saw" <note>original: "ειδον"</note> while others, like Codex Sinaiticus and the Vulgate, use the singular "he saw" <note>original: "ειδεν"</note>. **there is not**] A common Sahidic phrasing; some early manuscripts read "there was not." **other boat**] Several Greek and Latin manuscripts specify "another small boat" <note>original: "αλλο πλοαριον"</note>. **except-went up**] Various manuscripts omit the specific reference to "that" <note>original: "εκεινο"</note> boat, or slightly reorder the mention of the disciples.

<note>This apparatus compares ancient manuscript variations for the verses above.</note>

**Rabbi** <note>original: "rabban"</note>] Found in the Syriac (Curetonian and Sinaitic) versions. **you came** <note>original: "ⲛ̄ⲧⲁⲕⲉⲓ"</note>] Found in Sahidic manuscripts (l, etc.), Codex Sinaiticus <note>symbol: ℵ</note>, Codex Bezae <note>symbol: D</note>, Old Latin, Vulgate, Bohairic Coptic, and Syriac versions. However, Codex Sinaiticus and others use a Greek word meaning "you have arrived" <note>original: "γεγονας"</note>. **hither** <note>original: "ⲉⲡⲉⲓⲙⲁ"</note>] Found in manuscript 13 and others. Manuscript 28, the Armenian, and Ethiopic versions transpose this word before "arrived." **time** <note>original: "ⲡ̄ⲛⲁⲩ"</note>] Found in various Sahidic fragments; manuscript 91 adds "it is" <note>original: "ⲡⲉ"</note>.

**Verse 26** **Jesus answered... saying** <note>original: "ⲁ-ⲓ̄ⲥ ⲟⲩⲱϣⲃ̄"</note>] This phrasing is in Sahidic manuscripts. The major Greek Codices (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) and the Harklean Syriac read "Jesus answered them and said." The Bohairic version omits "to them" or "and." **Truly** <note>original: "ϩⲁⲙⲏⲛ"</note> **(second instance)**] Omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac. **you do not seek me** <note>original: "ⲡ̄ⲛⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄-ϣⲓⲛⲉ ⲛ̄ⲥ. ⲁⲛ"</note>] Omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus. The Syriac (Curetonian and Sinaitic) transposes this to "sought you me after signs." **signs** <note>original: "ⲙⲁⲉⲓⲛ"</note>] Manuscripts 91 and 114 use a specific spelling. Codex Bezae and some Old Latin versions add "and wonders." Bohairic manuscripts add "from me." **and**] Omitted in several Bohairic manuscripts.

**Verse 27** **work... perish** <note>original: "ⲙ̄ⲡⲣ̄ϩⲱⲃ-ⲧⲁⲕⲟ"</note>] Sahidic and Syriac versions. Codex Sinaiticus and Old Latin (b) use a Greek/Latin phrasing "work for the food not that which perishes." **for the food (second instance)**] This is present in the Sahidic, most major Greek Codices (Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae), and various versions (Bohairic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic). It is omitted in Codex Sinaiticus, several other Greek manuscripts, the Vulgate, and citations by early Church fathers like Clement and Augustine. The Syriac (Curetonian/Sinaitic) prefixes this with "work." **he/this one** <note>original: "ⲛ̄ⲧⲟϥ"</note>] Found in manuscript 91 and 114; omitted in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus. **will give to you** <note>original: "ⲡⲁⲧⲁⲁⲥ"</note>] Sahidic, various Greek manuscripts, and Syriac. Major Greek codices (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) read "the Father, God." Codex Alexandrinus omits "the Father."

**Verse 28** **therefore** <note>original: "ϭⲉ"</note>] Found in Sahidic and the Harklean Syriac. Manuscript 114 uses "but/and." Omitted in Codex Alexandrinus and most Syriac versions. **to him** <note>original: "ⲛⲁϥ"</note>] Sahidic and major Greek codices. The Old Latin (e) specifies "to him the Jews." **what** <note>original: "ⲟⲩ"</note>] A Greek manuscript (G) adds "then." **that we do** <note>original: "ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄-ⲛⲁⲁⲁϩ"</note>] Manuscript variations in Greek spelling for "we shall do."

<note>The following section is a technical "apparatus criticus," where scholars compare different ancient manuscript versions of the text above. Numbers like 13, 20, 91, and 92 refer to specific Coptic manuscript fragments.</note>

**we should work]** Manuscripts ⲃ, 91, 114; Manuscript 13 and 20 use a slightly different prefix; Manuscript m<sup>1</sup> uses another variant. <sup>29</sup> Found in 13, 20, ⲃ, 91, 92, 114, m<sup>1</sup>, and fragment fr<sup>a</sup>. **that you believe]** Variants in prefixing found in ⲃ, 114, m<sup>1</sup>, fr<sup>a</sup> versus 13, 20, 91. **in the one whom]** 13 and others; manuscript m<sup>1</sup> omits a letter; manuscript 114 has a different spelling. <sup>30</sup> Found in 13, 20, ⲃ, 91, 92, 114, m<sup>1</sup>. **so that we may see]** manuscript 20 varies; 13 adds a letter. **and believe]** 13, 20, m<sup>1</sup>; manuscript ⲃ and others prefix with "and"; manuscript 114 has a spelling error. **work]** manuscript 114 writes "his work." **which you (do)]** Manuscripts 91, 92, m<sup>1</sup> use a shorter relative form; 114 uses a different pronoun. <sup>31</sup> Found in 13, 20, ⲃ, 91, 92, 114, m<sup>1</sup>. **fathers]** Manuscripts 92 and 114 omit the initial "n". <sup>32</sup> Found in 13, 20, ⲃ, 91, 92, 114, m<sup>1</sup>. **the one who gave]** manuscript 114 varies the construction. <sup>33</sup> Found in 13, 20, ⲃ, 91, 92, 114, m<sup>1</sup>.

<note>This section compares the Coptic text to Greek (G), Latin (OL/Vg), Syriac (Syr), and other ancient versions.</note>

*we shall do* <note>original Latin: "faciemus"</note> in Old Latin and Vulgate; *we should do* <note>original Greek: "ποιηϲωμεν"</note> in Greek Codex Bezae and others; *we are doing* in some; *we should do* in Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and writings of Origen and Cyril. **that we should work]** 13 and others; *what should we work so that we may do* in Codex Bezae.

<note>The following section is a "critical apparatus." It records small differences found when comparing various ancient manuscripts. Scholars use these codes (like B, A, or Syr) to track how the text changed over centuries of copying.</note>

**Verse 41**
**Concerning him** <note>original: "ⲙⲡⲉϥⲙⲧⲟ"</note> — Found in manuscript 'c' and others; however, it is omitted in manuscript 69 and the Syriac Sinaitic version.
**Which came out of the heaven** <note>original: "ⲉⲧⲁⲩⲉⲓ-ⲧⲡⲉ"</note> — Found in manuscript 'c' and others. Some famous early Greek Bibles, like the Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Alexandrinus (A), and Codex Vaticanus (B), use the phrase "the one who came down from heaven," while other manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate use "the one who came down out of heaven."

**Verse 42**
<note>This entire verse is omitted in one version of the Bohairic Coptic Bible.</note>
**This** <note>original: "ⲡⲁⲓ"</note> — Found in manuscript 'c' and others; omitted in some Bohairic and Syriac copies.
**Jesus** <note>original: "ⲓⲥ̅"</note> — Found in the majority of early Bibles (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus), the Latin versions, and the Syriac. It is omitted in a few Greek manuscripts and some Bohairic and Armenian versions.
**Joseph** <note>original: "ⲓⲱⲥⲏⲫ"</note> — One Bohairic manuscript (Q) adds the title **"the carpenter"** after the name Joseph.
**This (man)** <note>original: "ⲡⲁⲓ"</note> — Variations exist where some versions say "that" or "and."
**His father** <note>original: "ⲡⲉϥⲉⲓⲱⲧ"</note> — Variation in the grammatical prefix in manuscript 91 and 114.
**And his mother** <note>original: "ⲙⲛ̅ ⲧⲉϥⲙⲁⲁⲩ"</note> — Found in manuscript 'c' and the Armenian version. Codex Sinaiticus and some Syriac versions omit this phrase.
**How** <note>original: "ⲡⲁϣ ⲛ̅"</note> — Variations in manuscripts include "and how," "how now," or "how now therefore."
**Saith he** <note>original: "ⲉϥϫⲱ"</note> — Found in most manuscripts; Codex Sinaiticus and the Vulgate add the word "this" or "this man."
**That I came out of the heaven** <note>original: "ϫⲉ ⲛ̅ⲧⲁⲩⲉⲓ-ⲧⲡⲉ"</note> — Found in manuscript 'c'. Other Greek Bibles (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus) and the Bohairic/Syriac versions use the phrasing "that I have come down from heaven."

**Verse 43**
**Jesus answered** <note>original: "ⲁ ⲓⲥ̅ ⲟⲩⲱϣⲃ̅"</note> — Most Greek manuscripts (Vaticanus, etc.) simply say "Jesus answered," but Codex Sinaiticus and the Vulgate say "Jesus therefore answered."
**Said he** — Some versions add "and" before this.
**To them** — Omitted in one Greek manuscript.
**Murmur not** — One Greek manuscript (69) asks "Why do you murmur?"

**Verse 44**
**It is not possible** <note>original: "ⲙⲙⲛ̅ ϣϭⲟⲙ"</note> — One Syriac version adds "for" here.
**My Father** <note>original: "ⲡⲁⲉⲓⲱⲧ"</note> — Most manuscripts say "the Father," but manuscript 'g', Cyril of Alexandria, and others include "my."
**And I also** <note>original: "ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲛⲟⲕ ϩⲱ"</note> — The page ends as Jesus begins to explain his role in raising believers.

# JOHN VI 44-50
<page-num>98</page-num>
<header>JOHN</header>

...and I, I shall raise him in the last day. ⁴⁵ It is written in the prophets: "And they shall all be taught by God." Every one who has heard from the Father and has learned, comes to me. ⁴⁶ Not that any one has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; this one has seen the Father. **Jesus.** ⁴⁷ Truly, truly, I say to you: he who believes in me has eternal life. ⁴⁸ I am the bread of life. ⁴⁹ Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. ⁵⁰ This, however, is the bread which comes out of heaven, so that if one eats of it, he may not die.

---

<note>The following lines are a critical apparatus, which compares different ancient copies of this text to show where they vary in spelling or wording.</note>

**I will** [raise him] — variations in the verb form appear in manuscripts 'g' and 20, as well as 114.
**Last** <note>original: "phae"</note> — spelled differently in manuscript 114.
**Verse 45** — Significant variations in the phrase "taught by God" <note>original: "peqjicbw n̄tm̄ pnoyte"</note> across manuscripts 13, 20, 91, and 114.
**Has heard** — The spelling of "heard" varies between the group 'g' and manuscript 91.
**The Father** — Manuscript 114 uses a slightly different form for "the Father" here.
**Verse 46** — "Not that" <note>original: "n̄ebol an"</note> shows minor spelling differences in manuscripts 13 and 114.
**Verse 47** — **Jesus** <note>original: "ⲓⲥ"</note> is explicitly noted in manuscript 91.
**To you** — Variation in the plural form "you" in manuscript 91.

---

<note>This section compares the Sahidic Coptic text above with other ancient languages and famous Bible manuscripts.</note>

**Verse 44**
**And I** <note>original: "ayw anok"</note> — The Coptic manuscripts 93 and others, along with the Bohairic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions, include "and." However, the earliest Sahidic manuscript (91*) and several major Greek manuscripts like Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), and Ephraemi Rescriptus (C) simply say **"I also"** <note>original: "anok zw"</note>.

**Verse 45**
**It is written** — Most manuscripts agree, but some Latin versions add the word "for" <note>original: "enim"</note>.
**The prophets** — Most versions use the plural; however, some Syriac versions use the singular "the prophet."
**They [shall be]** — Coptic and most ancient versions agree; however, some Greek manuscripts like Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A) use a slightly different grammatical connector.
**Every one who heard** — Most manuscripts use the past tense "the one who heard" <note>Greek: "ακουσας"</note>, but Codex Bezae (D) and some Latin and Syriac versions use the present tense "the one hearing."
**The Father** — Some Coptic manuscripts (13, 93, 114) specify "**my** Father" instead of "the Father."
**Was taught** — The Armenian version and most Coptic texts agree on the phrase "has learned" <note>Greek: "μαθων"</note>, though one Greek manuscript adds the phrase "the truth."

**Verse 46**
**One saw** — Manuscripts 13 and the Bohairic version agree with the Greek Codex Alexandrinus (A) and the Syriac and Armenian versions in their phrasing of "anyone has seen."

# JOHN VI 45-50
<page-num>99</page-num>
<header>JOHN VI 45-50</header>

...me draw him; and I also, I shall raise him in the last day. 45 It is written in the *prophets*: "They will be all taught of God." Every one who heard from the Father, and was taught, comes unto me. 46 Not indeed that anyone saw the Father, except he who is from God; this is he who saw the Father. 16. 47 *Verily, verily*, I say to you, he who *believes me* has the life forever. 48 I am the bread of the life. 49 Your fathers ate the manna in the desert, and they died. 50 But this is the bread which comes out of the heaven, so that if any

---

<note>The following notes compare different ancient versions of the Bible. Scholars use these abbreviations (like ℵ for Codex Sinaiticus or B for Codex Vaticanus) to track how the text changed as it was copied over centuries.</note>

**Verse 45** — Variations for "has seen" <note>original Greek: "heora."</note> and "anyone" <note>original Greek: "tis"</note> are found in manuscripts Sinai, Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, Bezae, and others. The word "whenever" <note>original Greek: "hotan"</note> is omitted in manuscript 'g' and 114.
**He saw** <note>original Coptic: "afnay"</note> — found in manuscript 'g' and 114.
**From the Father** <note>original Coptic: "ebol m-pi-ot"</note> — "from" <note>original Greek: "para"</note> is used in manuscripts Sinai, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus; while "out of" <note>original Greek: "ek"</note> is used in other Greek and Bohairic Coptic versions. 
**God** <note>original Coptic: "p-noute"</note> — used in manuscript 'g' and 114; while "the Father" <note>original Greek: "tou patros"</note> is used in Codex Sinai. 
**This one** <note>original Coptic: "pai"</note> — supported by the Syriac version. Other versions (Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic) use "that one."
**The Father** (the second mention) — "the Father" <note>original Coptic: "e-p-eiot"</note> is the standard reading; however, Codex Sinai and Codex Bezae use "God" <note>original Greek: "ton theon"</note>, and one Syriac version reads "God the Father."

**Verse 47** — **Me** <note>original Coptic: "eroi"</note> — "believes in me" <note>original Greek: "eis eme"</note> is found in manuscripts like Alexandrinus, the Latin Vulgate, and Bohairic Coptic; however, it is omitted in Sinai, Vaticanus, and the Armenian version. One Syriac version reads "believes in God."
**The life** <note>original Coptic: "p-onkh"</note> — "a life" <note>original Coptic: "ou-onkh"</note> is an alternative reading in some Bohairic manuscripts. Most Greek manuscripts use "life" <note>original Greek: "zoen"</note>.
**For ever** <note>original Coptic: "sha eneh"</note> — used in manuscripts 'g', 13, and 91. Other manuscripts use the adjective "eternal" <note>original Coptic: "n-o-u."</note>, while one Syriac version omits it entirely.

**Verse 48** — **Of the life** <note>original Coptic: "n-p-onkh"</note> — One Syriac version adds the phrase "which came down from heaven."

**Verse 49** — **Your fathers** <note>original Coptic: "neten-eiote"</note> — The Bohairic version uses this; some Greek manuscripts read "our fathers" <note>original Greek: "hoi p. hemon"</note>, while the theologian Origen omits "your."
**Ate** <note>original Coptic: "ouom"</note> — Codex Bezae and some Old Latin versions add "the bread" <note>original Greek: "ton arton"</note>.
**The manna** <note>original Coptic: "pi-manna"</note> — omitted in one Syriac version. Different manuscripts disagree on whether "the manna" should be placed before or after the word "wilderness" <note>original Greek: "eremo"</note>.
**They died** <note>original Coptic: "au-mou"</note> — Manuscript 'g' and others add the word "and" <note>original Coptic: "ay-o"</note> before this.

**Verse 50** — **But** <note>original Coptic: "de"</note> — "But this is" <note>original Latin: "hic est autem"</note> is found in some Bohairic and Syriac versions, though it is omitted in Sinai, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus.
**Which comes** <note>original Coptic: "et nēy"</note> — Greek manuscripts typically use "the one coming down" <note>original Greek: "ho-katabainon"</note>, while others use "which came down."
**That if** <note>original Coptic: "jekas ershan"</note> — "if" <note>original Greek: "ean"</note> is included in Codex Bezae and Latin versions, but omitted in Sinai, Vaticanus, and most Syriac versions.
**He-die** <note>original Coptic: "nnef-mou"</note> — Translated as "may not die" <note>original Latin: "non moriatur"</note> in Latin and Armenian. Some Greek manuscripts read "and not die" <note>original Greek: "kai mē apothanē"</note>, while one Syriac version curiously says "and die."

<note>The following technical notes compare different ancient manuscripts of the New Testament. The letters and symbols refer to specific historic books: ℵ is the 4th-century Codex Sinaiticus, B is the Codex Vaticanus, and abbreviations like Bo and Syr refer to the Coptic Bohairic and Syriac translations respectively.</note>

<gloss>64</gloss> **but-you** <note>Coptic: "oun-teten"</note>] Found in manuscript 13 and others. The Greek "there are some of you" <note>original: "eisin tines ex hymōn"</note> appears in the Received Text; "of you there are some" appears in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae; "there are of you some" appears in Codex Vaticanus. **believe not**] Manuscript 13 and others; the Bohairic manuscripts M and Q add "in me." **from**] Manuscript 6 and others. Greek manuscripts use "from" <note>original: "apo"</note> or "out of" <note>original: "ex"</note>. The Bohairic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions reorder this to "Jesus from the beginning." **Jesus**] Manuscript 6 and others. Codex Sinaiticus calls him "the Savior" <note>original: "ho sōtēr"</note>. **who-and**] Manuscript 13 and others. This is omitted in some Old Latin and Syriac versions, as well as Codex Sinaiticus. Bohairic manuscripts add "him." **who-up [betrayer]**] Manuscript 6 and others. Codex Vaticanus and others read "who is the one who will deliver him up." Codex Sinaiticus and others read "who was the one about to deliver him up." One Old Latin manuscript reads "who were those who would believe in him," skipping the mention of the betrayer.

<gloss>65</gloss> **and**] Manuscript 6 and others; omitted in some Bohairic and Syriac versions. **he was saying**] Manuscript 6 and others. The Syriac reads "he says," while the Ethiopic adds "to them." **to him**] Manuscript 6 and others. Some versions add "from above" <note>original: "anōthen"</note>. **the Father**] Found in manuscripts 13 and 101, and major Greek codices like Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Others, including manuscripts 6, 77, and 91, read "my Father."

<gloss>66</gloss> **because of this**] Manuscript 13, Bohairic, and Syriac. Codex Vaticanus and others read "from this" <note>original: "ek toutou"</note>. Some manuscripts add "therefore" <note>original: "oun"</note>. The Bohairic and Syriac versions imply "because of this word." **among his disciples**] Manuscripts 6, 77, 91. Other Greek codices use "out of his disciples." **his disciples**] Codex Sinaiticus omits "his." **went**] Found in manuscript 13 and most major ancient versions. **and**] Manuscript 6 and others; omitted in manuscript 77 and some Bohairic copies.

# JOHN VIII 48-53

<page-num>145</page-num>

**header**
-> JOHN VIII 48-53 <-

**signature**
L

...you are not of God. <gloss>48</gloss> The *Jews* answered, saying to him, “Do we not indeed say *well*, that you are a *Samaritan*, and there is a *demon* with you?” <gloss>49</gloss> Jesus answered, “Indeed there is not a *demon* with me; but (**a**) I honor my Father, and you, you despise me. <gloss>50</gloss> **I**, I do not seek for my glory: there is he who will seek and judge. <gloss>51</gloss> Truly, truly, I say to you, He who will keep my word will not see death forever.” <gloss>52</gloss> The *Jews* said to him, “Now we knew, that a *demon* is that which is with you: Abraham died and the prophets; and you, you say, ‘He who will keep my word will not taste death forever.’ <gloss>53</gloss> You, are you greater than our...

---

<gloss>48</gloss> The Bohairic, Syriac (manuscript j), Armenian, and Ethiopic versions add “to them.” Other Bohairic manuscripts (D₁, A₁, F₂) and Ethiopic add “said.” Certain Bohairic manuscripts (B, C₂, F₁, J₁, M, P, Q) add the phrase after “said to them.” The reading **ⲁϥⲓⲩ** <note>original Coptic variant</note> is found in manuscript Epsilon and others including 101. The term **ⲇⲉⲙⲱⲛ** <note>original Greek loanword: demon</note> is in the Bohairic; while "a demon" <note>original Coptic: ou-demon</note> appears in Bohairic manuscripts c and v. The word **ⲁⲩⲱ** (“and”) is found in manuscript Epsilon and 101, but is omitted in Bohairic manuscript M. For **ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲥ.** (“you despise”), manuscript Epsilon, 101, and the Old Latin (manuscripts d, q), Syriac (manuscripts g, s, h), and Armenian use a word meaning "you despise" <note>original Latin: spernitis</note>. Other Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) use "you dishonor" <note>original Greek: atimazete</note>, while Old Latin (e, l) and the Clementine Vulgate use "you have dishonored" <note>original Latin: inhonorastis</note>. For **ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲓ** (“me”), manuscript Epsilon and others, along with Armenian and Ethiopic, support this; however, an Armenian edition reads "him."

<gloss>50</gloss> **ⲁⲛⲟⲕ** (“I”) is supported by manuscript Epsilon, 22, 69, Bohairic (manuscripts E₂, c), Armenian, and the church fathers Chrysostom, Cyril, and Tertullian. Manuscript 41 and others, along with the major Greek manuscripts, add "but" <note>original Greek/Coptic: de</note>. The Syriac (manuscript s) reads "and I." Regarding the phrase **ⲡⲓ$\dagger$(ⲧⲉⲓ ⲟˡ)ϣ.** (“I seek not”), the Bohairic reads "I was not seeking." Bohairic manuscript E₂ prefixes this with "but" <note>original Coptic: alla</note>. For **ⲡⲁⲉⲱⲟⲩ** (“my glory”), Greek manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Ephraemi support this; manuscript Epsilon reads "the glory," and other Greek and Syriac (s) or Ethiopic sources read "the glory of myself." For the phrase **ϥ(ⲉϥ ⲟˡ)ϣ.** (literally "is being"), Bohairic manuscript v prefixes "because." For **ⲡⲉⲧⲛⲁϣ.** (“he [who] will seek”), Bohairic manuscripts D and N support this; other Bohairic and major Greek manuscripts read "he who seeketh." For **ⲡϥ̄(ⲡⲉϥ ⲟˡ)ⲕⲣ.** (“and judge”), Bohairic manuscripts B, D, and N read "and who will judge"; others read "and who judgeth."

<gloss>51</gloss> For **ⲡⲉⲧⲛⲁⲣ.** (“he [who] will keep”), various manuscripts and the Syriac (manuscripts g, s), Armenian, and Ethiopic read "whosoever shall keep" <note>original Greek: hos an tere</note>; major Greek manuscripts and Bohairic/Syriac (h) read "if anyone keeps" <note>original Greek: ean tis tere</note>. For **ⲛⲁⲛ** (“see”), manuscript c, Syriac (g, h), and Armenian use "see," while Syriac (g, 9, s) and Ethiopic use "taste."

<gloss>52</gloss> For **ⲡⲉϫⲉ-ⲛⲁϥ** (“said to him”), manuscript Epsilon and 86 support this; major Greek, Old Latin (a, b, e), Bohairic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Origen read "the Jews said to him." Manuscript 41 and others, along with Old Latin (f, c, f, l, q) and the Vulgate, read "the Jews therefore said to him." For **ⲛⲁϥ** (“to him”), manuscript Epsilon and Bohairic (B, C, c) include it, while it is omitted in several Old Latin and Vulgate sources. Regarding **ϫⲉ** (“that”), Syriac manuscript s adds "truly." Regarding **ⲁⲃⲣ.** (Abraham), Syriac manuscript s adds "for" <note>original Greek: gar</note>. For **ⲙⲛ̄ ⲡⲉⲡⲣ.** (“and the prophets”), manuscript Epsilon, Bohairic (Sinaiticus, B, N), and major Greek manuscripts support "and the prophets"; Bohairic manuscript D adds "and also the prophets." The word **ⲁⲩⲱ** (“and”) is found in manuscript Epsilon, but is omitted in Syriac (s), replaced with "but" in Ethiopic, and "and" <note>original Coptic/Greek: de</note> in Bohairic (D₂,₃). For **ⲡⲉⲧⲛⲁⲣ.** (“he [who] will keep”), manuscript Epsilon and others support this; manuscript m¹, Syriac (g, s), and Ethiopic read "he who keepeth." For **ϫⲓϯⲡⲉ** (“taste”), manuscript c and Syriac (g, h) support this, while manuscript B and others use "see" <note>original Greek: theorese</note>. The phrase **ϣⲁ ⲉⲛⲉϩ** (“forever”) is supported by most, but omitted in some early Greek and Latin sources and the Syriac (s).

<gloss>53</gloss> **ⲡⲉⲛⲉⲓⲱⲧ** (“our father”) is supported by major manuscripts and the Vulgate, but omitted in Greek manuscript D and some Old Latin sources.

# JOHN VIII 53-59

<page-num>146</page-num>

**header**
-> JOHN <-

...father Abraham] <gloss>53</gloss> who died, and the prophets died. Whom are you making yourself? <gloss>54</gloss> Jesus answered, "If I should glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, the one of whom you say concerning him, 'He is our God.' <gloss>55</gloss> And you have not known him. But I, I know him. If I should say, 'I do not know him,' I would be a liar like you. But I know him, and I keep his word. <gloss>56</gloss> Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day, and he saw it and was glad." <gloss>57</gloss> Then the Jews said to him, "You have not yet reached fifty years, and has Abraham seen you?" <gloss>58</gloss> Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you: before Abraham was, I am." <gloss>59</gloss> They picked up stones <note>The text ends here as they prepare to stone him for what they perceived as blasphemy.</note>

---

**Whom are you making** <note>Coptic: ekeire</note>] Manuscripts E and others read "you have made" <note>Coptic: ak-</note> in manuscript o¹ and the Bohairic <note>The dialect of northern Egypt</note> version. The spelling "to make" <note>Coptic: kiri</note> appears in several Bohairic manuscripts. <gloss>54</gloss> **our God**] This reading is found in the Sahidic manuscripts 70 and 110, as well as major Greek codices like Alexandrinus and Vaticanus, and the Latin, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions. However, the Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae read "your God." <gloss>55</gloss> **And**] Omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac version. **But**] Omitted in some versions. <gloss>58</gloss> **Before Abraham was**] Manuscript 41 and 43 use a slightly different grammatical form for "before."

---

**this who died** <note>Coptic: nai entafmou</note>] The Sahidic manuscript 86 and m¹ use this phrasing. The major Greek codices (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) use a relative pronoun <term>hostis</term> ("whoever"), while Codex Bezae and the Old Latin use "that" <term>hoti</term>. **and**] Some manuscripts use the word "with" instead of "and." The Ethiopic version adds "and than the prophets who died." <gloss>54</gloss> **answered Jesus**] Major manuscripts and the Syriac and Armenian versions follow this; however, the older Syriac versions say "Jesus saith to them," and the Ethiopic says "and Jesus answered and said to them." **if I glorify**] Variant spellings in the Greek and Latin manuscripts alternate between the present and future tense. **my Father**] The Sinaitic Syriac and Armenian versions simply read "the Father." **who [glorifies]**] Manuscript 86 and m¹ add the word "this."

<note>This section provides a "critical apparatus," comparing different ancient translations and manuscripts of the Bible to see how they differ.</note>

**If I say** <note>Coptic: e-ei-sh</note>] This reading appears in the Sinaitic Syriac and Sahidic manuscript 110. It corresponds to the Greek phrase "and if" <note>original: kai ean</note> found in Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus. The Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae use a slightly different Greek word for "even if" <note>original: kan</note>. **him (second instance)**] Found in manuscript 110; omitted in Codex Delta. **But**] Found in manuscript 110; the Sinaitic Syriac and Ethiopic versions use "and."

<gloss>56</gloss> **He rejoiced** <note>Coptic: af-r-</note>] Found in manuscripts 70 and 86, and the major Greek codices. Some manuscripts add the Greek word for "then" or "therefore" <note>original: de</note>. **Your father**] Found in the main Sahidic text, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions. Some Bohairic manuscripts <note>Northern Egyptian dialect</note> read "our father," while the Sinaitic Syriac omits the phrase entirely. **He was glad** <note>Coptic: af-t-</note>] Found in most manuscripts. Some add "in him," while others use the phrasing "he was being glad" or "he was delighting" or "he desired." **My day**] Found in most texts; one manuscript reads "the day." **And**] Found in the Syriac and Ethiopic; omitted in others. **He rejoiced**] Manuscripts 41, 86, and 110, along with the major Greek codices and other ancient versions, add "and" before this word.

<gloss>57</gloss> **They said**] Found in most versions; some use "they say." The Ethiopic adds "and" at the start. **Therefore** <note>Greek loanword: de</note>] Found in the major Greek codices and most Sahidic and Bohairic copies; omitted in some Syriac and Armenian versions. **To him**] Omitted in one Bohairic manuscript. **The Jews**] Omitted in one Syriac manuscript. **Thou... yet**] This uses the Greek word for "not yet" <note>original: oupō</note> found in most major codices. One manuscript uses "not even yet" <note>original: oudepō</note>. **Fifty**] Found in most versions; however, manuscript 239 and some writings of the church fathers Chrysostom and Pseudo-Athanasius read "forty" <note>original: tessarakonta</note>. **Year**] Some Bohairic manuscripts add "yourself." **And**] Omitted in one manuscript. **Saw you**] This reflects the Greek "has he seen you?" <note>original: eōraken se</note> found in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus and the Sinaitic Syriac. Other versions read "have you seen Abraham?" <note>original: eōrakas</note>.

<gloss>58</gloss> **Jesus said**] Found in the major Greek and Latin versions; some add "therefore" or "and." **Became** <note>Coptic: shōpe</note>] This matches the Greek "to be born/become" <note>original: genesthai</note> in the major codices. It is omitted in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin versions. **I am being** <note>Coptic: ti-shoop</note>] This is the famous "I Am" statement. The Sinaitic Syriac and Ethiopic versions translate this as "I was."

<gloss>59</gloss> **They therefore took**] Matches the Harklean Syriac; the Codex Bezae reads "then they took."

### Chapter IX

<gloss>1</gloss> And as he passed by, he saw a man who had been born <note>original Coptic: ϫⲡⲟϥ ("born him")</note> blind. <gloss>2</gloss> His disciples asked him, saying, "Rabbi <note>original: Hrabbei</note>, who is it that sinned? ---

<note>The following notes represent a critical apparatus. Scholars use these abbreviations to compare different ancient copies of the Bible. "c," "41," and "97" refer to specific Coptic manuscript fragments. Symbols like ℵ (Codex Sinaiticus), A (Alexandrinus), and B (Vaticanus) represent major 4th- and 5th-century Greek Bibles. "Syr" refers to Syriac translations, and "OL/Vg" refers to Latin versions.</note>

**saying** <note>original: ⲉϫⲱ</note>] Supported by Sahidic manuscript (c) etc., and the Syriac (Harklean) version... omitted in Codex Bezae (D), the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Syriac (Sinaitic)... the Syriac (Gwilliam) and Armenian say "and say"... other Syriac and Ethiopic versions say "and say to him."

**Rabbi** <note>original: ⲣⲁⲃⲃⲓ</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c) etc., and Greek Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi, Bezae, and Regius... Codex F etc., use the Bohairic and Syriac (Harklean) forms... the Syriac (Gwilliam) uses "Rabban"... omitted in the Syriac (Sinaitic).

**his parents** <note>original: ⲛⲉϥⲉⲓ</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c) etc., and the Greek text ("the parents of him") in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc... the Armenian version reads "his father and mother."

**that [he was born]** <note>original: ϫⲉⲕⲁⲥ</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c) etc., Syriac (Gwilliam and Harklean), and Armenian... Syriac (Gwilliam and Sinaitic) reads "who blind was born."

<gloss>3</gloss> **answered** <note>original: ⲁϥⲟⲩ</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c) etc., Syriac (Harklean), and Armenian... Syriac (Gwilliam) and Ethiopic read "saith to them"... Syriac (Sinaitic) reads "he saith to them."

**Jesus** <note>original: ⲛ̄ϭⲓⲓ︦ⲥ︦</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c) etc., Armenian, and Ethiopic... omitted in Syriac (Sinaitic)... some Greek manuscripts and Old Latin versions add "and said to them."

**even his parents** <note>original: ⲛⲉϥ ⲕⲉⲉⲓⲟⲧⲉ</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c) and manuscript 97, and Syriac (Gwilliam)... The Greek text in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus simply says "his parents."

<gloss>4</gloss> **it is right** <note>original: ϣϣⲉ</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c) and Greek Codex Bezae (D)... transposed after "us" in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus... manuscript 73 adds "therefore"... Syriac and Armenian add "and."

**for us** <note>original: ⲉⲣⲟⲛ</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c), the original hand of Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, and Regius; also Bohairic, Syriac (Jerusalem), Ethiopic, and the church fathers Cyril and Nonnus... "for me" is found in the corrected Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, Armenian, and Chrysostom... variants in Bohairic and other Sahidic fragments show a mixture of "us" and "me."

**sent me** <note>original: ⲧⲁⲟⲩⲟ</note>] Supported by corrected Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bohairic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic... "sent us" is found in the original hand of Sinaiticus, Codex Regius, and Cyril.

**as long as** <note>original: ⲉⲟⲥⲟⲛ</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c)... Greek uses "while" or "as" in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc... Bohairic uses "while."

**cometh** <note>original: ⲥⲡⲏⲩ</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c) and Bohairic... Syriac (Sinaitic) adds "but"... Syriac (Gwilliam) and Ethiopic add "for."

**when** <note>original: ϩⲟⲧⲉ</note>] Various readings in Sahidic fragments 41, 73, 110; omitted in fragments 43, 70, 86, 97.

**possible** <note>original: ⲙⲛ̄-ϭⲟⲙ</note>] Variant forms in several fragments; fragment 97 omits "any to work."

**in it** <note>original: ⲛ̄ϩⲏⲧⲥ</note>] Supported by Sahidic fragments and some Bohairic manuscripts and Syriac (Sinaitic)... omitted in major Greek codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus.

<gloss>5</gloss> **as long as** <note>original: ⲉⲟⲥⲟⲛ</note>] Greek Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus use "whenever"... Bohairic uses "as long as."

**I am in** <note>original: ϯϩⲛ̄</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c), Codex Bezae (D), Codex Regius (L), and ancient Latin/Vulgate versions... transposed in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus... Syriac (Sinaitic) reads "it is in"... Ethiopic reads "I was in."

**I am** <note>original: ⲁⲛⲅ</note>] Supported by Sahidic (c) and Armenian... Syriac (Sinaitic) adds "for."

**Verse 15**

<note>Additional comparative notes with Greek and Latin versions:</note>

Regarding **that day** <note>original: "ⲡⲉϩⲟⲟⲩ ⲉⲧⲙ̅"</note>, found in manuscript 75 and the Bohairic Coptic version. This matches Greek manuscripts like Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Vaticanus (B), and others. The word **and** <note>original: "ⲁⲩⲱ"</note> is missing in some Bohairic copies.

**Verse 15** 
**Asked him**: Supported by the majority of manuscripts and the Syriac and Armenian versions. The Greek uses **they asked** <note>original: "ⲉⲡⲏⲣⲱⲧⲱⲛ"</note>.

# JOHN IX 15-17

...his eyes. <gloss>15</gloss> Therefore the <term>Pharisees|A prominent Jewish religious group known for strict observance of traditional and written law</term> asked him again, "How did you receive your sight?" <note>literally: "How sawest thou out?"</note> But he said to them, "He smeared clay on my eyes, and I washed my face, and I saw [out]." <gloss>16</gloss> Some of the Pharisees said, "This man is not from God, because he does not keep the <term>Sabbath|The holy day of rest; according to some interpretations of the time, making clay counted as forbidden 'work'</term>." But others were saying, "How is it possible for a man who is a sinner to do such <term>signs|Miraculous acts that reveal divine power or identity</term>?" And a <term>division|Greek: 'schisma'; a sharp split in opinion</term> was among them. <gloss>17</gloss> They said again to the one who had been blind, "You, what [do you say about him?]"

---

**I washed my face** <note>original: "ⲁⲓⲉⲓⲁ ⲡⲁϩⲟ"</note>] Found in manuscripts 20 and others, and 86. The major Greek manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus) and the Armenian version use a word meaning **I washed myself** <note>original: "ἐνιψάμην"</note>. The Old Syriac version omits this phrase.

**I saw out** (received sight) <note>original: "ⲁⲓⲛⲁⲩ ⲉⲃ."</note>] Found in manuscripts 20 and others, 86, the Bohairic Coptic, the Syriac (Garkel), and Ethiopic versions. Some Bohairic manuscripts read **I see**. The major Greek manuscripts, certain Bohairic, Syriac (Harclean), and Armenian versions read **and I see** <note>original: "καὶ βλέπω"</note>. The Old Latin and one Syriac version read **and behold, I see** <note>original: "et ecce video"</note>. The Old Syriac (Sinaitic) reads **he opened them**.

<gloss>16</gloss> **said** <note>original: "ⲡⲉϫⲉ"</note>] Found in manuscript 110 and others. The Syriac (Harclean) and Armenian versions say **say**. The major Greek manuscripts, Bohairic Coptic, and Syriac (Garkel) read **they were saying** <note>original: "ἔλεγον"</note>. **some** <note>original: "ϩⲟⲉⲓⲛⲉ"</note>] The Old Latin, Bohairic, Syriac (Garkel/Harclean), and Armenian versions place this word after "Pharisees." It is omitted in some Greek manuscripts and added in others with the word **therefore**. The Ethiopic version reads **and there are those who say**. **out of** <note>original: "ⲉⲃ. ⲉⲃ"</note>] Omitted in some manuscripts. **this man is not from God** <note>original: "ⲡⲉⲓⲣ.-ⲡⲉ"</note>] The word order varies across manuscripts, including the Greek and Old Latin, though the meaning remains consistent: **this man is not from God** <note>original: "non est hic homo a deo"</note>. **because** <note>original: "ϫⲉ"</note>] Some Latin and Ethiopic versions use **who** <note>original: "qui"</note>. **he keepeth not**] The Old Syriac adds **and he made clay**. **such** <note>original: "ⲛⲉⲓ-ⲧⲉⲓⲙⲉ"</note>] Manuscript 110 reads **these** <note>original: "ⲛⲉⲓ"</note> omitting **such**. **and** <note>original: "ⲁⲩⲱ"</note>] Omitted in manuscript 110 and some Bohairic versions. **was being** <note>original: "ⲛⲉⲣⲉ"</note>] One Bohairic manuscript reads **occurred** or **became**. **division** <note>original: "ⲥⲭⲓⲥⲙⲁ"</note>] Some Bohairic manuscripts add **therefore**. The Old Syriac and Ethiopic versions read **and they were dividing one against one**.

<gloss>17</gloss> **said they** <note>original: "ⲡⲉϫ."</note>] The Ethiopic reads **and they said**. Major Greek and Syriac versions use the present tense **they say** <note>original: "λέγουσιν"</note>, while some use the past tense **they were saying** <note>original: "ἔλεγον"</note>. One Sahidic manuscript adds **therefore**. Some Bohairic versions prefix this with **again therefore**. The Old Syriac reads **and they say to him who was healed**. **again** <note>original: "ⲟⲩⲛ"</note>] This word's position varies in Greek, Latin, and Syriac manuscripts, or is omitted in some Sahidic and Latin copies. **to that one who was blind** <note>original: "ⲡⲏ ⲉⲧ ⲉⲛⲉϥ ⲟ ⲛⲃⲗⲗⲉ"</note>] Codex Sinaiticus reads **to the one formerly blind**, while other Greek manuscripts omit **formerly**. **thou, what do you say** <note>original: "ⲛⲧⲟⲕ ⲉ ⲕϫⲱ-ⲙⲟⲩ"</note>] The word order varies in the Greek and Bohairic versions between **What do you say?** and **You, what do you say?** **concerning him** <note>original: "ⲉⲧⲃ."</note>] The Greek reads **about yourself** <note>original: "περὶ σεαυτοῦ"</note> in some variations, but the context here refers to the man's opinion of Jesus.

<header>JOHN X 2–7</header>

[climb] over by another side, that (one) is a thief and is a robber. <gloss>2</gloss> But he who enters indeed through the door, he is the shepherd of the sheep. <gloss>3</gloss> This is the one for whom the gatekeeper <note>original: "porter"</note> usually opens, and the sheep usually hear his voice, and he usually calls his sheep by their names, and brings them out. <gloss>4</gloss> Whenever he brings out all those which are his, he usually walks before them, and the sheep usually follow him, because they know his voice. <gloss>5</gloss> But they would certainly not follow a stranger; instead, (**a**) they will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of the strangers. <gloss>6</gloss> Jesus spoke this proverb <note>original Greek loanword: "paroimia," referring to a figure of speech or parable</note> to them; but those (men) did not understand what the things were which he said to them. <gloss>7</gloss> He said [to them again...]

---

<note>The following notes are part of the "Apparatus Criticus," where scholars compare this Coptic version to other ancient copies of the Bible in Greek, Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic, and Armenian. The numbers (20, 43, etc.) identify specific Coptic manuscript fragments.</note>

**all those—his** [Coptic: *nete.-têr.*]] Found in several versions, including the Old Latin (manuscripts b, c, f, f2, l, q), the Bohairic Coptic, and Cyril of Alexandria. Manuscripts 20, 43, 108, and 137, and the Bohairic, use a phrasing like "those which are all his." Other Greek manuscripts like Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$), Codex Vaticanus (B), and Codex Bezae (D) use the Greek phrase <note>original: "panta ta idia"</note> meaning "all his own." The Old Latin manuscripts a and e, and Armenian versions, vary slightly. Some Latin versions (b, c, f, f2, l) read "all his sheep" <note>original: "oves suas omnes"</note>. The Syriac (j) reads "them," while the Ethiopic reads "all of them." Other Syriac versions read "his flock" (g) or "his beasts" (s).

**the sheep** [Coptic: *nes.*]] Found in manuscripts 20, 92, 108, 137, the Bohairic, and Armenian. The Syriac (g) reads "his own sheep," the Syriac (s) reads "his own flock," and the Ethiopic reads "his sheep."

**they know** [Coptic: *sesooun*]] Found in 20, 108, and 137. The Syriac (s) reads "the flock knows his voice."

<gloss>5</gloss> **they were not following** [Coptic: *nnet.*]] Found in 20, 41, 92, 99, 108, 137, and the Harclean Syriac (h). The Syriac versions (g and s) read "the flock does not go." **indeed** [Coptic: *de*]] Found in 20, 41, 92, 99, 108, 137; omitted in the Armenian. **but—him** [Coptic: *alla-mmof*]] Found in 20, 41, 99, 108, 137. Omitted in fragment E*. **of the strangers** [Coptic: *nn-shmmo*]] Found in 20, 41, 92, 99, 108, 137, and the majority of Greek manuscripts. Fragment 110, the Bohairic, and several Syriac (g, s, h) and Ethiopic versions use the singular "of the stranger." Old Latin versions (a, b, c, f, f2) and Lucifer of Cagliari read "his" <note>original: "eius"</note>, while Old Latin (e) reads "that one's" <note>original: "illius"</note>.

<gloss>6</gloss> **this proverb** [Coptic: *teiparaoimia*]] Found in 20, 108, 137. The Bohairic version (F) adds "but." **this—Jesus**] The Syriac (s) reads "this Jesus spoke with them in a parable." **but those** [Coptic: *nê de*]] Found in 20, 108, 137, Greek manuscripts A and B, and Ethiopic. Fragment 99 reads "but these." Codex Sinaiticus ($\aleph$) reads "and," while the Armenian reads "and they." **what—said** [Coptic: *ou pety-khô m.*]] Found in 20 and 137. Greek manuscripts use "what things they were that he spoke." Fragments 99 and 108, and the Latin, Vulgate, and Syriac (g) use the phrase "what was spoken" <note>original: "quod locutus est"</note>. Omitted in Syriac (s). **to them** [Coptic: *nau*]] Found in 20, 108, 137. Omitted in Syriac (s). One Greek manuscript (69) adds "Jesus."

<gloss>7</gloss> **said—them** [Coptic: *pekh.-nau*]] Found in 20, 92, 108. Many Greek manuscripts and the Latin (a) include the word "again" in various positions: "again to them" <note>original: "palin autois"</note> or "to them again" <note>original: "autois palin"</note>. The Bohairic reads "again he said to them" or "again he spoke to them."

### Comparison with Other Ancient Versions

**(Verse 7) ...but said to them again]** as found in the Syriac and some Latin versions. **omits "but"]** in the Syriac. **again said to them]** in the Syriac (Sinaitic) and Armenian. **and again said to them]** in the Ethiopic. **Jesus]** found in manuscript 20, etc., but omitted in the Old Latin (b). **to you]** found in most Sahidic manuscripts; transposed before **I say** in Codex Vaticanus (B). **the shepherd]** found in most Sahidic manuscripts; but the Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) and the Bohairic Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic read **the door**. **of the sheep]** found in most Sahidic and Bohairic Coptic, and the Armenian and Ethiopic; the Syriac reads **of the flock**.

<header>JOHN 10:8–12</header>

Jesus said to them therefore again, "*Truly, truly,* I say to you, I am the shepherd of the sheep. $^8$ All who came are thieves and are robbers; but the sheep did not hear them. $^9$ I am the door: if anyone should go in through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and come out, and find a place of feeding <note>or pasture</note>. $^{10}$ The thief is not accustomed to come for any reason, except that he should steal and slaughter and destroy; I, I came so that they should take life, and take an abundance. $^{11}$ I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd is accustomed to lay down his life for his sheep. $^{12}$ But the hired hand, who is not a shepherd, this one whose own the sheep are not, is accustomed to see the wolf coming, and leave the sheep and flee; and the wolf is accustomed to carry them off and scatter them,

### Critical Notes on the Variations

$^9$ **The door** <note>Sahidic: "pro"</note>] fragment **k** and others, manuscript 137... add *of the flock* in the Syriac (Sinaiticus version), add *of the true sheep* in the Ethiopic. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **if** <note>Sahidic: "er"</note>] fragment **k** and others (92, 108, 137), Armenian version... *and all who* in the Syriac (Sinaiticus). &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **and-in** <note>Sahidic: "auo nshahe ef"</note>] fragment **k** and others, manuscript 92 (137?)... omitted in Codex Alexandrinus... omitted *and* in the Bohairic (Coptic) and Armenian versions. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **feeding** <note>Sahidic: "moone"</note>] fragment **k** and others, manuscript 92 (108)... manuscript 110 and some Bohairic versions read **walking** <note>Sahidic: "mooshe"</note>.

$^{10}$ **The thief** <note>Sahidic: "prefjioute"</note>] manuscripts 20, 92, 99... add *but* <note>original Greek: "de"</note> in the Syriac (Sinaiticus) and Ethiopic. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **I** <note>Sahidic: "anok"</note>] manuscripts 20, 92, 99... add *but* <note>original Greek: "de"</note> in Codex Bezae, Old Latin, Bohairic, Syriac, and Ethiopic. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **I-abundance** <note>Sahidic: "anok-aionion"</note>] omitted in manuscript 110; the phrase *and they might have* <note>original Greek: "kai echōsin"</note> is omitted in Codex Bezae. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **a life** <note>literally "a life," Sahidic: "ouonāe"</note>] manuscripts 20, 92... add *eternal* <note>original Greek: "aiōnon"</note> in Codex Sinaiticus, Syriac, and Ethiopic. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **an abundance** <note>Sahidic: "oujōte"</note>] fragment **k**, manuscript 92; reads *abundant* <note>original Greek: "perisson"</note> in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus... reads *more abundant* <note>original Greek: "perissoteron"</note> in other Greek codices and the writings of Athanasius.

$^{11}$ **the good shepherd (2nd time)**] fragment **k** and others... omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts... prefixed with *and* in Bohairic and Syriac... prefixed with *but* in Ethiopic. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **is-down** <note>Sahidic: "shafka," part of "lay down"</note>] fragment **k** and others; reads *lays down* <note>original Greek: "tithēsin"</note> in Codex Sinaiticus (corrected), Syriac, Armenian, and the writings of Clement and Origen... reads *gives* <note>original Greek: "didōsin"</note> in Codex Sinaiticus (original hand), Codex Bezae, Old Latin, Vulgate, Bohairic, and the writings of Augustine. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **his sheep**] fragment **k** and others, Bohairic, Ethiopic... reads *of the sheep* <note>original Greek: "tōn probatōn"</note> in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus... reads *sheep* in Armenian... reads *his flock* in Syriac.

$^{12}$ **but** <note>original Greek: "de"</note>] reads *but the hired hand* in Codex Alexandrinus, Old Latin, Vulgate, Bohairic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, and the writings of Eusebius and Chrysostom... add *the false* in Syriac (Sinaiticus)... omitted in Codex Vaticanus and some Old Latin. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **who-shepherd**] Bohairic and Syriac... omitted in Syriac (Sinaiticus)... prefixed with *and* <note>original Greek: "kai"</note> in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and Bohairic. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **this-not**] Syriac (Sinaiticus)... prefixed with *and* in Syriac and Ethiopic. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **is-see**] *when he seeth* in Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **and (1st time)**] omitted in some manuscripts, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **the sheep**] mentioned twice... reads *the flock* in Syriac (Sinaiticus). &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **and flee**] adds *because he is a hired hand* <note>original Latin: "quia mercennarius est"</note> in Old Latin. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **and (2nd time)**] omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **to carry them off**] Armenian and Ethiopic... omitted *them* in Codex Bezae, Old Latin, Vulgate, and Syriac.

### Critical Apparatus: Sahidic Coptic Variations

### Critical Apparatus: Manuscript Variations

<note>This section compares the Sahidic Coptic text above with other ancient manuscripts to show how the wording differs across history.</note>

$^{28}$ **And I** <note>original: "ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲛⲟⲕ"</note>] Found in Manuscript 20 and others, including Manuscript 76 and the Bohairic <term>Bohairic: The Coptic dialect of Lower Egypt</term> (manuscripts c₁*Q). Other versions, including the Bohairic, Greek Codex Sinaiticus, and Armenian, read "my hands" (plural).

$^{29}$ **My Father** (the first instance)] Supported by most major manuscripts (A, B, Latin, Syriac, etc.) and Cyril of Alexandria. Manuscript 69, the Bohairic, and the Armenian read "the hands" (plural). **My Father** (the second instance)] Found in Sahidic, Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Bezae (D), the Latin Vulgate, and Bohairic. It is omitted in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B), and by early fathers like Basil and Chrysostom.

### Critical Apparatus: Textual Variations

<note>This section compares the Sahidic Coptic text with other ancient translations. Scholars use these notes to trace how the Bible's wording changed as it was copied by hand over centuries.</note>

**Verse 32**
The phrase "and by what works" is found in Greek manuscript 69. "Because of what" appears in the Old Latin <note>original: "propter quid"</note> manuscript e. The Bohairic version <term>Bohairic: The Coptic dialect of northern Egypt</term> reads "because of which work therefore."
The Coptic phrase **ⲉⲣⲟϥ ⲙⲉ** <note>original: "against him"</note> is supported by manuscripts 20, 76, the Greek manuscripts A (Codex Alexandrinus) and D (Codex Bezae), the Old Latin, Bohairic, and Syriac traditions, as well as the church fathers Epiphanius, Theodoret, and Hilary. 
In Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Vaticanus (B), and Codex Regius (L), this phrase is moved to appear before the word "stones."

**Verse 33**
**The Jews answered** <note>original: "ⲁⲩⲟⲩⲱϣⲃ ⲛⲓ-ⲓⲟⲩⲇⲁⲓ"</note>: This reading is found in manuscript 20, Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Vaticanus (B), and many others. 
*   The Syriac version reads: "The Jews say to him."
*   Some versions add "saying" (Greek D, Bohairic, Syriac, Armenian).
*   Old Latin and some Bohairic manuscripts add "they said."
*   **Concerning** <note>original: "ⲉⲧⲃⲉ"</note>: Found in manuscript 20 and 76.
*   **Because** <note>original: "ϫⲉ"</note>: Found in manuscripts 69, 110, and Syriac versions.
*   **Blasphemy** <note>original: "ϫⲓⲟⲩⲁ"</note>: Manuscript 69 and 110 read "you blaspheme."
*   **Because** <note>original: "ϫⲉ"</note>: Found in manuscript 20, Codex Sinaiticus (א), and Cyril of Alexandria.
*   **You, being a man** <note>original: "ⲛ̄ⲧⲟⲕ-ⲣⲱⲙⲉ"</note>: The Armenian version and others support this. Codex Sinaiticus (א) and Codex Vaticanus (B) use the Greek phrasing "you, being a man." 
*   **You make yourself** <note>original: "ⲉⲕⲉⲓⲣⲉ ⲙ̄ⲙⲟⲕ"</note>: Found in most Coptic manuscripts.

**Verse 34**
**Jesus answered**: Manuscript 69 adds the word "again." The Syriac reads "he says."
**To them**: Omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts.
**Written**: <note>original: "ⲛ̄ⲏⲥϩⲃ"</note> The phrasing "thus written in" is found in Syriac versions.
**Your law**: <note>original: "ⲡⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲛⲟⲙⲟⲥ"</note> Found in Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Vaticanus (B), and the Vulgate. However, the word "your" is omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (א*) and by early fathers like Tertullian, Cyprian, and Hilary.
**I** <note>original: "ⲁⲛⲟⲕ"</note>: Omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (א*).

**Verse 35**
**If he called**: Manuscript 69 and some Greek versions add "therefore" <note>original: "ⲇⲉ"</note>.
**The word of God became [sent]**: <note>original: "ⲁⲡⲛ̄. ϣⲱⲡⲉ"</note> Found in Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Vaticanus (B), and the Old Latin.

**Verse 40**
**He went** <note>original: "ⲁϥⲃⲱⲕ"</note>: Found in manuscript g, 76, and some Bohairic manuscripts. Most Greek manuscripts (ℵ, B, etc.) and the Syriac read "and he went away" <note>original: "\kappa\alpha\iota \alpha\pi\eta\lambda\theta\epsilon."</note>.

**To the place** <note>original: "ⲉⲡⲙⲁ"</note>: Found in manuscript g, 76, and most Bohairic versions. Omitted in some Greek manuscripts and Chrysostom.
**He remained** <note>original: "ⲁϥϭⲱ"</note>: Found in manuscript 69 and 76. Manuscript 20 and others add "and" <note>original: "ⲁⲩⲱ"</note> before it, following Greek Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A).
**There** <note>original: "ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ"</note>: Found in manuscripts 20 and 76. Manuscript 69 reads "at that place" <note>original: "ⲙ̄ⲡⲙⲁ ⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ"</note>. Omitted in the Syriac.

$^7$ **afterwards** <note>original: "ⲙⲛⲛⲥⲱⲥ"</note>] *after this* in the Bohairic tradition <note>a northern Coptic dialect</note> .. It is omitted in Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. **let us go**] Prefixed with the word *come* in the Syriac and Armenian versions. **again**] Found in many early Greek minuscules and versions (Old Latin, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic). $^9$ **answered [and] said**] This wording is found in manuscript 20. Other major Greek codices and the Armenian simply say *Jesus answered*. Another Syriac version uses *he who*. **in the day**] Found in manuscript 20 and the Bohairic. Codex X and some other Coptic versions say *in the light*. **because**] Manuscript 20 and the Bohairic. Other Bohairic variations use *and*. **this world**] Found in manuscripts 20 and 110. Other variations simply say *the world* or *this*.

$^{10}$ **if**] The Bohairic, Syriac, and Ethiopic use the phrasing *he who*. **and**] Omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts.

### Textual Variants and Manuscript Notes
<note>This section compares different ancient versions of the Bible, including the Coptic (Bohairic and Sahidic), Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic, and Greek manuscripts.</note>

^20 **therefore** [original: *de*]] Found in the Harklean Syriac manuscript; omitted in the Bohairic (p) and Armenian versions. The Syriac (g) reads "but," while the Sinaitic Syriac and Ethiopic versions read "and." 
**came** [original: *asei*]] Found in Bohairic manuscripts (B, D, A1, E, J, N, O, Q, S, 26). Omitted in the Harklean Syriac. Some Bohairic manuscripts add "she rose," while one (F) reads "they came." The Syriac (g, s) and Ethiopic read "she went out," and the Armenian reads "she went to meet him."
**Mary** [original: *Maria*]] Found in manuscript 20 and others. Omitted in Bohairic manuscript A. Manuscript 33 uses the form "Mariam."
**therefore** [original: *de*]] Found in Armenian and Ethiopic versions; the Sinaitic Syriac reads "and."

^21 **therefore** [original: *de*]] Found in manuscript 20 and the Harklean Syriac. Omitted in the Armenian version. The Syriac (g, s) and Ethiopic read "and."
**Lord** [original: *p-khristos*]] Found in manuscripts 20, 95, Bohairic (M), Syriac (g), and Armenian. Omitted in Codex Vaticanus (B) and Sinaitic Syriac. The Bohairic, Syriac (g), and Ethiopic versions read "my Lord."
**my brother would not have died** [original: *nere-pe...*]] Found in manuscript 20 and the Bohairic. Various Greek manuscripts (Codex Ephraemi, etc.), the Old Latin, Vulgate, Harklean Syriac, and Armenian read "the brother died." Other major Greek codices (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, etc.) show slight variations in the word order of "not," "died," and "brother."

^22 **but even now** [original: *alla-on*]] Found in manuscript 20 and the Bohairic. Matches the Greek in Codex Sinaiticus (corrected) and Alexandrinus, the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Syriac (g). Codex Sinaiticus (original) and Vaticanus, along with the Old Latin (a), read "and now." The Bohairic (BN) and Ethiopic read "and now also."
**all things** [original: *hōb*]] Found in manuscript 20 and Syriac versions (g, 37, h). The major Greek codices read "whatever." The Bohairic, Sinaitic Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic also read "whatever."
**will give them** [original: *nataay*]] Literally "will give them." Found in manuscript 20 and others. The major Greek codices (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus), as well as the Bohairic, Harklean Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic, add the word "God."

^23 **said** [original: *peje*]] The Ethiopic version adds "and" before this. **to her** [original: *nas*]] Omitted in Bohairic manuscript q.

^24 **said** [original: *peje*]] The Ethiopic version adds "and" before this. 
**he will rise** [original: *fna-tōns*]] Found in manuscripts 20, 110, and Bohairic. Omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac.
**in the resurrection** [original: *khn tanastasis*]] Omitted in certain Greek manuscripts (X, Delta, Lambda). The Ethiopic version adds the phrase "of the dead."

^25 **said** [original: *peje*]] Matches the Greek "eipen" in the major codices. Manuscript 69 reads "says." Some manuscripts add "but" or "therefore." The Ethiopic adds "and."
**and the life** [original: *ayō pōnh*]] Omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac.
**he who believes** [original: *petnahoute*]] The Syriac (g) adds "and" before this.

²⁸ **Manuscripts 20, 70, 95, 96, 110**: General agreement across these copies. 
²⁹ **Manuscripts 20, 70, 96, 110**: General agreement across these copies.

### Textual Variations and Ancient Witnesses
<note>Scholars use these notes to compare the Coptic Bible with other ancient translations. The abbreviations refer to different languages: Arm (Armenian), Bo (Bohairic Coptic), Syr (Syriac), Eth (Ethiopic), OL (Old Latin), and Vg (Latin Vulgate). Greek manuscripts are indicated by letters like ℵ (Sinaiticus), A, B, and C.</note>

**Verse 28** 
In the Armenian version, the text adds: <note>original: "adest vocat"</note> "is present and calls." 
**The teacher** [original: ⲡⲥⲁϩ / *psah*]: Found in Coptic manuscripts 20, 70, 96. The Syriac Harklean version uses *rabban* (Teacher). The Ethiopic version adds "behold" at the start of the sentence.

**Verse 29** 
**But** [original: ⲇⲉ / *de*]: This connective word appears in Coptic manuscripts 20 and 70, as well as the early Greek manuscripts Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others. It is omitted in manuscripts such as Alexandrinus and the Latin Vulgate, which use "and" instead. 
**When she heard**: Manuscript 20 and others include this. One Bohairic Coptic version omits "heard." 
**She rose**: In manuscripts 20 and several major Greek copies, this is in the past tense. Some Greek and Latin versions use the present tense ("she rises"). The Syriac Sinaiticus manuscript describes her as having "sprang up and eagerly went."
**Quickly**: Found in manuscript 20 and some Bohairic copies. Many Greek manuscripts add "and."
**Came**: There is a variation between "came" and "is coming" across the Greek and Latin traditions. 
**Out**: Present in manuscript 20 and several Bohairic versions.
**Unto him**: Manuscript 20 supports this, while Armenian versions often specify "to Jesus."

**Verse 30** 
**Jesus**: The placement of the name varies within the sentence across almost all ancient manuscripts. One Bohairic version uses "the Lord" instead of "Jesus." 
**But**: Supported by the Syriac and some Latin versions. 
**Had not yet**: Variations in the Syriac suggest "not until then." 
**Still**: Present in many early Greek and Latin manuscripts but omitted in Codex Alexandrinus and the Ethiopic version. 
**Was in**: Manuscripts vary on the exact word order.
**Met**: One Bohairic version translates this as "came to him."

**Verse 31** 
**The Jews**: Some Syriac versions specify "also those Jews" or "those also who were comforting Mary." 
**Therefore**: Omitted in some Coptic and Syriac manuscripts. 
**Who and**: Manuscripts 20 and others include the connector "and." 
**Seen**: Some versions add "but" or "because they saw." 
**Mary**: Spelled in Greek as *Mariam* in several major codices. One Syriac version simply says "she."

### Critical Notes on the Text
<note>These notes compare the Sahidic Coptic text above with other ancient versions of the Bible, such as the Syriac (Syr), Bohairic Coptic (Bo), Armenian (Arm), and Ethiopic (Eth), as well as famous Greek codices like Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Vaticanus (B).</note>

**quickly** [original: ϩⲛ̄-ϭⲉⲡⲏ / *hn-tsepi*]] Mentioned in manuscript 95... *thus in amazement* in the Sinaitic Syriac version. **came** [original: ⲁⲥⲉⲓ / *asei*]] in manuscript 95, Bohairic, and Curetonian Syriac... omitted in some Syriac manuscripts... prefixed with "and" <note>original Greek: $\kappa\alpha\iota$</note> in Greek manuscripts Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus, and the Bohairic and Harklean Syriac. **out** [original: ⲉⲃⲟⲗ / *ebol*]] to him in Bohairic manuscript 26. **they followed** [original: ⲁⲩⲟⲩⲁϩⲟⲩ / *auuahou*]] in manuscripts 20 and 95... prefixed with "and" in Bohairic... adds "even they" in the Armenian. **saying** [original: ⲉⲩϫⲱ / *eujō*]] in manuscripts 20, 95, Alexandrinus, and the Old Latin, Vulgate, and some Syriac versions... "thinking" <note>original Greek: $\delta o\xi\alpha\nu\tau\epsilon\varsigma$</note> in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and other Greek codices... the Bohairic says "they were thinking"... the Syriac says "for they supposed." **there** [original: ⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ / *mmau*]] in manuscript 20... omitted in Bohairic manuscript Q.

# JOHN 11:37–41

Therefore the Jews said, "See how he loved him!" 
³⁷ But some among them said, "This man who opened the eyes of the blind man, was it not possible for him also to keep this man from dying?" 
³⁸ Jesus, therefore, again groaning within himself, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone was laid upon it. 
³⁹ Jesus said to them, "Take away the stone." Martha, the sister of the deceased, said to him, "Lord, by now he smells, for it is his fourth day <note>This refers to the Jewish belief that the soul departs the body after three days, making the fourth day the point of absolute, irreversible death and decomposition.</note>." 
⁴⁰ Jesus said to her, "Did I not say to you that if you should *believe*, you will see the glory of God?" 
⁴¹ Therefore they took away the stone.

->**Critical Notes on the Coptic Text**<-

**believed**] split across lines as **be-lieved** in Manuscript 57. Verse ⁴⁶ is supported by Manuscripts 20, 24, 57, 75, 96, 101, 108, 110, and 115. **some**] variants in spelling found in 20, 24, and 57. Verse ⁴⁷ supported by 20, 24, 37, 57, 75, 96, 101, 108, 110. **into the Sanhedrin**] Manuscripts 37, 57, 75, 96 use the standard form; Manuscripts 20, 101, 108, 110 use a slightly different prepositional form. Verse ⁴⁸ is supported by 20, 37, 57, 75, 101, 108, 110. Verse ⁴⁹ supported by 20, 37, 57, 101, 108, 110. Verse ⁵⁰ supported by 20, 37, 57, 101, 108, 110. **is profitable**] Manuscript 1 uses a slightly different verb form for "it is beneficial."

---

->**Comparative Variants from Greek, Latin, and Other Versions**<-

**having seen** <note>Original Greek: θεασαμενοι</note>] found in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus. The Coptic variants "and they saw" <note>Original: ⲁⲩⲱ ⲁⲩⲛⲁⲩ</note> are found in Manuscripts 24 and 75 and the Syriac (Harclean) version. The Latin <note>Original: videntes</note> also uses "seeing." This phrase is omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac. **that which he did**] Supported by the Coptic and Greek Codices Alexandrinus (second hand), Vaticanus, Ephraemi Rescriptus, and Bezae; also in Old Latin, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Some versions add "Jesus" or "our Lord Jesus" as the subject. **in him**] Omitted by Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (corrected); the Sinaitic Syriac reads "from that hour believed in Jesus."

⁴⁶ Verse omitted in the Sahidic manuscript "S." **but**] Omitted in some Bohairic <note>The Coptic dialect of the Nile Delta</note> manuscripts, but included in Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic. **the Pharisees**] Manuscript 13 and others read "the chief priests and the Pharisees." The Sinaitic Syriac reads "those who believed not but went to the Pharisees." **they informed them**] Manuscript 24 and Greek Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus prefix this with "and." **the things which**] Various Greek and Latin versions show minor differences in the relative pronoun used here.

⁴⁷ **therefore**] Found in most Coptic manuscripts and the Harclean Syriac. Omitted in some Bohairic and Armenian. Manuscripts 24 and 75 use "but" instead. **the Pharisees**] Codex 69 reads "the elders" <note>Original Greek: οι πρεσβυτεροι</note>. **the council** <note>Original: ⲡⲥⲩⲛⲉⲇ(ⲣⲓⲟⲛ)</note>] Most manuscripts; some versions add "and made a plot."

### The Plot Against Jesus

⁴⁶ But some of them went to the **Pharisees** and told them the things which Jesus had done. ⁴⁷ The chief priests and the **Pharisees** therefore gathered the council together and said, "What are we doing? For this man is performing many signs. ⁴⁸ If we let him go on like this, everyone will **believe** in him; and the **Romans** will come and take away from us our place <note>Original: ⲡⲉⲛⲙⲁ (pen-ma). In this context, "our place" likely refers to the Temple in Jerusalem or their standing in the holy city.</note> and our nation." ⁴⁹ But one of them, named **Caiaphas**, being the high priest for that year, said to them, "You know nothing at all, ⁵⁰ nor do you consider that it is profitable for us that one man should die for..." <note>The text breaks off here mid-sentence, concluding on the next page with "...the people."</note>

---

->**Textual Variants and Critical Notes**<-

**Verse 46**
**against Jesus**] <note>original: "κατα του ̅ι̅υ"</note> Added in the Syriac (Sinaitic) version and several Greek minuscules (13, 69, 124, 127, 254, 346).

**Verse 47**
**and they said**] <note>original: "ⲁⲧⲱ ⲡ."</note> Found in Coptic manuscripts 20, 24, 96, and others. The Greek Codices Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A), and Vaticanus (B) read "and they were saying" <note>original: "και ελεγον"</note>; other Greek manuscripts read "saying" <note>original: "λεγοντες"</note>. The Bohairic Coptic (B) omits "and."
**what**] <note>original: "ⲟⲩ"</note> Found in manuscripts 20, 96, etc. Some Greek manuscripts add "then" <note>original: "ουν"</note>.
**that we do**] <note>original: "ⲡⲉⲧⲛⲁⲁϣ"</note> Supported by Coptic manuscripts 20, 96, and the Bohairic version. The Greek Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus use "we are doing" <note>original: "ποιουμεν"</note>. Manuscript 108 reads "that you do."
**many**] <note>original: "ϣⲁϥ"</note> Found in most manuscripts. Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin versions read "such things" <note>original: "τοιαυτα"</note>.
**signs**] <note>original: "ϣⲁⲉⲙ"</note> The Bohairic version phrases this as "many are the signs which this man doeth."

**Verse 48**
**if we**] <note>original: "ⲉⲡϣ."</note> Supported by most Coptic and Syriac versions. Codex Bezae (D) and the Bohairic version add "and" at the beginning.
**permit him**] <note>original: "ⲕⲁⲁϥ"</note> Coptic manuscripts 20, 75, 101. Some Syriac versions omit "him."
**will believe**] <note>original: "ⲛⲁⲡⲓⲥⲧ."</note> Standard future tense. Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ*) and Old Latin manuscript (ff) use a specific Greek future form.
**our place**] <note>original: "ⲁⲡⲉⲛⲙⲁ"</note> The order varies across versions; some place "our" before "nation," others after "place." The Syriac (Sinaitic) version reads "our city."

**Verse 49**
**Caiaphas**] <note>original: "ⲕⲁⲓⲫ."</note> Spelled differently across manuscripts; Codex Bezae (D) uses "Kephas."
**being the high priest**] <note>original: "ⲉⲡⲁⲣⲭ. ⲡⲉ"</note> Found in most versions. The Syriac (Sinaitic) version adds "their [high priest]."
**for that year**] <note>original: "ⲛⲧⲉⲣ.-ⲙ̅ⲙ̅ⲁⲩ"</note> One Syriac version reads "in that year."
**to them**] <note>original: "ⲛⲁⲩ"</note> Omitted in manuscript 110.
**not anything**] <note>original: "ⲁⲛ ⲛ̅ⲗⲁⲁⲩ"</note> The Bohairic version uses a different Coptic negation <note>original: "ⲛ̅ϩⲗⲓ ⲁⲛ"</note>.

**Verse 50**
**for us**] <note>original: "ⲛⲁⲛ"</note> Found in Codex Alexandrinus, Old Latin, and Syriac. However, Codices Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), and the Bohairic version read "for you" <note>original: "υμιν"</note>.
**one**] <note>original: "ⲡⲟⲩⲱⲧ"</note> The Bohairic version uses a word meaning "alone" or "only."

->**Textual Variants and Critical Notes**<-

**Verse 50**
**for the people**] <note>original: "ϩⲁ ⲡⲗⲁⲟⲥ"</note> The Sinaitic Syriac version reads "on behalf of the whole people."
**nation**] <note>original: "ⲡⲉⲑⲛⲟⲥ"</note> The Armenian version reads "people"; the Harklean Syriac and Ethiopic versions also use "people."

**Verse 51**
**this**] <note>original: "ⲡⲁⲓ"</note> The Sinaitic Syriac adds "this word."
**himself**] <note>original: "ⲙⲁⲩⲁⲁϥ"</note> Omitted in some Bohairic Coptic, Harklean Syriac, and Ethiopic manuscripts. The Curetonian Syriac reads "of his own will," and the Sinaitic Syriac reads "of his own mind."
**for that year**] <note>original: "ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲣⲟⲙⲡⲉ ⲉⲧⲙ̄ⲙⲁⲩ"</note> Omitted in some Old Latin and Sinaitic Syriac versions. The Greek Codex Bezae omits the word "that" <note>original: "εχεινου"</note>.
**that**] <note>original: "ϫⲉ"</note> The Sinaitic Syriac reads "because that."
**Jesus**] <note>original: "ⲓⲥ"</note> Some Bohairic Coptic manuscripts read "the Christ."
**nation**] <note>original: "ⲡⲉⲑⲛⲟⲥ"</note> The Armenian version reads "people," the Harklean Syriac also uses "people," and the Ethiopic reads "all the people."

**Verse 52**
**not**] <note>original: "ⲁⲛ"</note> Some Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus corrected) add "but" <note>original: "δε"</note>.
**that**] <note>original: "ϫⲉⲕⲁⲥ"</note> Some Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) and the Bohairic Coptic add "and" <note>original: "και"</note>.
**who were scattered**] <note>original: "ⲉⲧϫⲟⲟⲣⲉ ⲉⲃⲟⲗ"</note> Omitted in some Greek minuscules (69 and 251).
**he should gather them**] <note>original: "ⲉϥⲉⲥⲟⲟⲩⲅⲟⲩ"</note> The Sinaitic Syriac reads "should be gathered."
**to one place**] <note>original: "ⲉⲩⲙⲁ ⲛ̄ⲟⲩⲱⲧ"</note> Translates the Greek "into one" <note>original: "εις εν"</note>. Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts place this phrase before "gather."

**Verse 53**
**from**] <note>original: "ϫⲓⲛ"</note> The Harklean Syriac and Ethiopic add "and." The Sinaitic Syriac and Armenian add "but" or "therefore."
**the day**] <note>original: "ⲡⲉϩⲟⲟⲩ"</note> Some manuscripts (Sahidic 37, 57, and Greek versions) add "therefore."

<note>This section compares different ancient copies of the Bible. The numbers (37, 108, etc.) refer to specific Coptic manuscripts, while symbols like ℵ and B refer to major Greek codices.</note>

### Scholarly Notes on Traditions
<note>The editor here compares the Coptic text against Greek, Latin, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic traditions to see which ancient "family" of manuscripts the Sahidic Coptic belongs to.</note>

**Verse 7: [that she might] keep]** Found in most Sahidic manuscripts and the Greek Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Vaticanus (B), and others. Also found in the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Bohairic Coptic. However, Codex Alexandrinus (A) uses a different Greek verb tense <note>original: tetērēken - "she has kept"</note>.

**My burial]** The word "my" is omitted in the Greek Codex Bezae (D) and some Syriac versions.

**Verse 8: For...]** Omitted entirely in Codex Bezae (D) and the Sinaitic Syriac. 
**But... always]** Omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ*) and some Syriac versions.

**Verse 9: A great crowd... learned]** Various traditions handle this differently. The Greek Codex Bezae (D) and Old Latin say "great crowds heard." The Bohairic Coptic says "but they knew." The Armenian version suggests "when a great [multitude] knew."

**He is there]** Most Sahidic manuscripts agree with the Syriac. The Ethiopic and some Syriac versions specify "Jesus is there."

**They came]** The Sinaitic Syriac adds the word "thither" <note>to that place</note>.

**Not because... only]** Some manuscripts (like Codex Bezae and parts of the Old Latin) omit the word "only."

**That also]** Most Coptic and Greek manuscripts (ℵ, A, B) include the word "also" <note>original: kai</note>, but it is omitted in Codex Bezae (D) and the Vulgate.

**He raised]** Some manuscripts (Codex Bezae and some Bohairic) specify "whom *Jesus* raised" rather than just "he raised."
