# JOHN XII 8–13

->### JOHN<-

...her, that she should keep it for the day of my embalming <note>The Coptic text refers to the preparation of a body for burial</note>. **^8** For the poor are with you always; but I, I am not with you always. **^9** But a great multitude out of the *Jews* knew that he is there; and they came not because of Jesus only, but also that they should see Lazaros, whom he raised out of those who are dead. **^10** Took counsel therefore the chief-*priests*, that they should put to death Lazaros also. **^11** Because many *Jews* were going because of him, and they were believing Jesus. 

**28.** <note>Section 28 in the ancient numbering system</note> **^12** The next day a great multitude of those who came to the feast, when they had heard that Jesus is coming to the Hierusalem <note>Jerusalem</note>, **^13** they took branches of the palm-trees, they came out to meet him, and they cried out,

---

### Critical Notes on Manuscript Variations
<note>This section compares various ancient versions. Abbreviations like "Eth" refer to Ethiopic, "Syr" to Syriac, "Bo" to Bohairic Coptic, and letters like "א, A, B" to major Greek Bible codices.</note>

Ethiopic version [**those who are dead** <note>Coptic: ⲛⲉⲧⲙ</note>] Manuscript 37 and others; the Greek "of the dead" <note>original: των νεκρων</note> found in Codex Bezae; omitted in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus; adds "Jesus" <note>original: ⲓ̅ⲥ̅</note> in Codex Alexandrinus.

**^10** **therefore** <note>Coptic: ⲇⲉ</note>] Manuscript 37 and others; omitted in the Bohairic and Armenian versions; found in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and the Harklean Syriac; the Sinaitic Syriac and Ethiopic read "and." **the chief priests** <note>Coptic: ⲛ̄ⲁⲣⲭ.</note>] Manuscript 37 and others; manuscript 115 reads "**the Jews and the chief priests**" <note>original: [ⲛ̄ⲓⲟ]ⲩⲇⲁⲓ ⲙⲛ̄ ⲛ̄ⲁⲣⲭ.</note>; prefixes "and" in Codex Vaticanus. **Lazaros also** <note>Coptic: ⲛ̄ⲕⲉⲗ.</note>] Manuscript 37 and others; omitted "also" in the Ethiopic version.

**^11** **because... him** <note>Coptic: ⲭⲉ–ⲉⲧⲃⲏⲏⲧϥ̄</note>] Manuscript 37 and others; the Sinaitic Syriac reads "for because of Lazarus"; the Bohairic reads "because because of him"; the Greek "because many because of him" <note>original: οτι πολλοι δι αυτον</note> in major Greek codices; omitted in the Armenian version. **Jews** <note>Coptic: ⲛ̄ⲓⲟⲩⲇ.</note>] Manuscript 37 and others; manuscript 110 reads "among the Jews"; the Greek "of the Jews" <note>original: των ιουδ.</note> in major Greek codices; "out of the Jews" in Bohairic and Georgian Syriac; placement varies in other versions; omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac. **were going... and** <note>Coptic: ⲃⲏⲕ–ⲁⲩⲱ</note>] Omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac. **and** <note>Coptic: ⲁⲩⲱ</note>] Manuscript 37; omitted in Bohairic manuscript M. **were believing** <note>Coptic: ⲛⲉⲩⲡ.</note>] Manuscript 37 and 115; the Greek "believed" <note>original: επιστευσαν</note> in manuscript 69 and others.

**^12** **his morrow** <note>meaning: "the next day"</note>] Manuscript 37, 108, 115; the Bohairic adds "therefore"; the Syriac and Ethiopic prefix "and"; the Sinaitic Syriac adds "he went out and came to the mount of Olives, and." **a multitude** <note>Coptic: ⲟⲩⲙ.</note>] Manuscript 37 and others; the Greek "the crowd" <note>original: ο οχλ.</note> in Codex Vaticanus and Codex Bezae; the Sinaitic Syriac reads "those many multitudes." **much** <note>Coptic: ⲉⲡⲁϣ.</note>] Omitted in certain Bohairic manuscripts. **because** <note>Coptic: ⲭⲉ</note>] Manuscript 115 reads "but" <note>original: ⲇⲉ</note>. **Jesus** <note>Coptic: ⲓ̅ⲥ̅</note>] Placement varies in Greek and Armenian versions. **Jerusalem** <note>Coptic: ⲑⲓⲉⲩⲣⲟⲩⲥⲁⲗ[ⲏⲙ]</note>] Various spellings of Jerusalem <note>original: ιεροσο-λυμα</note> across different manuscripts.

**^13** **branches** <note>Coptic: ⲛ̄ⲃⲉⲛⲃⲁ</note>] Most manuscripts; Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus read "the branches." **of the palm-trees** <note>Coptic: ⲛ̄ⲛ̄ⲃⲛ̄ⲛⲉ</note>] Greek "of the palm trees" <note>original: των φοινι-κων</note> in major codices; "from the palm-trees" or "out of palms" in other versions.

# JOHN XII 13–19

->### JOHN<-

...and they cried out: "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel!" **^14** And Jesus, having found a young donkey, sat upon it, just as it is written: **^15** "Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your King is coming to you, sitting on an ass's colt." <note>This is a quotation from the Prophet Zechariah 9:9.</note> **^16** His disciples did not understand these things at first; but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things were written about him, and that they had done these things to him. **^17** The crowd that was with him bore witness <note>meaning they testified to others</note> that he had called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead. **^18** For this reason also the crowd went out to meet him, because they heard that he had performed this sign. **^19** The Pharisees therefore said to one another:

---

### Critical Apparatus: Textual Variants (Part I)
<note>This section compares the Sahidic Coptic text above with other ancient manuscripts. Numbers like 110, 115, and 61 refer to specific Coptic papyri or parchments. "Bo" refers to the Bohairic (Northern) Coptic dialect.</note>

**Israel** <note>original: ⲙ̅ⲡⲓⲥ̅ⲣ̅ⲁ̅ⲏ̅ⲗ̅</note>] Manuscript 115 [reads] "of Israel." Manuscripts 110, 61 [agree with the main text].
**Verse 14**] Found in manuscripts 110, 115, 61.
**found a...** <note>original: ϩⲉ ⲉⲩ.</note>] Manuscript 115 writes it as one word.
**donkey** <note>original: ⲉⲓⲱ</note>] Bohairic (Manuscript F) reads "donkey"; other Bohairic manuscripts use variant spellings <note>original: ⲓⲱ, ⲉⲱ</note>.
**Verse 15**] Found in manuscripts 110, 115, 61.
**to you** <note>original: ⲉϩⲉ.</note>] Manuscript 115 mistakenly writes "in you" <note>original: ⲉϩⲛⲉ.</note>.
**upon** <note>original: ⲉϫⲛ̅</note>] Manuscript 110 reads "on top of" <note>original: ϩⲓϫⲛ̅</note>.
**Verse 16**] Found in various Sahidic fragments.
**understand these...** <note>original: ⲉⲓⲙⲉ ⲉⲡ.</note>] Written as one word in some manuscripts.
**Verse 17**] Found in various Sahidic fragments.
**Verse 18**] Found in various Sahidic fragments.
**he performed** <note>original: ⲁϥⲣ̅</note>] Manuscript 61 writes a variant form.
**Verse 19**] Found in Manuscript 110 and others.
**Pharisees** <note>original: ⲫⲁⲣⲓⲥ.</note>] Abbreviated in several manuscripts.

---

### Critical Apparatus: Textual Variants (Part II)
<note>This section compares the Coptic against Greek, Latin, Syriac, and other ancient versions. Scholars use this to trace how the Bible changed as it was copied and translated across the ancient world.</note>

**and** <note>original: ⲁⲩⲱ</note>] Found in Sahidic and Bohairic; omitted in some Armenian versions.
**they cried out** <note>original: ⲁⲩⲱϣⲕ.</note>] Sahidic and some Bohairic manuscripts; the Greek manuscripts (Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) use words meaning "they were shouting" <note>original Greek: εκραυγαζον or εκραζον</note>.
**that** <note>original: ϫⲉ</note>] Found in most Coptic and Latin versions; many Greek manuscripts and the Syriac/Armenian versions add the word "saying" <note>original Greek: λεγοντες</note>.
**Hosanna** <note>original: ⲱⲥⲁⲛⲛⲁ</note>] Various minor spelling differences in Greek manuscripts.
**blessed is he** <note>original: ϥⲥⲙ.</note>] Found in most Sahidic manuscripts; omitted in the Sinaitic Syriac version.
**in the name [of the Lord]**] Found in most versions; omitted in one Old Latin manuscript.
**the King** <note>original: ⲡⲣ̅ⲣⲟ</note>] Most Coptic and Greek manuscripts include this; some Latin versions omit it; some Greek and Bohairic versions add "and" before "the King."
**Israel**] Standard across most ancient versions.
**Verse 14: but Jesus [found]**] Most Coptic and Greek versions; the Sinaitic Syriac version reads "but Jesus was riding."
**as it is written**] One Syriac version adds "in Zechariah the prophet."
**Verse 15: the daughter** <note>original: ⲧϣⲉⲉⲣⲉ</note>] Follows the Greek "the daughter"; some early Greek manuscripts omit the article "the."
**Zion**] Standard across versions.
**thy King**] Omitted in Codex Alexandrinus.
**to thee** <note>original: ⲛⲉ</note>] Found in Coptic, Latin, and some Syriac manuscripts; omitted in the major Greek codices. One Latin version adds "gentle, sitting" <note>original Latin: mansuetus sedens</note>.
**of donkey** <note>original: ⲛ̅ⲉⲓⲱ</note>] Bohairic and Syriac add "the son [of a donkey]."
**Verse 16: his disciples**] Found in Coptic and major Greek manuscripts; some add the word "but" <note>original: ⲇⲉ</note>.

# JOHN XII 14-19

->### JOHN<-

"Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of [the] Israel!" **^14** But Jesus, having found a young donkey, mounted it, just as it is written: **^15** "Fear not, Daughter of Zion; behold, your King is coming to you, sitting upon an ass's colt." <note>This is a citation of Zechariah 9:9, linking Jesus to the promised peaceful king of Israel.</note> **^16** His disciples did not understand these things at first; but when Jesus had been glorified, then they remembered that these things were written concerning him, and these things were what they had done to him. **^17** The multitude that was with him was bearing witness <note>meaning they were testifying or telling others</note> that he had called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead. **^18** Because of this, the multitude also came out to meet him, because they heard that he had performed this sign. **^19** The Pharisees, therefore, said to one another:

### Critical Apparatus: Textual Variants
<note>This section compares the Coptic text above with other ancient manuscripts. Scholars use these notes to see how the Bible's wording changed slightly as it was copied into different languages like Latin, Greek, and Syriac.</note>

**Verse 16**
"...and this his disciples" <note>Found in the Armenian version</note>
**these things** <note>original Coptic: ⲉⲛⲁⲓ</note>] Found in Coptic manuscripts 110 and 115. Translated at the beginning in <note>Greek Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus</note>.
**at first** <note>original Coptic: ⲛϣ.</note>] Found in manuscript 110 and the <note>Syriac Harclean version</note>.
"at that time" <note>Found in the Syriac version of Georgius</note>.
"these things" <note>original Greek: ταυτα</note> moved to the beginning in the <note>Ethiopic version</note>.
**Jesus** <note>original Coptic: ⲓ̅ⲏ̅ⲥ̅</note>] Found in manuscripts 110 and 115.
"our Lord" <note>Found in the Syriac Sinaiticus version</note>.
**then** <note>original Coptic: ⲧⲟⲧⲉ</note>] Found in manuscripts 110 and 115, and the Armenian version. Omitted in <note>Syriac versions of Georgius and the Sinaiticus</note>.
**they remembered** <note>original Coptic: ⲁⲩⲉⲣⲡⲙ.</note>] Found in various Coptic fragments.
"the disciples" <note>original Greek: οι μαθ.</note> added in some Greek manuscripts and <note>Bohairic (Northern Coptic) manuscripts M, Q, and V</note>.
**these things and** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲉⲣⲉ-ⲁⲩⲱ</note>] Found in manuscript 110. Omitted in <note>Bohairic manuscript A</note>.
**concerning him** <note>original Coptic: ⲉⲧⲃ.</note>] Found in Coptic fragments, Codex Bezae, and the <note>Vulgate (Latin)</note>.
"upon him" <note>original Greek: επ αυτω</note> found in <note>Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus</note>.
"from him" <note>original Latin: ab eo</note> found in <note>Old Latin Codex Colbertinus</note>.

**Verse 17**
**was bearing witness** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲉϥⲣⲙ.</note>] Found in manuscript 110 and the Bohairic version.
"therefore" <note>original Greek: ουν</note> added in most Greek codices and the <note>Syriac Harclean version</note>.
"the crowd which was with him was declaring" <note>Found in the Syriac Sinaiticus version</note>.
**that** <note>original Coptic: ϫⲉ</note>] Found in manuscript 110 and <note>Old Latin codices</note>.
"when" <note>original Greek: οτε</note> found in <note>Codex Sinaiticus and the Vulgate</note>.
**raised him** <note>original Coptic: ⲧⲟⲩⲛⲟⲥϥ</note>] Found in manuscripts 110 and others.
"made him live" <note>Found in the Syriac Sinaiticus version</note>.
**those who are dead** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲉⲧⲙ.</note>] Found in manuscript 110.
"in the sepulchre" <note>Added in Bohairic manuscript F</note>.

**Verse 18**
**because also** <note>original Coptic: ⲉⲧⲃⲉ-ⲟⲛ</note>] Found in <note>Codices Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus</note>.
"and all those men ran to meet him" <note>Found in the Syriac Sinaiticus version</note>.
**the multitude met him** <note>original Coptic: ⲁ-ⲉϩⲧϥ</note>] Found in many Coptic and Greek manuscripts.
"the crowds met him" <note>Found in Codex Bezae and the Bohairic version</note>.
**they heard** <note>original Coptic: ⲁⲩⲥ.</note>] Found in most major Greek codices and Latin versions.

**Verse 19**
**therefore** <note>original Coptic: ⲇⲉ</note>] Found in <note>Codices Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus</note> and the Vulgate.

# JOHN XII 19–24

->### JOHN<-

"...You see <note>The Pharisees are speaking to one another.</note> that we are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him!" **^20** Now there were some Greeks <note>original: ⲟⲩⲉⲉⲓⲉⲛⲓⲛ; likely referring to Greek-speaking Gentiles or "God-fearers" who respected Jewish traditions.</note> among those who had come up to worship during the festival. **^21** These people approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and they made a request of him, saying: "Sir, we wish to see Jesus." **^22** Philip went and told Andrew; then Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. **^23** But he answered them, saying: "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. **^24** Truly, truly, I say to you: unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies,"

---

### Textual Variations and Fragmentary Notes
<note>This section details differences found in various ancient manuscripts of the Bible. The letters and numbers (like א, A, B, or 110) refer to specific historical copies of the New Testament used by scholars to reconstruct the original text.</note>

**Verse 20**
Coptic manuscripts 110, 6$^1$, and o$^1$ contain various notations regarding the Greek pilgrims.

**Verse 21**
**from**] Manuscript 6$^1$ uses a slightly different preposition.
**Galilee**] Spelled with a minor variation in manuscript o$^1$.
**we wish**] A variation in manuscript 6$^1$ suggests "we seek."

**Verse 24**
**grain**] Spelled differently in manuscript 76.
**upon**] Variant found in the Bohairic <note>the dialect of Lower Egypt</note> tradition.

---

### Critical Apparatus: Comparative Readings
<note>Scholars compare the Sahidic Coptic text (the main text above) with other ancient versions like Greek, Syriac, and Latin to see how the wording evolved.</note>

**Verse 19**
**"You see"**] Found in Coptic manuscripts and many others. Manuscript 110 and some Bohairic copies read **"We see."**
**"We gain"**] Found in manuscripts 110 and 6$^1$, as well as the Old Latin and the Vulgate. Other Greek manuscripts (including Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus) and the Syriac read **"You gain."**
**"Behold"**] <note>original: ⲉⲓⲥ</note> Matches the Bohairic and certain Greek additions.
**"The world"**] Standard reading. Some manuscripts (Codex Bezae, the Vulgate, and Syriac versions) add the word **"whole"** (i.e., "the whole world").

**Verse 20**
**"Greeks"**] The Bohairic and major Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) read "certain Greeks." Other versions vary, with some Syriac texts calling them **"the nations,"** **"the profane,"** or **"the Heathen."**
**"Among"**] <note>original: ⲉⲃⲟⲗ ϩⲛ̄</note> Missing in some Greek fragments; the Syriac reads **"who had come up."**
**"In the feast"**] Manuscript 110 and major Greek codices. The Bohairic version phrases this as **"to the feast that they might worship."**

**Verse 21**
**"Therefore"**] Found in most manuscripts. Omitted in some Old Latin and Syriac copies.
**"Bethsaida"**] Spelling varies slightly between the "Bethsaida" and "Bessaida" forms across Coptic and Greek traditions.

# JOHN XII 20-24

->### JOHN<-

"You see <note>The Pharisees are speaking to one another.</note> that we gain nothing: behold, the *world* has gone after him." **^19** **^20** But there were Greeks <note>original: ⲟⲩⲉⲉⲓⲉⲛⲓⲛ; referring to Gentiles who had adopted Jewish customs.</note> among those who came up to worship during the feast. **^21** These therefore came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee; and they besought him, saying, "Lord, we wish to see Jesus." **^22** Philip came and told Andrew; but Andrew and Philip told Jesus. **^23** But he answered them, saying, "The hour has come that the Son of Man should be glorified. **^24** Truly, truly, I say to you, that unless a grain of wheat falls upon the earth and dies, it is destined to remain [alone]..."

---

### Textual Apparatus
<note>This section compares different ancient versions of the Gospel of John to identify variations in the text across different languages and manuscript traditions.</note>

**Verse 21**
**they besought him**] Omitted in the Bohairic <note>The Coptic dialect of Northern Egypt.</note> (manuscript F₁*) and Armenian traditions. The Sahidic <note>The Coptic dialect of Southern Egypt.</note> manuscript ⲕ and others use a Coptic form meaning "they-besought-him" <note>original: ⲁⲩⲥⲉⲡⲥⲡⲱⲗⲥ</note>. In Greek manuscripts M and X, the word is "they asked" <note>original: ερωτησαν</note>; while in the Codex Sinaiticus (א) and Codex Vaticanus (B), it is "they were asking" <note>original: ηρωτων</note>. One manuscript (69) reads "they said."
**saying**] Manuscript g and others follow this, while the Syriac (Philoxenian) reads "and say to him."
**Lord**] Found in manuscript g and others. The Sinaitic Syriac reads "my Lord," while manuscript U* and 28 omit the word.

**Verse 22**
**Philip]** Found in manuscript ⲕ and others, as well as the major Greek codices (א, A, B) and the Bohairic tradition. Manuscript g and Bohairic manuscript M add the word "but" <note>original: ⲇⲉ</note>. The Philoxenian Syriac reads "and came," while the Sinaitic Syriac says "and Philip went, and he said to Andrew."
**to Andrew]** Found in manuscript g and others. Some Syriac versions add "his brother."
**but [Andrew and Philip] said]** Various traditions differ on the phrasing: "Andrew however and Philip spoke" (Old Latin manuscript c), "Andrew again with Philip came, they said to Jesus" (Bohairic), and "Andrew and Philip say to Jesus" (Armenian).
**to Jesus]** Found in manuscript ⲕ and the major Greek codices. The Bohairic manuscript B reads "to our Lord Jesus."

**Verse 23**
**he]** Manuscript g and ⲕ support this. Major Greek codices read "But Jesus." The Sinaitic Syriac reads "saith to them Jesus."
**answered]** Manuscript g, ⲕ, and the Latin Vulgate include this. Some Greek manuscripts (א, B, L) use a slightly different verb form <note>original: αποκριναται</note>. The Sinaitic Syriac omits the word entirely.
**saying]** Supported by manuscript g and ⲕ. The Bohairic reads "said he," and the Syriac reads "and said."
**to them]** Found in manuscript g, ⲕ, and the Bohairic. Greek codices (א, A, B) transpose this word to appear before "saying."

**Verse 24**
**upon the earth]** Supported by manuscript ⲕ and the Bohairic tradition. Greek codices (א, A, B) read "into the earth." The Syriac transposes this phrase to appear after the word "dies."
**and die]** Supported by manuscript ⲕ and manuscript 37. It is omitted in the Bohairic manuscript ⲕ.

<meta>This page continues the discourse following the arrival of the Greeks. Jesus has just introduced the metaphor of the grain of wheat that must die to produce fruit. # JOHN
->### JOHN<-

...it remains alone. But if it should die, it produces much fruit. **^25** He who loves his soul <note>Coptic: ⲯⲩⲭⲏ (psyche); can mean "soul," "life," or "self."</note> will lose it, and he who hates his soul in this world will find it for eternal life. **^26** If therefore anyone serves <note>original: ⲇⲓⲁⲕⲟⲛⲉⲓ; to minister or serve as a deacon.</note> me, let him follow me; and the place where I am, there my servant also shall be. If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him. **^27** Now my soul is troubled. And what shall I say? "My Father, save me from this hour"? But for this cause I have come up to this hour. **^28** My Father, glorify your name. Then a voice came out from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." **^29** The crowd that was standing there and hearing said...

---

**^25** Manuscripts ⲕ, 76, 92, 101, 110, and others. The reading "this" <note>original: ⲡⲉⲓ</note> is found in ⲕ, 76, 92; while 101 and 110 use the definite article "the" <note>original: ⲡⲓ</note>.
**^26** Manuscripts g, ⲕ, 76, 92, and 110. Variation at "If anyone serves": Manuscript 92 and fragments use "serves" while 101 and 110 use "the one who." For "honor him": manuscripts ⲕ, 76, 110 differ slightly from 92.
**^27** Manuscript 37 starts here; also 76, 92, 110. Manuscript 92 repeats "this" twice.
**^28** Manuscripts 37, 76, 92, 101, 110.
**^29** Manuscripts g, 37, 76, 92, 101, 110.

---

**it remains** <note>original: ϣⲁⲥⲱⲱ</note>] Manuscript ⲕ and others; also found in the Syriac (Sinaitic) version.
**if it should die** <note>original: ⲉⲥϣⲁⲛⲙⲟⲩ</note>] Manuscript ⲕ and others; some versions add "fall [and die]" as in the Syriac (Sinaitic).
**^25** **he who loves** <note>original: ⲡⲉⲧⲙⲉ</note>] Manuscript ⲕ and others; the Ethiopic version reads "but he who."
**will lose it** <note>original: ϣⲁⲥⲟⲣⲙⲉⲥ</note>] Manuscript ⲕ and others. <header>JOHN XIII 2-5</header>

...his own, who were in the world, he loved them unto the uttermost. <sup>2</sup> And when a supper had happened, the devil having already cast [it] into the heart of Judas the son of Simon the Iscariot, that he should deliver him up; <sup>3</sup> knowing Jesus that the Father gave all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and he is going to God, <sup>4</sup> he rose from the supper, he laid his garments down, he took a towel, he bound himself with it. <sup>5</sup> And he cast water into the basin <term>basin (lakane): a Greek loanword for a wash-bowl</term>, he began to wash the feet of the disciples, and to wipe them with the towel with which he was bound.

---

<note>The notes below document variations in the text found in different ancient manuscripts. Abbreviations like "Syr" refer to Syriac, "Arm" to Armenian, "Eth" to Ethiopic, and "Bo" to the Bohairic dialect of Coptic. Greek manuscripts are noted by letters (ℵ, A, B, D).</note>

**because &c]** Syriac (Sinaitic) reads "because." **Jesus knew]** Armenian version. **and when Jesus knew]** Ethiopic version.
**Jesus]** Found in manuscript 1, Codex Alexandrinus (A), Old Latin (manuscripts b, f, m, q), Bohairic, Syriac, Armenian, and the writings of Chrysostom and Cyril.
**omitted]** Omitted by Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Vaticanus (B), Bezae (D), and others, as well as Old Latin (a, c, e, ff), the Vulgate, and Ethiopic.
**the Father]** Found in manuscript 1 and others.
**his Father]** Manuscript 94.
**and (first instance)]** Found in manuscript 20 and others. Omitted in Bohairic (manuscripts B, H). Codex Bezae (D) and Syriac add "that" <note>original: "ⲟⲧⲓ" (hoti)</note>.
**is going]** Found in manuscript 20 and others. Manuscript m1 reads "goeth." Bohairic and major Greek codices (ℵ, B) add "again."

⁴ **he rose]** Found in manuscript 20, etc., and 41 (though omitted in 36, 92, 94, 95). Matches the Latin "surrexit" <note>original: "surrexit" (he rose)</note> in Old Latin, Bohairic, Syriac (Sinaitic), and Ethiopic. Major Greek manuscripts use "is raised" <note>original: "εγείρεται" (egeiretai)</note>.
**from]** Found in manuscript 20 and 41. Corresponds to the Greek "out of" <note>original: "εκ" (ek)</note> in major codices. Syriac (Sinaitic) omits "out of the supper and."
**he laid]** Found in manuscript 20 and 41, along with Old Latin, Bohairic, and Syriac. Major Greek codices use "lays aside" <note>original: "τίθησιν" (tithēsin)</note>.
**his garments]** Manuscripts 36, 41, 92, 94, 95, Codex Bezae, Old Latin, Vulgate, Bohairic, Syriac, and Ethiopic. Manuscripts 20 and 129 use the singular "garment." Major Greek codices and Armenian omit "him" or use "the garment."
**he took]** Manuscript 20 and 41. Bohairic adds "and." Major Greek codices use "and taking" <note>original: "και λαβών" (kai labōn)</note>.
**he bound himself with it]** Manuscript 20, etc. Major Greek codices use "he girded himself" <note>original: "δι(περι)εζωσεν εαυτον"</note>. Syriac and Ethiopic use "he girded his loins" or "put it on his loins."

⁵ **and]** Manuscript 20 and 36, Bohairic, Syriac, and Ethiopic. Omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts. Major Greek codices use "then" <note>original: "ειτα" (eita)</note>; Armenian uses "and then."
**he cast water]** Manuscript 20, 36, 248, Old Latin, Bohairic, and Syriac. Major Greek codices use "pours" <note>original: "βαλλει" (ballei)</note>. Some Greek manuscripts and Armenian read "taking water, he pours."
**water]** Manuscript m1 reads "the water."
**basin]** Manuscript 20 and others. Syriac uses "a washing vessel."
**he began]** Manuscript 20 and others, and Bohairic. Major Greek codices and other Bohairic manuscripts add "and."
**the disciples]** Manuscripts 20, 36, 95, and major Greek codices. Manuscript g, Codex Bezae, Old Latin, Bohairic, and Ethiopic read "his disciples."
**to wipe them]** Manuscript g and major Greek codices. Some Greek manuscripts and Syriac (Sinaitic) use "he wipes" <note>original: "εκμασσει" (ekmassei)</note>.
**the towel]** Manuscript g and others. Codex Δ omits "the."

<note>The following section is a "critical apparatus," a scholarly record of differences found in ancient manuscripts. The numbers refer to specific papyrus or parchment fragments, while abbreviations like "Syr" or "Eth" refer to other ancient translations.</note>

$^{28}$ **but-knew]** Supported by manuscript 20 and others (possibly 95). The Sinaitic Syriac version reads: *and his disciples knew not*.
**but <note>original: de</note>]** Supported by 20 and others, including 95. This word is omitted in manuscript 115, Codex Vaticanus (B), and manuscripts 157, 248, 435, and some Bohairic Coptic versions. Manuscripts 63, 253, and 259 use **for** <note>original: gar</note>. The Sinaitic Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions read *and*.
**to him]** Found in 20 and others, including 95. Omitted in some Bohairic Coptic versions.

$^{29}$ **were]** Found in manuscript group *g* and others, 95, and the Harklean Syriac. Manuscript m¹ reads **when had**, while some Bohairic and Syriac versions use the simple past **thought**.
**some]** The Syriac and manuscript group *g* add *of them*.
**for <note>original: gar</note>]** Found in manuscript group *g*, 13, 20, 44, 95, and major Greek codices (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus), and the Syriac. Omitted in manuscript 251 and some Bohairic versions. Others read **but** <note>original: de</note> or **indeed** <note>original: men</note>. The Ethiopic reads *and*.
**since]** Found in manuscript group *g* and others, 13, 95, and the Bohairic. Major Greek codices use a slightly different form of the word. Codex Bezae (D), the Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, and Armenian use **because** <note>original Latin: quia</note>.
**Jesus]** Found in manuscript group *g*, 13, 95, and the Armenian. Omitted in others. One Bohairic manuscript reads *the Lord*.
**said]** Found in manuscript group *g*, 13, the Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic. Some Syriac versions read *gave commandment*.
**we]** Manuscript 13 reads **you (plural)**.
**or]** Found in manuscript group *g*, 13, and 95. The Sinaitic Syriac reads *and*.

$^{30}$ **when-taken]** Found in manuscript group *g* and others. Some Syriac versions read *took-and*.
**therefore]** Found in manuscript group *g* and the Harklean Syriac. One Syriac version reads *then rose Jesus and took*, while the Ethiopic reads *and*.
**the bread]** Found in manuscript group *g*, 95, and several Bohairic manuscripts. The major Greek codices and the Armenian simply say "the morsel."
**that]** Found in manuscript group *g*, 95, and major Greek codices. The word is moved or omitted in various Latin and Syriac versions. Some versions specify *Judas* instead of "that one."
**immediately]** Found in manuscript group *g*, 95, Codex Alexandrinus, and some Syriac versions. In many other versions (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Vulgate, Bohairic), this word is moved to after the phrase "went out."
**but]** Found in manuscript 13 and others. Omitted in some Bohairic and Ethiopic versions. The Armenian reads *and*. The Sinaitic Syriac reads *but the time was night*.

$^{31}$ **when-out]** Found in manuscript 13, most major Greek codices, the Vulgate, and Bohairic. Other versions like the Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic read *and when...*
**said Jesus]** Found in manuscript 13, 44, and some Syriac and Armenian versions. Other Greek manuscripts and the Ethiopic use slightly different phrasing, such as *Jesus says* or *then saith to them Jesus*.
**now]** Found in manuscript 20, 44, and the Syriac. The Sinaitic Syriac reads *behold henceforth*. The Ethiopic adds *therefore*.

"has happened that" [original: $\gamma\epsilon\gamma o\nu\epsilon\nu$ $\omicron\tau\iota$], etc., found in Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, etc., the Bohairic Coptic, the Harklean Syriac, and the Armenian versions. **to us** [original: ⲛⲁⲛ]] Found in manuscript 85; some Old Latin and Church Father versions (Lucifer of Cagliari) place this before "about to" [original: $\mu\epsilon\lambda\lambda$]. The main Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) and others place it differently. 

**and not** [original: ⲛⲧⲙⲟⲛ]] Manuscript 85 reads this way; manuscripts 91 and 92 add "and." 

**manifest**] This word is omitted in the main Greek codices and several Coptic and Syriac versions.

²³ **answered** [original: ⲁ-ⲟⲩⲱϣ.]] Found in manuscripts 85, 91, 92. The Bohairic version adds "but." The phrase "Jesus answered" [original: $\alpha\pi\epsilon\kappa\rho\iota\theta\eta$ $\iota\eta\sigma\omicron\upsilon\varsigma$] is found in the major Greek codices and the Ethiopic version.

**said he** [original: ⲡⲉⲭⲁϥ]] Found in 85 and 91; the major Greek manuscripts use "and said" [original: $\kappa\alpha\iota$ $\epsilon\iota\pi.$]. 

**to him** [original: ⲛⲁϥ]] Found in 85 and 91, but omitted in the Bohairic and some Sinaiticus versions.

**if one** [original: ⲉⲣϣⲁⲛ ⲟⲩⲁ]] Found in 85, 91, and 92, and the Syriac and Armenian. Other Syriac versions read "he who."

**he will keep** [original: ϥⲛⲁϩ.]] Found in 85, 91, and Bohairic. Several Greek manuscripts use a slightly different tense of "keep."

**will love him** [original: ⲛⲁⲙ.]] 85 and 91 follow this.

**we come** [original: ⲧⲛ̄ⲡ.]] Found in 85, 91, and 92. The major Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) and the Bohairic read "we will come" [original: $\epsilon\lambda\epsilon\upsilon\sigma\omicron\mu\epsilon\theta\alpha$]. Codex Bezae and some Old Latin and Syriac versions use the singular "I will come" [original: $\epsilon\lambda\epsilon\upsilon\sigma\omicron\ma\iota$].

**and make** [original: ⲛ̄ⲧⲛ̄ⲧ.]] Manuscripts 85 and 91. Codex Bezae and some Latin and Syriac versions use the singular "I will make" [original: $\pi\omicron\iota\eta\sigma\omicron\ma\iota$]. Manuscript 95 erroneously reads "and you make."

**an abiding place with him** [original: ⲙⲟⲛⲙⲁ-ⲧⲏϥ]] Found in 85 and 92. Major Greek manuscripts use "a dwelling with him" [original: $\mu\omicron\nu\eta\nu$ $\pi\alpha\rho$ $\alpha\upsilon\tau\omega$]. Some Latin versions read "we will remain with him" or "we remain with him."

²⁴ **he who [does not love]** [original: ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲛ̄ϥⲙⲉ]] Found in 92; some versions add "but" or "and."

**keeps not** [original: ⲛ̄ϥⲉ.]] Found in manuscript 85. The Bohairic and others read "will not keep."

**my word** [original: ⲡⲁϣ.]] Found in 92 and some Syriac/Armenian versions. Major Greek manuscripts use the plural "my words" [original: $\tau\omicron\upsilon\varsigma$ $\lambda\omicron\gamma\omicron\upsilon\varsigma$ $\mu\omicron\upsilon$].

**the word** [original: ⲡϣ.]] Found in 85 and 91. Some Latin and Armenian versions add "my" [original: $\omicron$ $\epsilon\mu\omicron\varsigma$].

**is** [original: ⲡⲉ]] Found in 85. Omitted in some other manuscripts.

**that of the Father** [original: ⲡⲁⲡⲉⲓ-ⲱⲧ]] Found in 85 and 95. Some manuscripts and early Church writers (Chrysostom, Didymus) omit this phrase.

²⁵ **these** [original: ⲛⲁⲓ]] Found in Bohairic. Some versions add "but" or "and."

**with you** [original: ⲉⲁⲧ.]] Manuscript 95. Other versions vary between "while I remain with you" or "from you."

## XV.
I am the true vine, and my Father is the gardener <note>original: ⲡⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲉ (p-uoeie); literally a husbandman or vinedresser</note>. ² Every branch in me which will not give fruit, he will cut it off; and every branch which will give fruit, he will cleanse <note>or prune</note> it, so that it should give more fruit. ³ From now on you, you are clean because of the word which I said to you. ⁴ Remain in me, and I in you: according as the branch which will not give fruit of itself, except it remain in the vine, thus you also unless you should remain in me. ⁵ I am the vine, you are the branches: he who will remain in me, and I in him, this one

<note>The following notes are a "critical apparatus," comparing this Coptic text with other ancient translations of the Bible. Scholars use these to understand how the wording of the New Testament changed or was preserved across different cultures.</note>

**Scholarly Citations and Variants:**

Chrysostom and Hilary. The word **and** (Coptic: ⲁⲩⲱ) appears in manuscript 20, possibly 95, a¹, m¹, and the Syriac and Armenian versions, but is omitted in manuscript 85.
The word **the gardener** (Coptic: ⲡⲟⲩⲟⲉⲓⲉ) appears in manuscript 20 and others, including 95, but is omitted in certain Greek manuscripts like Codex Delta and Codex Athous Lavrensis.

² The word **branch** (Coptic: ϣⲗⲃ) appears in manuscript 20 and others; manuscript m¹ adds "therefore," while the Syriac Sinaiticus version uses "vine."
For the phrase **in me**, manuscript 20 and others agree, while the Armenian version says "which is in me."
For the phrase **he will cut it off** (Coptic: ϥⲛⲁⲥⲟⲗⲡϥ), manuscript 20 and the Bohairic Coptic agree. Old Latin versions use the word *tollet* <note>original: Latin "he takes away"</note>. Major Greek codices (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) use *airei* <note>original: Greek "he takes away"</note>. Some Latin versions add "Father."
For **every branch** (Coptic: ϣⲗⲃ ⲛⲓⲙ), manuscripts 20 and Ethiopic agree; it is omitted in some Bohairic and Greek manuscripts.
For the word **fruit** (Coptic: ⲕⲁⲣⲡⲟⲥ), some versions add "but good."
For the phrase **he cleanses it** (Coptic: ϥⲡⲁⲧⲉ̄), manuscript 20 and the Vulgate agree with the Greek *kathairei* <note>original: Greek "he prunes" or "he purifies"</note>.
The word **more** (Coptic: ⲉⲟⲩⲉ) is placed after "fruit" in several early versions like the Vulgate and the writings of Clement and Eusebius.

³ This verse is omitted in the Codex Bezae.
The phrase **from now** (Coptic: ϫⲓⲛ ⲧⲉⲛⲟⲩ) is in manuscript 20 but omitted in m¹; some Syriac and Ethiopic versions add "and" or "but."
For the word **you**, manuscript m¹ adds "you also."

⁴ For the phrase **remain in you**, it is omitted in manuscript m¹ and Codex Bezae.
For **and I**, some versions add "also."
For the phrase **according as** (Coptic: ⲕⲁⲧⲁ), some Greek manuscripts use "for just as."
For the word **alone** (Coptic: ⲙⲁⲩⲁⲁϥ; literally "by itself"), it is found in most but possibly omitted in one manuscript.
For **you also**, Greek and Latin versions vary between "and you" and "neither you."
For the phrase **unless you remain in me**, the Syriac Sinaiticus reads "nothing can you do apart from me."

⁵ For the word **I**, the Codex Bezae and some Syriac versions add "for" or "because."
For the word **you**, some Bohairic and Syriac versions add "and" or "but."
For **and I**, some versions omit "and" or add "also."

<note>The following notes are a "critical apparatus," where the translator compares different ancient Coptic manuscripts (numbered 20, 73, 77, 85, etc.) and other early versions of the Bible to see where the wording differs.</note>

**Coptic Manuscript Variations:**

⁶ In several manuscripts, for the word **in** (Coptic: *hrai*), manuscript m¹ uses a slightly more emphatic form (*ehrai*).
⁷ For the phrase **and if** (Coptic: *nte*), manuscript 77 adds "and" before it. In the phrase **remain in you**, manuscript 77 adds the word "in" twice. For the phrase **whatever you wish**, some manuscripts (95 and a¹) use a different future tense marker.
⁸ In the phrase **that you should give**, manuscripts 73 and 77 use a slightly different grammatical form than manuscript 20. For the phrase **a fruit**, manuscript 20 and others omit the article "a." For the word **disciples**, manuscript 77 uses a slightly different spelling (*mathetēs*).
⁹ For the phrase **just as**, manuscript 20 uses a different relative marker than the others.
¹⁰ For the word **commandments**, manuscripts 73 and m¹ use a shortened spelling. For the phrase **you will remain**, manuscript a¹ uses a double future marker.

---

**Comparison with Other Ancient Versions:**

**this**] Found in manuscript 20 and others; corresponds to the Greek word for "thus" (οὕτως) in some Greek manuscripts; the Syriac version adds "but"; the Ethiopic version translates this as "he then."
**any thing**] Found in manuscript 20 and others; omitted in the Greek Codex Bezae (D*) and some Old Latin versions; however, the Old Latin manuscript (a) adds the phrase "unless one remains in me."
⁶ **unless one remain**] Supported by most manuscripts, including the famous Greek Codices Sinaiticus (א), Alexandrinus (A), and Vaticanus (B), and the Syriac version. A different reading ("he who will not remain") is found in some citations.
**they cast him**] Literally translated from the Coptic, though some citations use the future "they will cast him."
**and-up**] Refers to the branch being "withered." Omitted in manuscript 77 and the Ethiopic version; the Syriac version translates this as "which is withered."
**they-them**] Refers to gathering the branches. Supported by most Greek and Latin manuscripts. However, several Greek manuscripts (including Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae) and the Vulgate use a singular "it" (Greek: συναγ. αὐτὸ / *synagousin auto*) instead of the plural "them."
**and-flame**] Refers to throwing them into the fire. Omitted in some citations and certain Bohairic Coptic manuscripts.
**the fl.**] Refers to "the fire." Supported by most major Greek manuscripts; however, it is omitted in some Greek citations by fathers like Cyril of Alexandria.
**burn them**] The Coptic uses the plural "them," whereas some citations and the Syriac version use the singular "burn him." The Ethiopic version omits this phrase entirely.

<note>The following section is a scholarly comparison of different ancient Bibles. It shows how the Sahidic Coptic text (represented by manuscript numbers like 20, 73, etc.) differs from early Greek manuscripts like the Codex Sinaiticus (א), Codex Vaticanus (B), and others.</note>

### Textual Variations and Comparisons

**Verse 7** 
**If you remain** <note>Coptic: ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲱ̣</note>: The Sahidic Coptic follows the reading found in the famous Greek manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), Alexandrinus (A), and Vaticanus (B). Some Latin and Syriac versions add "but" (*de*).
**Ask** <note>Greek: αιτει / αιτησασθε</note>: There is a debate here in the ancient world between the command "Ask!" (found in the Sahidic and the major Greek codices A, B, and D) and the future promise "You shall ask" (found in Codex Sinaiticus and others).
**To you** <note>Coptic: ⲛⲏⲧⲛ̄</note>: Most manuscripts include this, though Codex Bezae (D) and some Old Latin versions omit it.

**Verse 8** 
**Was glorified** <note>Coptic: ⲁϥϫⲓ</note>: Most Sahidic manuscripts use the past tense, whereas some Bohairic Coptic manuscripts say "shall be glorified."
**My Father** <note>Coptic: ⲡⲁⲉⲓ</note>: Follows the Greek and Armenian versions; the Syriac simply says "the Father."
**Much** <note>Coptic: ⲉⲛⲁⲱ̣</note>: The word order for "much fruit" varies in Codex Bezae (D) and the Ethiopic version.
**And become** <note>Coptic: ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲱ̣</note>: The Sahidic agrees with the major Greek manuscripts (B, D, L) using a form that implies a result ("so that you become"), while Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus use a future tense ("and you will become").
**To me** <note>Coptic: ⲛⲁⲓ</note>: Most sources read "my disciples," but some Greek and Syriac sources read "to me disciples."

**Verse 9** 
**My Father** <note>Coptic: ⲡⲁⲉⲓⲱⲧ</note>: The Sahidic and Syriac include "my," while the major Greek manuscripts (א, A, B) simply say "the Father."
**I also** <note>Coptic: ⲁⲛⲟⲕ ϩⲱ</note>: Translates the Greek *kagō*.
**You** <note>Coptic: ⲧⲏⲩⲧⲛ̄</note>: Most sources agree on the placement, though Codex Vaticanus (B) and Codex Bezae (D) move the word order.
**In** <note>Coptic: ϩ̄ⲡ</note>: Minor variation in manuscript 77.
**My love** <note>Coptic: ⲧⲁⲁⲅⲁⲡⲏ</note>: The Sahidic and Syriac versions use a possessive form, while the Greek manuscripts use a slightly more formal phrasing ("the love that is mine").

**Verse 10** 
**My love**: Most manuscripts agree, though the Old Latin version (e) omits "my."
**I also** <note>Coptic: ϩⲱ</note>: Sahidic matches the Greek *kagō*.
**My Father**: The Sahidic, Bohairic, and Syriac include "my," while Codex Vaticanus (B) and several Old Latin versions omit it.
**I remain** <note>Coptic: ϯⲥⲉⲉⲧ</note>: The Sahidic uses a present tense ("I remain"), matching the Greek present tense *menō*. Some later Greek manuscripts use the future *menō* ("I will remain").

### JOHN XVI 4-8

...will be doing these things to you, because they knew not my Father, *nor* knew they me. ⁴ These things I said to you, that if the hour should come ye should remember, that I, I said them to you; but these things I said not to you from the beginning, because I was with you. ⁵ But now I shall be going unto him who sent me; and no one among you asketh me, "Whither art thou going?" ⁶ But because I said these things to you, the grief filled your heart. ⁷ But I, I am saying to you the truth: it is profitable for you that I, I should go; for unless I go, the <term>Paraclete</term> <note>original: ⲡⲁⲣⲁⲕⲗⲏⲧⲟⲥ (paraklētos); a Greek loanword used in Coptic meaning 'Advocate,' 'Helper,' or 'Comforter.'</note> is not coming unto you; but if I should go, I shall send him unto you. ⁸ And that one, if he should come, will reprove the world concerning—

---

<note>The following notes represent a 'critical apparatus.' Scholars use these abbreviations to compare the Coptic text with other ancient versions like Greek (א, A, B), Syriac (Syr), Armenian (Arm), and Ethiopic (Eth). The symbols like 'g' or '20' refer to specific ancient hand-written copies.</note>

**Verse 4:** **omitted** in the Bohairic <note>A dialect of Coptic from Lower Egypt.</note> manuscript Q. $\quad$ **to you** (the second time it appears): found in manuscript 20 and others, manuscript 108, and the first hand of manuscript alpha. Omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus <note>original: א*; one of the oldest and most important Greek Bibles.</note>. $\quad$ **these** (the second time it appears): found in group g, others, 108, and alpha-1. The Syriac (Sinaitic) version reads: **these (things), because I said not.** $\quad$ **these... to you**: omitted in manuscript 92 due to a copying error where the eye skips between similar word endings <note>original: 'homeotel' (homoeoteleuton).</note>. $\quad$ **but** <note>original: ⲇⲉ (de), a Greek conjunction.</note>: found in group g, others, and alpha-1. Omitted in the Syriac (Philoxenian and Sinaitic versions) and Armenian. $\quad$ **I said not**: found in (group g), others, alpha-1, Lectionary 28, Bohairic, Syriac (Philoxenian, Harklean, and others), Armenian, and Ethiopic. It is **transposed** <note>placed in a different order</note> after the word "but" in the Greek manuscripts Sinaiticus (א), Alexandrinus (A), and Vaticanus (B), and the Harklean Syriac. The phrase "from the beginning to you" is transposed in Greek manuscripts D, 33, 157, 254. Omitted "to you" <note>original: υμιν (hymin)</note> in manuscripts 63 and 69.

**⁵ but** <note>original: ⲇⲉ (de)</note>: group g, others, and manuscript 41. Omitted in Bohairic (Q). $\quad$ **I-going** <note>original: ⲉⲓⲁⲛ (eian)</note>: found in (group g?), others, manuscript 41, and (Bohairic). The Greek reads "I go" <note>original: υπαγω (hypagō)</note> in Alexandrinus and Vaticanus; Codex Sinaiticus (א) reads "I, I go." The Sinaitic Syriac reads "that I go." $\quad$ **him who**: found in (group g), others, and manuscript 41. Greek manuscript 69, Bohairic (manuscript N), and Ethiopic read "the Father who." $\quad$ **and**: group g, others, and manuscript 41. Omitted in Bohairic (M) and (Sinaitic Syriac). $\quad$ **me**: group g, others, and manuscript 41. Swapped position before the verb "ask" in manuscript 69. $\quad$ **art thou going**: group g, others, and manuscript 41. Codex Sinaiticus (א) reads "he goes" <note>original: υπαγει (hypagei)</note>.

**⁶ but** <note>original: αλλα (alla)</note>: group g, others, and manuscript 41. Omitted in Alexandrinus (A). Syriac (Philoxenian and Sinaitic) reads "for" <note>original: γαρ (gar)</note>. $\quad$ **because**: group g, others, manuscript 41, and Bohairic (manuscripts A, C, H, O, P, Q). Omitted in manuscript m (first hand) and some Bohairic. Greek manuscript Lambda reads "when" <note>original: οτε (hote)</note>. $\quad$ **these**: group g, others, and manuscript 41. Omitted in Greek manuscripts Lambda, 71, 127, and three others, and Bohairic (P). $\quad$ **the grief**: group g and others. Greek and Syriac (Philoxenian and Sinaitic) add "and came" before this.

**⁷ I** (the first time): manuscript 20, others, and (41). Omitted in manuscript 101 <note>original: ⲓⲟⲓ</note>. $\quad$ **to you** (the first time): group g, others (41), Sinaiticus (א), Alexandrinus (A), Vaticanus (B), and others. Swapped position before the verb "I say" in several Greek manuscripts (K, L, Y, Pi, 33, etc.), Old Latin (a), and the writings of John Chrysostom and Cyril. Omitted in Armenian (versions c and d). $\quad$ **it is profitable**: group (g), others, and (41). Manuscript m adds "for" <note>original: γαρ (gar)</note>. $\quad$ **I** (the second time): group g, others, and manuscript 41. Bohairic (L and M) reads "but if." $\quad$ **I-go**: manuscript 20 and others. Sinaitic Syriac reads "when I go." $\quad$ **but** <note>original: ⲇⲉ (de)</note>: manuscript 20 and others. Omitted in manuscript 69 and some Bohairic. Bohairic (P) reads "for." $\quad$ **send him**: manuscript 20 and others. Sinaitic Syriac reads "send the Paraclete."

**⁸ and** (the first time): group (g), others, manuscript 41, and alpha-1. Sinaitic Syriac reads "but." $\quad$ **if-come**: group g and others.

<header>JOHN</header>

> ⁹ ...so that the word which he had spoken might be fulfilled: “Of those whom you gave to me, I have not lost even one of them.” ¹⁰ Simon Peter then, having a sword, drew it and struck the servant of the high priest <note>original: "archiereus"</note> and cut off his right ear. Now the name of the servant was Malchus. ¹¹ Jesus said to Peter, “Put your sword into its sheath. The cup which my Father has given me, shall I not drink it?” ¹² Then the military cohort <note>original: "speira," a Roman unit of several hundred men</note> and the commander <note>original: "chiliarchos," a leader of a thousand</note> and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him. ¹³ And they led him to Annas first, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was the high priest <note>original: "archiereus"</note> for that year. ¹⁴ Caiaphas was the one who had advised the Jews that it is profitable for one man... <note>The text breaks off, implying "to die for the people"</note>

---

⁹ **Manuscript variants for Verse 9:** Found in manuscripts g, 14, 85, 95, 97, 110, etc.  
¹⁰ **Manuscript variants for Verse 10:** Found in g, 14, 85, 95, 97, 110, etc.  
**sword** <note>original: "sēfe"</note>] spelled as "sēbe" in manuscript 110.  
**struck** <note>original: "reht"</note>] spelled as "rōht" in manuscript 14 and 85.  
**high priest** <note>original: "archiereus"</note>] abbreviated or spelled "archeiereus" in manuscript 97.  
**cut off** <note>original: "selp"</note>] spelled "slp" in manuscript m1.  
¹¹ **Manuscript variants for Verse 11:** Found in g, 14, 85, 95, 97, 110, etc.  
**shall I not** <note>original: "ntina"</note>] the negative marker "n" is omitted in manuscript 97.  
¹² **Manuscript variants for Verse 12:** Found in g, 14, 85, 92, 95, 97, 110, etc.  
**cohort** <note>original: "speira"</note>] spelled "spi." in 14.  
**commander** <note>original: "chiliarchos"</note>] spelled "cheil." in 97.  
**of the** <note>original: "nn."</note>] spelled "nne." in 110.  
**officers** <note>original: "hypēretēs"</note>] Various spellings of this Greek loanword appear across manuscripts 97, 110, 14, 85, 92, and 95, as well as in the Bohairic Coptic traditions.  
¹³ **Manuscript variants for Verse 13:** Found in g, 14, 85, 92, 95, 97, 110, m1.  
¹⁴ **Manuscript variants for Verse 14:** Found in g, 14, 85, 92, 95, 97, 110, m1.  
**who had**] manuscript 95 uses a slightly different relative pronoun form.  
**to the Jews**] manuscript 95 reads "with the Jews."  
**it is profitable**] spelled differently in 92 and m1.  
**a man**] spelled "ouōme" in m1 (a scribal error).

---

⁹ **the word**] manuscript 14 etc. / Armenian versions (codices c and d) add "of Jesus."  
**those whom you gave**] manuscript 14 etc. / The Syriac (g 9) reads "all those."  
**I lost not**] manuscript 97, m1, 14 etc. / The Sinaitic Syriac version follows this. Manuscripts 85 etc. add "any" <note>original: "laau"</note>, matching the Bohairic.  
**out of them**] manuscript g etc. / Codex Alexandrinus and other Greek/Syriac/Latin versions vary the word order: "I lost none of them" or "none out of these."

¹⁰ **therefore** <note>original: "ce"</note>] manuscript 14 etc. / Matches Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and Syriac. Manuscript 110 and Old Latin (q) use "but/and" <note>original: "de"</note>. The Ethiopic also uses "and."  
**Peter**] Coptic manuscripts / The Syriac (Palestinian and Sinaitic) uses the name "Kepha."  
**having it**] Coptic manuscripts / The Sinaitic Syriac reads "drew a sword."  
**and**] 14 etc. / Omitted in 97 and some Bohairic manuscripts.  
**the servant** (first mention)] Coptic manuscripts 14, g, etc. / Matches Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae, Old Latin, Bohairic, and Syriac. Codex Alexandrinus and Vaticanus place this word later in the sentence.  
**the name**] 14 etc. / Matches Codex Bezae and others; omitted in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus.  
**and/but** <note>original: "de"</note>] 14 etc. / Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions use "and."  
**of the servant** (second mention)] 14 etc. / Manuscript m1 and Codex Bezae read "of that servant."

# ->JOHN XVIII 24-29<-

Jesus said, "If I spoke evilly, bear witness concerning my evil; but if *well*, why do you beat me?" ²⁴ Then Annas sent him, bound, to <term>Caiaphas</term><note>The high priest; original: "Kaiphas"</note> the chief priest. ²⁵ Meanwhile, <term>Simon Peter</term><note>original: "Simōn Petros"</note> was standing, warming himself; they said to him, "Are you also one of his disciples?" He denied it, saying, "No." ²⁶ One of the servants of the chief priest, being a relative of the man whose ear Peter cut off, said, "Did I not see you in the garden with him?" ²⁷ *Again* Peter denied it, and immediately a rooster crowed. ²⁸ After these things, they took Jesus from Caiaphas into the <term>Praetorium</term><note>The Roman governor's palace; original: "praitōrion"</note>; it was morning, and they did not enter the Praetorium themselves so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the <term>Passover</term><note>The Jewish festival; original: "paskha"</note>. ²⁹ Therefore <term>Pilate</term><note>original: "Pilatos"</note> came out to them and said:

---

### Critical Notes on the Text

**Verse 23-24:** The Ethiopic version reads "saying" [original: ⲉϥϫ.] following the Greek "and he said" [original: και ειπεν] found in <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term><note>A 4th-century Greek Bible manuscript</note>, <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term><note>A 5th-century Greek manuscript</note>, and <term>Codex Vaticanus</term><note>A 4th-century Greek manuscript</note>, as well as Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions. The Greek "he says" [original: λεγει] is found in Codex Alexandrinus and minuscules. Omitted in Bohairic Coptic manuscripts B and L.

**Verse 26:** **said** [original: ⲡⲉϫⲉ]] some manuscripts add "therefore" [original: ουν]. The Armenian and Ethiopic read "and saith," while the Syriac reads "and answered." **one** [original: ⲟⲩⲁ]] found in several Greek codices; manuscript 14, Bohairic, Syriac, and Ethiopic add "to him" [original: ⲛⲁϥ]. **being a kinsman** [original: ⲉⲧⲥⲩⲅ-ⲅⲉⲛⲏⲥ]] matches the Greek "the kinsman" [original: ο συγγ.] in various manuscripts, Syriac, Armenian, and <term>Old Latin</term><note>Latin translations of the Bible predating the Vulgate</note>. For Peter: the Armenian and Syriac versions vary the name or phrasing.

**Verse 27:** **again** [original: ⲡⲁⲗⲓⲛ]] found in manuscript 14 and Armenian; manuscript 20 adds "but/and" [original: ⲇⲉ]; Codex Sinaiticus and others add "therefore" [original: ουν]; the Syriac and Ethiopic read "and again." **denied** [original: ⲁϥⲁⲣ.]] the word order is changed in manuscript 69 and some Latin versions. **Peter** [original: ⲡⲉⲧⲣ.]] omitted in some Old Latin versions; the Syriac adds "I know him not."

**Verse 28:** **after-took** [original: ⲁⲩⲛⲓ.-ϫⲓ]] found in manuscript 14; Greek "they lead therefore" [original: αγουσιν ουν] in Codex Sinaiticus and others, the <term>Vulgate</term><note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note>, and Church Fathers like <term>Chrysostom</term><note>Early Church Father known for his preaching</note> and <term>Cyril</term>. The Syriac adds "and when it dawned." **from-Praetorium** [original: ⲉⲃⲟⲗ-ⲡⲣⲁⲓ.]] found in manuscript 14; Old Latin reads "to Caiaphas in the Praetorium" [original: ad C. in praet.]. **Caiaphas** [original: ⲕⲁⲓⲫⲁⲥ]] Old Latin and Bohairic add "chief priest" [original: principem sac.]; Syriac adds "and led him." **it was** [original: ⲡⲉ]] manuscript 14; Syriac adds "that they might deliver him to the governor." **and** [original: ⲁⲩⲱ]] manuscript 14; Syriac uses "but" [original: ⲇⲉ]. **that-defiled** [original: ϫⲉⲕⲁⲥ-ⲥⲱϣϥ]] omitted in Bohairic manuscript P. **but that they** [original: ⲁⲗⲗⲁ ⲉⲧⲉ.]] manuscript 14 and Armenian; Ethiopic reads "and that they"; Bohairic and Syriac read "until they." **should eat** [original: ⲉⲧⲉ-ⲟⲩⲱⲙ]] manuscript 14; Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus and Latin versions add "so that" [original: ινα].

**Verse 29:** **therefore** [original: ⲇⲉ]] found in Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and Bohairic versions; omitted in Armenian.

# ->JOHN<-

**Verse 39-40 Variations**
Ethiopic version... *omits* the word in the Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Regius, and other manuscripts... *prefixed* with the word "again" in the Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others (though *omitted* in many Greek and Old Latin versions, the Syriac, and the writings of John Chrysostom). **saying [Coptic: ⲉⲧⲕ.]** is found in manuscripts 14 and others... but *omitted* in manuscript 93 and some Old Latin sources. **do not release [Coptic: ⲙⲡ(ⲉⲣ)ⲕⲁ]** is found in manuscripts 14, 101, and the Bohairic Coptic, but *omitted* in the major Greek codices. **Barabbas (1st mention)**... some manuscripts *add* "to us." **Barabbas (2nd mention)**... some versions *add* the word "this [one]." **robber [Coptic: ⲥⲟⲟⲛⲉ]**... some Old Latin versions describe him as a "notorious robber" <note>original Latin: insignis latro</note> and the Syriac and Ethiopic call him a "chief robber."

**Textual Variants and Manuscript Notes:**

**so that you also may believe**] manuscript 95... **36** manuscripts 20, 93, 95, 110... **bone** <note>original Coptic: "kas"</note>] spelled as "kees" in manuscripts 93, 110... **37** manuscripts 20, 93, 95, 110... **38** manuscripts 20, 93, 95, 110, 132... **being a disciple**] manuscript m1 has a slight grammatical variation in the prefix... **of the Jews**] manuscript m1 has a variant spelling... **take**] manuscript 110 adds a suffix "it"... **39** manuscripts 20, 93, 110, 132... **Nicodemus**] spelled "-umos" in 110, 132... **he who had [come]**] manuscript 132 uses a different relative pronoun... **weighing**] manuscript 132 uses a different verb form.

---

**Cross-References and External Versions:**

**blood-water**] found in manuscript 20 and others, also in the Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic versions. Note: The Greek manuscripts Y and the Bohairic Coptic, along with Eusebius, reverse the order to **"water-blood"** <note>original Greek: "hydōr-haima"</note>. 
**35** This verse is omitted in the Old Latin manuscript (e). **true witness**] Supported by manuscripts 20, 93, 95, 96, 110, and the Bohairic. The Greek phrase **"true is his witness"** <note>original Greek: "alēthēs estin hē martyria autou"</note> is found in manuscripts H, Y, and others, as well as the Vulgate and Syriac. 
**and that one**] Manuscripts 20, 93, 95, 96, 110 support the Coptic reading. The Greek uses **"that one"** <note>original Greek: "ekeinos"</note> in Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus. 
**ye also**] Supported by major Greek manuscripts and Syriac; omitted in some Bohairic and Armenian copies.
**36 for** <note>original Greek loanword: "gar"</note>] Omitted in Armenian; replaced with **"but"** <note>original Greek: "de"</note> in some Greek and Old Latin copies. **happened**] Supported by Bohairic and Syriac. **shall not be bruised/broken out of him**] Various Latin versions use **"shall not break"** <note>original Latin: "confringent" or "comminuetis"</note>. The phrase **"out of him"** <note>original Greek: "ap' autou"</note> follows the Septuagint translation of Numbers 9:12.
**37 saying**] Omitted in some Old Latin manuscripts.

<note>The following section details "textual variants"—differences found between various ancient copies of the Bible. These notes help scholars understand how the text was preserved and changed in different languages and regions.</note>

**7** In Manuscript 75 and the Armenian version, "therefore" <note>original Coptic/Greek: *de*</note> is omitted. In Manuscript 132, the Syriac, and the Ethiopic versions, the word "therefore" is present. &nbsp;&nbsp; **Peter]** Omitted in Manuscript 75, Manuscript 132, and the Syriac. &nbsp;&nbsp; **he bound himself]** Translated from the Coptic *afmorf*. Manuscript 43 and others read this; however, the Syriac reads "he girt his loins" and the Armenian reads "he put on [his clothes]." &nbsp;&nbsp; **he leapt]** Translated from Coptic *afhitf*. Manuscript 43 and others use this. The Codex Bezae <note>An ancient Greek and Latin manuscript from the 5th century.</note> uses a similar Greek word for "leaped," while the Syriac says "he fell." The major Greek manuscripts—Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus—along with the Bohairic and Armenian, say "he threw himself." &nbsp;&nbsp; **into the sea]** Manuscript 43 and others. The Syriac version adds "that he might come to Jesus," while another Syriac manuscript adds "and was swimming and coming."

**8** **the other disciples... the ship]** The Syriac version transposes this to say "and the rest of the disciples were coming after the shore." &nbsp;&nbsp; **therefore]** <note>original Coptic/Greek: *de*</note> Added in the Bohairic, Sinaiticus, and Armenian. &nbsp;&nbsp; **the ship]** Manuscript 43 and others. The Codex Sinaiticus adds "other" <note>original Greek: *allō*</note>. &nbsp;&nbsp; **but... cubits]** This phrase is omitted in the Syriac version. &nbsp;&nbsp; **two hundred]** Manuscript 43 and others. One Old Latin manuscript <note>Codex Vercellensis</note> reads "twenty" <note>original Latin: *viginti*</note>. &nbsp;&nbsp; **the net]** The Armenian manuscripts vary between "the net" and "the nets." &nbsp;&nbsp; **of the fish]** Manuscript 43 and others. Manuscript 91 reads "under the fish." The Syriac omits this, while the Ethiopic says "with the fish."

**9** **when they moored]** Manuscript 43 and others. The Greek manuscripts Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus use a word meaning "as they landed." &nbsp;&nbsp; **therefore]** <note>original Coptic/Greek: *de*</note> Found in Manuscript 75 and most major Greek and Bohairic copies, but omitted in some Armenian and Bohairic versions. &nbsp;&nbsp; **to the shore]** Manuscript 43 and others. Some Greek copies say "onto the land." &nbsp;&nbsp; **they saw]** Manuscript 43 and others. The Codex Sinaiticus and most major Greek manuscripts use "they see," while some Syriac and Ethiopic versions say "they found." &nbsp;&nbsp; **a fire... it]** Manuscript 43. The Armenian reads "a fire of coals and a fish upon it." The major Greek manuscripts and Syriac read "a charcoal fire lying there and a fish" <note>original Greek: *anthrakian keimenen kai opsarion*</note>. The Old Latin and Ethiopic read "burning coals and a fish" <note>original Latin: *carbones incensos et piscem*</note>. The Syriac says, "in front of Jesus coals of fire and the fish put on them." &nbsp;&nbsp; **and [bread]** Found in Manuscript 43 and the Syriac. The major Greek manuscripts say "lying there and bread."

# JOHN

...to Jesus, "Lord, but what about this one?"

²² Jesus said to him, "If I want him to remain <note>original Coptic: "etrefchō"</note> until I come, what is that to you? You, follow me." ²³ This word <note>original Coptic: "pei-shakhe"</note> therefore went out among the brothers, that that disciple would not die. Yet Jesus did not say to him that he would not die, but, "If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?" ²⁴ This is the disciple who testifies concerning these things and the one who wrote them; and we know that his testimony is true. ²⁵ There are also many other things that Jesus did; if they were written one by one, I say—

---

### Critical Apparatus

**Verse 21**
**to Jesus:** Found in Sahidic manuscripts 20 and 104. Manuscript 132 reads "to our Jesus." Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus) and others read "to Jesus." Codex Bezae (Greek) reads "to the same Jesus." Omitted in some versions.
**Lord:** Found in 20, 104 (with "is"), and 132. Omitted in Codex Sinaiticus (א). Bohairic and Syriac versions read "my Lord."
**but:** Found in 20, 104, and Bohairic. Omitted in other Bohairic versions.

**Verse 22**
**Jesus:** Found in 20 and 132. Omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts.
**if:** Found in 20, 104, and 132. This matches the Old Latin and Vulgate readings.
**for-remain:** Found in 20 and 132. Codex Bezae (Greek) reads "to remain thus." Bohairic translates this as "to leave him." Omitted in some Bohairic versions.
**what is that to you:** Found in 20 and 132. The Syriac (Gospels) reads "to thee what to thee?" Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, etc.) read simply "what [is it] to you?" Armenian versions read "what care is it to you?"
**follow me, thou:** Found in 20 and 132. Various Greek manuscripts and versions show different word orders for "you" and "me." Bohairic and Ethiopic read "but you, follow me." Syriac (Sinaiticus) prefixes this with "now."

**Verse 23**
**this word:** Found in 20 and 132. The word "this" <note>original Greek: "outos"</note> is omitted in some Greek witnesses.
**therefore:** Found in 20, and major Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, etc.). Omitted in some Bohairic. Manuscript 132 and other Bohairic versions use "but" <note>original Greek: "de"</note>. Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopic use "and."
**the brothers:** Found in 20, 104 (likely), and 132. Codex Bezae and Armenian add "and they thought." Syriac (Sinaiticus) reads "the disciples."
**Jesus-him:** Found in 132 and some Bohairic. Manuscripts 20 and 104 read "but Jesus did not say to him." Other major Greek (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) and Bohairic/Syriac versions read "but Jesus did not say." Some Greek (Alexandrinus, Bezae), Latin, and Armenian versions read "and Jesus did not say."
**he-die not:** Found in 20, 104, 132, and Bohairic versions.

### JOHN XXI 22-25

²² Jesus said to him, “If I should wish for him to remain until I come, what is that to you indeed? You, follow me.” ²³ This word therefore went out among the brothers: “That disciple will not die.” Yet Jesus did not say to him that he will not die, but (<gloss>if</gloss>) “If I should wish for him to remain until I come, what is that to you indeed?” ²⁴ This is the disciple who bears witness concerning these things, and he who wrote these things; and we know that his witness is true. ²⁵ But there are many other works which Jesus did; if these should be written one by one, I say—

---

**Verse 23 variations**
**die** <note>original Latin: "thneskeis"</note>: Found in Codex Bezae and Old Latin (manuscript e).
**if** <note>original Coptic: "efshan"</note>: Found in Sahidic manuscripts 20, 104, 132. This matches Old Latin (a, b, c) and the Vulgate. Omitted in some other Latin versions.
**for-remain** <note>original Coptic: "etrefchō"</note>: Found in 20, 104, 132 and the Syriac. The Armenian and other Syriac versions read "that this should remain."
**who art thou indeed?** <note>original Coptic: "ntk-nt."</note>: Found in 20 and 104. This corresponds to the Greek "what is that to you?" <note>original Greek: "ti pros se"</note> found in the corrected Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and Codex Bezae, as well as the Old Latin, Bohairic Coptic, and Ethiopic. The Old Latin (c) adds "follow me." This phrase is omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus and some Syriac and Armenian versions.

**Verse 24 variations**
**who-witness**: Found in Codex Vaticanus and Cyril of Alexandria.
**these**: Found in manuscript 20. Manuscript 132 and others read "this." Old Latin (a, e) reads "concerning Jesus." The Syriac adds "all."
**and-wrote**: Found in manuscript 20. The original hand of Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus read "and the one who wrote." Manuscript 132 and the Bohairic versions use a slightly different phrasing: "and he, he [is the one who wrote]." The Old Latin (a) reads: "and who wrote these things we know and we know."
**and we know**: Matches the Greek <note>original Greek: "ho kai oidamen"</note>.
**is his witness**: Found in Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, as well as the Old Latin, Vulgate, and Bohairic. Some versions (Vaticanus, Codex Bezae) vary the word order, placing "is" at the end: "his witness true is."

**Verse 25 variations**
**but there are**: Manuscript 20 and the Bohairic and Syriac include the word "but" <note>original: "de"</note>, while manuscript 104 omits it. The entire verse is omitted in the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus.
**many works**: Found in 20. Manuscript 132 omits "many." Greek and Latin manuscripts include "and many other things."
**which Jesus did**: Matches Old Latin, Bohairic, and Syriac versions.
**Jesus**: Codex Bezae adds "Christ." Some Greek and Syriac manuscripts add "in the presence of his disciples." One Old Latin manuscript adds "which are not written in this book."
**one (by one)** <note>original Coptic: "oua oua"</note>: Literally "one one." Omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts.
**I say**: Found in 20. This matches the Greek <note>original Greek: "oimai," meaning "I suppose"</note> found in the corrected Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus, as well as Bohairic and Armenian. Omitted in Syriac and Ethiopic. Manuscript 104 adds "to you." One Bohairic manuscript reads "I know."
**not the world**: Found in 20, 104, Bohairic, and Syriac. This matches the Greek <note>original Greek: "oude-ton kosmon"</note> found in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Armenian.

The extensive critical apparatus compares the Coptic text against major Greek codices and early translations in Latin, Syriac, and Armenian.</summary>

### JOHN

[...I suppose] that the world would not contain the books that they will write.

---

**will contain** <note>original Coptic: "nashp"</note> (as seen in manuscript 104) will contain] <note>original Greek: "chorēsein"</note> found in the corrected Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and the original hand of Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus .. *would not be sufficient* found in the Syriac versions (Sinaitic and Curetonian) .. <note>original Greek: "chorēsai"</note> found in Codex Alexandrinus, the corrected Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus, Codex Bezae, etc., the Old Latin, and the Vulgate .. **to be able to contain** <note>original Latin: "capere posse"</note> found in Old Latin manuscripts (a, g, q), the Clementine Vulgate, and the Armenian version (*sufficient to bear*) **which will be written** <note>original Coptic: "etounas..."</note>] found in the corrected Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, and several numbered Greek manuscripts, the Old Latin versions, the Clementine Vulgate, the Syriac (Peshitta and Harclean), and the Armenian .. some manuscripts add *Amen* such as Codex Basiliensis, Old Latin (c, f), Ambrosiaster, Ethiopic, and Cyril.

**Closing Title (Subscription).** **According to Jo[hn]** (manuscript 104) .. **With God** <note>original shorthand: "sunth," likely "in deo"</note> **The Gospel according to John** (manuscript 20), **Gospel according to John** <note>original Greek: "euaggelion kata iōannēn"</note> found in the corrected Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus, Codex Cyprius, and others.

# JOHN XXI

that the world will not contain the books which will be written.

Armenian .. <note>original Greek: "kata iōannēn"</note> **According to John** (Codex Vaticanus) .. <note>original Greek: "telos tou kata iōannēn euaggeliou"</note> **End of the Gospel according to John** (Codex Cyprius, Codex Petropolitanus, manuscript 473, and others) ..
<note>original Greek: "euagg. kata iōannēn etelesthē archetai euagg. kata loukan"</note> **The Gospel according to John is finished; the Gospel according to Luke begins** (Codex Bezae) .. *the Gospel according to (cata in manuscript e) John ends, begins according to (prefixed by "Gospel" in manuscripts d and f) Luke* (Old Latin manuscripts b, d, e, f) ..
*according to John ends, begins according to Luke, amen* (Old Latin manuscript q) ..
*end of the Gospel according to John, beginning of according to Luke* (Old Latin manuscript a) ..
*end of the Gospel according to (cata in Vulgate manuscripts) John* (Old Latin manuscript g and various Vulgate manuscripts) .. *end of the Gospel of John* (Old Latin manuscript c) .. <note>original Greek/Bohairic: "euaggelion zōēs kata iōannēs"</note> **Gospel of life according to John** (Bohairic Coptic version) .. the closing title is omitted in some Bohairic manuscripts (C₂ʳ, Δ₄ʳ, F₁ʳ, J₃, T)

<meta>This page transitions from the collation of fragmentary Gospel verses seen on the previous page to a specific list of chapter headings, known as "Tituli" (Latin for "titles"). These lists served as a table of contents in ancient Coptic Bibles. The following text compares two primary sources: Manuscript Paris Weill-108 and Manuscript Sayce 2 (indicated by the letter "S"). These headings provide insight into how early Egyptian Christians categorized the narratives of the Gospel of Luke.</meta>

## CHAPTER HEADINGS OF ST. LUKE FROM MANUSCRIPTS PARIS WEILL-108
## AND SAYCE 2

These are the chapters <note>original: "kephalaion", a Greek loanword used in Coptic for chapter divisions</note> according to Luke:
->They number 83 chapters <note>The Coptic numeral "pg" represents 83: "p" (80) + "g" (3).</note><-
->of the Gospel according to Luke <note>Manuscript Sayce 2 (S) includes this specific subheading.</note><-

1. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Concerning the enrolment <note>original: "apographē", referring to the Roman census at the time of Jesus' birth.</note>
2. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The shepherds <note>S includes this.</note>
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Simeon
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Anna the prophetess <note>The word "prophetess" is omitted in S.</note>
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The word which happened unto John <note>original: "Iōhannēs" (John the Baptist). S reads: "Concerning John".</note>
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Those who asked John <note>S reads: "Concerning the multitudes".</note>
7. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The temptation of the Savior <note>The phrase "of the Savior" is omitted in S.</note>
8. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The one who had the spirit of a demon <note>The demoniac. S reads: "Concerning the demoniac".</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the technical errata of previous volumes to an introduction describing the methodology used in constructing "The Text" of this critical edition. It explains the symbols, the script types (uncials), and the linguistic choices made by the editors regarding Sahidic and Bohairic dialects.</meta>

<page-num>373</page-num>

## THE TEXT

The text is printed continuously from the fragments, with breaks only at the chapters, except in the first chapter, where two breaks occur. Section marks and numbers are indicated in the <term>Apparatus</term> <note>The collection of notes at the bottom of a page that lists variations and evidence from different manuscripts.</note> by § for small and ¶ for large divisions of the text. In Matthew, Mark, and Luke the <term>Greek uncials</term> <note>A style of large, rounded capital letters used in ancient Greek manuscripts from the 3rd to 8th centuries.</note> of the large divisions are given to show that in these books the numbering of the divisions agrees with the Greek, whereas in John the numbering is given in <term>Coptic uncials</term> because a numbering system differing from the Greek and agreeing with the <term>Bohairic</term> <note>A dialect of Coptic used primarily in the Nile Delta; it eventually became the official liturgical language of the Coptic Church.</note> appears. 

In the short account of the fragments, the occurrence of sectional marks will be noted. Marks occur in the earlier fragments, but numbers are not seen until a later time, and the <term>Ammonian sections</term> <note>An ancient system of dividing the four Gospels into 1,165 numbered sections to help readers find parallel passages.</note> are written in only three manuscripts, one of which is not earlier than the ninth century; and the others, of much later date, are paper <term>lectionaries</term> <note>Books containing a collection of scripture readings used for Christian worship services.</note>, in the latest of which the numbers are written in a kind of <term>cursive</term> <note>A flowing style of handwriting used for faster composition.</note> hand with the <term>Arabic</term> word for "small" <note>Arabic: صغير (saghir)</note> over them, and without any indication of the <term>Eusebian canons</term> <note>A system of ten tables created by Eusebius of Caesarea to show where the different Gospels tell the same stories.</note>. Square brackets in the text signify the loss of letters or words in the fragment. 

In constructing the text, the chief guide was agreement with the so-called <term>Neutral Text</term> <note>A family of manuscripts, such as Codex Vaticanus, that 19th-century scholars believed was the most accurate reflection of the original New Testament.</note> with which the earlier fragments were usually in accord. After this, some importance in deciding the text was given to <term>Western influence</term> <note>A text type found in manuscripts like Codex Bezae, known for its frequent additions and paraphrasing.</note>, which was found to be not as powerful as supposed. Frequently, in the case of the omission of conjunctions, it was presumed that the version in its earliest form shows a survival of the old <term>Egyptian asyndeton</term> <note>A grammatical style in which words or phrases are joined without connecting words like "and" or "but."</note>, and that the Greek word "but" <note>original Greek: δὲ (de)</note> was originally the connecting word before the <term>Sahidic</term> <note>The dialect of Coptic used in Upper Egypt, which produced some of the earliest Christian translations.</note> equivalent for "and" <note>original Greek: καὶ (kai)</note> became used. Only in this way can the practice of the manuscripts be explained. Greek words were always preferred to Coptic in the text as probably belonging to the earliest version, and agreement with the Bohairic dialect was avoided.

<summary>This page outlines the editorial standards for the edition, explaining the numbering systems for Gospel divisions and the scholarly preference for the Neutral Text and Sahidic dialect over later influences.</summary>
<keywords>textual criticism, New Testament, Sahidic Coptic, Bohairic Coptic, Ammonian sections, Eusebian canons, manuscript fragments, Egyptian asyndeton</keywords>
