### THE APPARATUS <note>The "Apparatus Criticus" is the section at the bottom of a scholarly text that lists all the variations found in different ancient manuscripts, allowing researchers to see every version of a verse.</note>

Gothic letters <note>A heavy, decorative typeface used here specifically to denote fragments written on papyrus.</note> represent the few *papyrus* <note>An early form of paper made from the pith of the papyrus plant.</note> fragments, and Gothic *cit* <note>original: "cit," short for the Latin "citatio," meaning a reference or citation.</note> represents a citation written on papyrus. Greek cursive letters are used for the *bilingual* fragments written in Greek and Sahidic <note>The southern dialect of the Coptic language.</note>. Ordinary small letters mark the *paper* fragments. Ordinary numbers stand for the *parchment* <note>A writing surface made from processed animal skins, usually more durable than papyrus or paper.</note> fragments. Lectionaries <note>Books containing specific portions of the Bible organized for reading during church services.</note> are indicated by a small *l* placed above the letter or number. Curved brackets mean that the fragment is imperfect in the verse, and cannot be relied upon for that verse except when specially cited among the authorities for or against a given reading. If a note of interrogation <note>A question mark.</note> be placed within the bracket, it means that there is some imperfection of the writing, but that the reading may be regarded as certain. Elsewhere a note of interrogation implies uncertainty. Occasionally ‘fr’ <note>original: "fr," short for "fragment."</note> will appear, and means a later inserted unidentified fragment probably belonging to some of those in the Register.

In the upper part of the Apparatus verse numbers are printed, and following them come the letters and numbers giving the authorities <note>The specific ancient manuscripts that support a particular version of the text.</note> for every single verse. These authorities are arranged as far as possible according to their supposed date. The signs § and ¶ for small and large divisions are placed after the letter or number to which they belong, and if a <term>Coptic letter</term> <note>Coptic used its alphabet as a numbering system; a horizontal line over a letter indicated it was a numeral.</note>, with line over it be seen, it shows the number of the large Greek or Coptic sections, and in <term>Matthew</term>, <term>Mark</term>, and <term>Luke</term> it will be found to correspond with the Greek uncial <note>A style of large, block-like capital letters used in early Greek manuscripts.</note> in the text: after this Coptic letter are placed the authorities which give it. This part of the Apparatus is devoted chiefly to <term>orthographic phenomena</term> <note>The study of spelling variations and how words were written by different scribes.</note> and practically all the small variants of this kind are given of all the fragments, from which fact may be obtained some idea of the care and scholarship of the scribes. It may be noted here that only one <term>MS. (73)</term> <note>Manuscript number 73.</note> appears to have suffered any systematic correction. When citing the authorities for a given reading the first authority in the verse list is always cited; if there are more than one other authority without brackets,

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of the editorial methodology for the critical apparatus. <header>THE APPARATUS</header>

If preceded by **L**, it signifies the text was taken from the Leyden collection of fragments <note>Referring to the National Museum of Antiquities in Leiden, Netherlands, which houses significant Egyptian and Coptic manuscript fragments.</note>.

When curved brackets are used in the middle of a word, the enclosed letters, words, or numbers refer only to the letter immediately preceding it. For example, **ⲉϥ(ⲃ 111)ⲓ** <note>original: "ef(b 111)i"</note> means that manuscript **111** writes the word as **ⲉⲃⲓ** <note>original: "ebi"</note>. Sometimes, for the sake of clarity, a whole syllable may have to be written, such as **ⲧⲉϥ(ⲧⲩ̅ 70 134)ⲥⲓⲝ** <note>A technical notation showing how manuscripts 70 and 134 vary in their spelling of this specific Coptic word.</note>.

## TRANSLATION

The order of the words has been kept more strictly than in the translation of the Bohairic <note>The dialect of the Coptic language originating from the Nile Delta (northern Egypt), which became the standard liturgical language of the Coptic Church.</note> version. The word **ⲇⲉ** <note>original: "de," a Greek-derived particle</note> has always been translated as "but," and this word, when followed by **(ⲁ)** <note>Short for the Greek-derived word "alla."</note>, also renders the meaning "but" <note>original: "alla," a stronger Greek word for "but" or "on the contrary."</note>. In other respects, the rules of that previous translation have been followed with slight modifications; for instance, using "when he had" instead of "having." 

The periphrasis <note>A roundabout way of speaking or using more words than necessary to express an idea.</note> for the passive voice has been translated as the passive whenever the original Greek text uses the passive. Additionally, when the frequentative form <note>A grammatical form indicating an action that happens repeatedly or habitually.</note> of the Coptic language is used, the phrase "wont to be" represents that form where the Greek uses the ordinary passive. Greek proper names are preserved exactly in their own letters whenever possible—for example, *Nazōraios* <note>meaning "the Nazarene"</note> (volume 1, page 321), which is in italics by error. If this is not possible—for example, "*a Kyrenæan man*" <note>meaning "a man from Cyrene," a city in modern-day Libya</note> (page 333)—italics are used. All other translated Greek words that were borrowed by the Coptic language are also printed in italics.

Square brackets `[]` imply words used by the Coptic language that are not required by English grammar, while curved brackets `()` supply words which are necessary for the English idiom to make sense.

## NOTES ON THE FRAGMENTS OF <term>MSS.<gloss>Manuscripts; documents written by hand rather than printed.</gloss></term>

In the following remarks upon the materials used for this edition, the word **fragment** will be used rather than the word **manuscript**, because only one complete volume is found among them. Although no pains have been spared in identifying leaves and pieces of leaves that have been scattered across different collections, some which are listed separately in the <term>Register<gloss>The editor’s formal catalog or list used to track and organize the various pieces of the manuscripts.</gloss></term> may actually belong to the same volume, while others grouped under a single number might really form parts of different volumes. Photography and careful description of fragments can help identify which pieces belong together, but certainty is only reached when the text continues perfectly from one detached leaf to the next.

Except when noted as being copied by another person, all the sources cited in this edition—including the published works of <note>Oscar von Lemm (1856–1918) was a prominent scholar of Coptic studies whose work is vital for identifying manuscript fragments.</note> **Dr. von Lemm**—have been <term>collated<gloss>The process of comparing the editor's copy against the original manuscript to ensure every letter and mark is accurate.</gloss></term> by the editor.

Regarding <term>Papyrus<gloss>A writing surface made from the pith of the papyrus plant, used before parchment became the primary material for books.</gloss></term>, four large, practically continuous sections of text have recently been discovered. One of these had been preserved with sufficient accuracy by the copy made by <note>Des Rivières was an early collector and copyist whose transcriptions are often the only record of manuscripts that have since been lost or damaged.</note> **Des Rivières**, which can be found in the Library of **Munich**. These papyri were not scrolls but books <note>Technically called a "codex," these are early versions of the modern book format with bound pages.</note>, and are written in a bold, upright, regular hand. This style does not resemble the Greek writing of the fourth century, which some of the <term>Sahidic<gloss>The dialect of the Coptic language used in Southern (Upper) Egypt, where many of these ancient fragments were found.</gloss></term> parchment resembles. Fragment **g** shows earlier letter forms and appears to be written by two different hands. The fragment published by **Pistelli** <note>Ermenegildo Pistelli, an Italian scholar who specialized in ancient papyri.</note> and attributed by him to the fifth or sixth century leans forward and joins some of the letters, giving it a less formal appearance. The fragment **Brit. Mus. 955 (e)**, which should have been categorized with the <term>lectionaries<gloss>Books containing specific portions of scripture appointed to be read during church services.</gloss></term>, resembles the very latest style of writing found on parchment from the eleventh century.

By far the largest amount of text is written on **Parchment**, dating perhaps from the fifth to the fourteenth century. Only one specific date occurs in the entire collection of fragments, and this is **A. D. 985** (<term>A. MART. 701<gloss>The "Year of the Martyrs" (Anno Martyrum), the calendar system used by the Coptic Church, which begins in 284 AD. Adding 284 to 701 gives the year 985 AD.</gloss></term>). This date is found in a <term>homiletic<gloss>Related to a sermon or religious discourse.</gloss></term> work recently acquired by the **British Museum** containing the **Praise of St. John the Baptist**.

In dealing with this formidable collection of fragmentary documents, a rough threefold classification may be employed, depending upon some very obvious features of the writing and the layout of the page. **Class i** contains chiefly the smaller pages of text, usually featuring smaller, regular writing with...

Bodleian Hunt. 3 is a paper lectionary of the months Athor <note>Hatour, roughly November</note>, Mshir <note>Meshir, roughly February</note>, and of Paskha <note>Easter/Passover season</note>, *i. e.* Lent. It contains rough Arabic beginnings of lections <note>readings</note>, and is probably of the 13th century. Hunt. 4, 14th century, is a paper fragment of John, numbered for the leaves like Bohairic MSS. <note>manuscripts</note>, giving occasionally the Ammonian sections and canons <note>a system for dividing the Gospels for cross-referencing</note>. Hunt. 5, Friday <note>Greek: Paraskeve</note> lections, rubrics in Coptic and Arabic, foliated, section numbers, e.g. Mark 14:66 <term>ⲝⲍ̅</term> <note>67</note> which is rightly repeated at 15:1 and 6, <term>ⲟⲏ̅</term> <note>78</note> again is right for lections beginning Luke 22:47, 56, 66, then <term>ⲟⲑ̅</term> <note>79</note> follows correctly for 23:11, and <term>ⲗⲑ̅</term> <note>39</note> is the right Sahidic number for John 19:1, 13th century.

Vatican 90 has a lection from Luke which is found copied exactly among the Munich fragments of Des Rivières (Munich 8). 99 is a complete volume with lectionary for Holy Week in Sahidic and Arabic and worthy of publication, though not earlier than the 13th century.

Of the other lectionary fragments 1¹ and 2¹ are probably 9th century <note>Roman numeral IX</note>, *a*¹—9¹ 10th century <note>X</note>, 10¹—27¹ 11th century <note>XI</note>, 30¹—36¹ 12th century <note>XII</note>, 40¹—*h*¹ 13th century <note>XIII</note>, 46¹—*o* 14th century <note>XIV</note>.

# NOTES ON THE FRAGMENTS OF MSS. <note>MSS: An abbreviation for manuscripts</note>

<page-num>384</page-num>

...to phenomena of initial letters and ornament or the numbering of pages. Probably all the manuscripts of this and Class II <note>Class II: A category defined earlier in the work, likely referring to a specific chronological or stylistic group of manuscripts</note> had numbers on every page and quire <note>quire: A gathering of folded sheets of parchment or paper, usually four or eight, sewn together as part of a book</note> numbers in regular course. Comparatively very few fragments have preserved a quire number and still fewer any ornamental treatment of the last and first page of the quire. In these later fragments, at least two kinds of initial letters appear, and the Apparatus <note>Apparatus: The specialized academic notes and symbols used to document variations in a text</note> records the two kinds with sufficient accuracy by means of the signs § and P. Ornament is often attached to the initials, and a characteristic sameness in color and form prevails. Compared with the **Bohairic** <term>Bohairic: The dialect of the Coptic language used primarily in Northern Egypt (the Nile Delta)</term>, it is smaller in design, and interlacing work is less common, but in a very few instances far greater spirit and invention is shown. However, there is hardly any attempt at representing the scenes described, such as those found in the great parchment manuscript of the National Library <note>Refers to the Bibliothèque Nationale de France in Paris</note> and the smaller paper volume in the *Institut Catholique* of Paris, nor any imitation of the Byzantine pictures of the Evangelists <note>The writers of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John</note> which are found in the manuscripts of Paris and Cairo.

In reference to **papyrus g** <note>papyrus g: A specific fragmentary manuscript designated by the letter 'g' in this catalog</note>, the following particulars may be of some interest. The editor was told at Munich that the originals of Des Rivières' <note>Marquis de Rivières, a 19th-century French collector</note> copy preserved in the Library had been destroyed in the bombardment of Alexandria <note>The 1882 naval bombardment by the British Royal Navy</note>. On returning to England, by the kind suggestion of Mr. Leatham, of Miserden Park, Gloucestershire, he found them in the possession of Henry Martyn Kennard, Esq., well known as a collector of Egyptian antiquities. The papyrus had been obtained from a foreman of the Engineering Company which undertook the recent improvement of the harbor of Alexandria. It is very gratifying to be able to add that, since the printing of these Notes, the public-spirited owner has presented the fragments, together with a much larger number of non-Biblical pieces, to the **British Museum**.

The number of fragments may be reckoned as follows:
*   For **Matthew**: 187 fragments; **Lectionaries**: 35 <term>Lectionaries: Books containing specific scripture readings for daily or weekly church services</term>
*   For **Mark**: 76 fragments; **Lectionaries**: 17
*   For **Luke**: 152 fragments; **Lectionaries**: 42
*   For **John**: 210 fragments; **Lectionaries**: 32

This gives a total of 751. The papyrus passages are included in these figures, but are not reckoned according to each fragment: the passages in each gospel are reckoned as one for each indicating Gothic letter.

Of the whole body of fragments, Nos. 8, 13, 14, 21, 37, 73, 108, 110, 114, a¹, 6¹, 26¹, b¹, f¹, g¹, m¹ give text from all the four gospels; while Nos. g, 9, 18, 20, 50, 64, 70, 86, 91, 109, 4¹, 13¹, 19¹, 33¹, 48¹, l¹ give text from three.

As regards the amount of consecutive text in each supposed manuscript, No. 111 has the whole of **Matthew** chapters 11–26 and **Luke** chapter 5 (and 6); No. 91 has **Luke** chapters 9–16, 18–22 (and 24), and **John** chapters 2–7; No. 114 has **Mark** chapters 3–8...

## ESTIMATE OF THE VERSION

Two general observations may be made in regard to the whole body of fragments. The first is the freedom from corrections and the consistency of the orthography <note>orthography: the conventional spelling system of a language</note> of individual MSS. <note>MSS: an abbreviation for "manuscripts"</note> As noticed above, only one MS. appears to have been extensively corrected. The second observation is the unanimity of the readings. Variants appear, as is only natural in so large a number of MSS. of different dates, but these variants are few, and their scarcity may be connected with the fact that so many of the fragments have come from the same place, the White Monastery <note>A famous center of Coptic scholarship in Upper Egypt, once led by Saint Shenoute the Archimandrite.</note>.

To give an illustration of this unanimity of readings, if we take the *Selected Readings* <note>original: "Delectus"</note> drawn up in the *Appendices to the Stephanic New Testament* <note>original: "Appendices ad Novum Testamentum Stephanicum," referring to a scholarly work based on the editions of Robert Estienne (Stephanus)</note> under the supervision of Dr. Sanday, only three fluctuations will be noticed among fifty-four readings in Matthew; three also among the twenty-two in Mark; none at all among thirty readings in Luke; and only one among thirty-five in John. This singular unanimity must be qualified by the comparative paucity <note>paucity: a small amount or scarcity</note> of fragments for each passage, twelve being the highest number, and this number occurs only twice among these selected readings: but one of the appearances of twelve MSS. happens in John vii. 53, where all the fragments omit that verse and the following eleven verses of chapter viii <note>This refers to the "Pericope Adulterae" (the woman caught in adultery), a passage famously absent from the oldest and most reliable Greek and Coptic manuscripts of the Gospel of John.</note>. Strangely enough some words of this passage have been found written in Sahidic upon a stone ‘pottery shard’ <note>original: "ostrakon"</note> in the British Museum and published in the catalogue by Mr. Hall, who made this interesting discovery.

In estimating the character of the Version the following figures will give some idea of the position which it holds. They have been compiled by the editor during correction of proofs, and do not refer to variation of particles. Beside them, under the head of ‘miscellaneous’, were collected the readings of other early <term>uncials: manuscripts written in large, rounded capital letters, typical of the 4th-8th centuries</term> and <term>cursives: manuscripts written in a running, joined hand</term> when varying

Having previously compared the Sahidic to the Bohairic version and the "Neutral" Greek text-type (Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus), the author now examines specific readings from the Gospels of Mark, Luke, and John to determine the Sahidic's relationship to "Western" textual variants.</meta>

# ESTIMATE OF THE VERSION #

The Sahidic version agrees with the Bohairic version in their support of the **Neutral readings** <term>Neutral readings: A scholarly category for early biblical texts, mainly from Egypt, that were thought to be free from later alterations.</term>.

In the Gospel of Mark, the Sahidic supplies 47 readings. In these, the Sahidic differs from the Neutral text in eight instances and shows a division between different manuscripts only twice. In chapter xiv, verse 68, the significant manuscripts 73 and 108, along with 127, provide the Neutral reading. In chapter vii, verse 4, there are three Sahidic variations of the reading "and couches" <note>Original Greek: καὶ κλινῶν (*kai klinōn*); this refers to the ritual washing of dining furniture.</note>. Not a single purely **Western** <term>Western reading: A style of early biblical text known for adding extra details or paraphrasing, often found in early Latin and Syriac translations.</term> form occurs in the Sahidic version among these readings from the second Gospel.

Of the 65 readings selected from the Gospel of Luke, one of the three manuscripts (designated as 129) omits the phrase *on the same day* in chapter ix, verse 37, which is the unique reading found in the other two manuscripts. All six manuscripts use the phrase *covered for burning* <note>Original context: Luke xxiv. 32; this refers to the hearts of the disciples "burning" within them on the road to Emmaus, though the Sahidic manuscripts here show a specific variation in how they describe that feeling.</note> in chapter xxiv, verse 32, which supports the Western reading. Manuscript 91 includes the addition *and thus it must be* in chapter xxiv, verse 46, which goes against the other two manuscripts that confirm the Neutral omission. However, with these three exceptions, the Sahidic agrees consistently with the Neutral reading in all other selected locations.

In 40 readings taken from the Gospel of John, 11 Sahidic readings vary from the Neutral, and six take the Western form. One of these, the word *given*, in chapter vii, verse 39, is paraphrased because of the difficulty of expressing a passive verb in the Coptic language. Two combinations of readings occur at chapter i, verse 18 and chapter i, verse 34: *God the only Son* and *the Son the chosen* <note>These are famous textual variants; chapter i, verse 18 usually reads either "the only begotten Son" or "the only begotten God," while chapter i, verse 34 varies between "the Son of God" and "the Chosen of God."</note>. In no case is there any variation among the Sahidic manuscripts themselves, which are quite numerous for most chapters of John.

From this investigation of selected readings, the same result as before is obtained. The Western readings show a slight but clear superiority in number over other variations, while the main stream of the text is Neutral. This Neutral text—now regarded as the early **Alexandrian** <term>Alexandrian form: The tradition of biblical manuscripts preserved in Egypt, valued for its accuracy.</term> form and also seen in the Bohairic—is maintained even more firmly in the Sahidic. Furthermore, the large number of Western readings included in the selections by the scholars **Westcott and Hort** <note>Brook Foss Westcott and Fenton John Anthony Hort were 19th-century scholars whose edition of the Greek New Testament revolutionized the field.</note> makes this case more significant, even though those authors omitted the description of the stone at the tomb, which is a remarkable example of the twelve major Western additions.

Version and the relation of the **Sahidic** <term>Sahidic: The dialect of the Coptic language used primarily in Upper (Southern) Egypt; it was the first dialect into which the Bible was translated.</term> to the **Bohairic** <term>Bohairic: The dialect of Coptic from the Nile Delta (Lower Egypt), which eventually became the liturgical language of the Coptic Church.</term> which the writer in the *Encyclopædia Biblica* iv. 5008–10 has expressed.

As for the **Sahidic manuscripts** <term>MSS: An abbreviation for 'manuscripts,' referring here to hand-copied ancient documents.</term> themselves, the fragments are seldom long enough to determine satisfactorily the real character of the entire documents, and the longest are naturally the more recent. If longer and earlier fragments are discovered greater diversity may appear, but at present there is not much sign of variation. *Matthew* 111 and the lectionary <term>lectionary: A book containing specific portions of Scripture organized for reading during church services throughout the year.</term> *m¹* seem to have a slightly different vocabulary from the rest: thus manuscript 111 reads "that which belongs to him" <note>original: **ⲉⲧϣⲟⲟⲡ ⲛⲁϥ**</note> for "that which he has" <note>original: **ⲉⲧⲛ̄ⲧⲁϥ**</note>, "they brought them" <note>original: **ⲁⲩⲉⲓⲥⲟⲩ**</note> for "bring them" <note>original: **ⲛⲓⲥⲟⲩ**</note>, "they did" <note>original: **ⲁⲩⲣ̅**</note> for "they came" <note>original: **ⲁⲩⲉⲓ**</note>, "the shore" <note>original: **ⲡⲉⲕⲣⲟ**</note> for "the land" <note>original: **ⲡⲕⲁϩ**</note>, "they being on board" <note>original: **ⲉⲩⲧⲁⲗⲉⲏⲩ**</note> for "they being safe" <note>original: **ⲉⲩⲟⲩⲟϫ**</note>—joined in this last case by manuscript 73—and "inform" <note>original: **ⲧⲁⲙⲉ**</note> for "say it" <note>original: **ϫⲟⲟⲥ**</note>; the lectionary *m¹* reads "at this place" <note>original: **ϩⲓⲙⲁⲓ**</note> for "in this manner" <note>original: **ⲛ̄ⲧⲉⲓϩⲉ**</note>, and "cup" <note>original: **ⲁⲡⲟⲧ**</note> for "cup" <note>original: **ϫⲱ**</note>. 

Manuscripts 73, 111, 134 and *m¹* show signs of conforming to the Bohairic, and 111 shows signs of conforming to the Greek as in the Gospel of *Matthew* xiii. 15, 17, 27 and xxi. 4. It has been observed that the Bohairic manuscript group D A E etc. give special support to the Sahidic in the Gospel of *Matthew*, but this tendency is not maintained in the Gospel of *Mark*. The Bohairic manuscript *M*, which is known to have been brought from the **Monastery of St. Anthony** <note>A famous Coptic Orthodox monastery located in an oasis in the Eastern Desert of Egypt, founded by the followers of Saint Anthony the Great.</note> in the Eastern Desert, bears traces of Sahidic influence, as also manuscript *r* now in the Library of the Patriarch at Cairo, but probably written by the same scribe as the manuscript of the Epistles and Acts which still reposes on the shelf of a Sahidic Library in **Dair al Muharraq** <note>Also known as the Monastery of the Virgin Mary at Al-Qusiya, this is a significant Sahidic-speaking monastic site in Upper Egypt.</note>. The peculiarities also of Bohairic manuscripts *F* and *K* sometimes suggest an affinity with the Sahidic.

## THE DATE OF THE VERSION

According to the opinion of <term>Harnack</term><note>Adolf von Harnack (1851–1930) was an influential German theologian and church historian who studied the early spread of Christianity.</note> expressed in the second edition of his *Expansion of Christianity* no trust-worthy information concerning the origin of the religion of Christ in Egypt exists; though he remarks that the traditional list of the <term>Patriarchs of Alexandria</term><note>The succession of bishops who led the Christian church in Egypt, beginning traditionally with St. Mark.</note> ought not to be lightly disregarded.

With the accession of <term>Demetrius</term><note>The twelfth bishop of Alexandria (188–232 AD), known for organizing the Egyptian church and overseeing the school of Alexandria.</note> in A. D. 188 the real history of the Egyptian Church may be said to begin. During his long patriarchate he appointed four bishops, and his successor <term>Heraclas</term><note>A student of Origen who later became the bishop of Alexandria (232–248 AD).</note> as many as twenty, which indicates a rapid progress of the Church. <term>Clement of Alexandria</term><note>An early Christian teacher (c. 150–215 AD) who sought to unite Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note>, born about A. D. 150, speaks of the Christians spreading over all the land, and while <term>Origen</term><note>One of the most prolific and influential early Christian scholars (c. 184–253 AD).</note> in his discussion with <term>Celsus</term><note>A 2nd-century pagan philosopher whose criticisms of Christianity are preserved primarily in Origen's rebuttal.</note> admits that the number of Christians was small in the early part of the third century, yet there were enough to persecute under the rule of <term>Decius</term><note>A Roman Emperor who, in 250 AD, issued an edict requiring everyone in the Empire to perform a sacrifice to the Roman gods, leading to widespread Christian martyrdom.</note> in A. D. 250.

Considering the ease with which some of the ancient Egyptian beliefs might be adapted to the creed and teaching of Christians, and that there was probably an heretical <term>Gospel of the Egyptians</term><note>A non-canonical (apocryphal) text used by early Christians in Egypt, likely written in the 2nd century.</note> in the second century, we can hardly deny the likelihood of an early propagation of the faith. If with Harnack, relying on <term>Leipoldt</term><note>Johannes Leipoldt (1880–1965), a scholar whose work was fundamental to the study of the Coptic language and Egyptian Christianity.</note>, 'we may conjecture, though we cannot prove, that the <term>Sahidic Version</term><note>The translation of the Bible into the dialect of Coptic used in Upper (southern) Egypt.</note> partly goes back to the third century', there seems some reason for supposing that need of a <term>vernacular</term><note>The everyday language spoken by the common people, rather than the formal Greek used by the ruling elite.</note> Version arose as early as the time of Demetrius.

Where history fails us, the internal character of the Sahidic supplies confirmation of a date earlier than the third century. Being fundamentally of the older <term>Alexandrian type</term><note>A category of New Testament manuscript tradition associated with Alexandria, generally considered by scholars to be very accurate and close to the original texts.</note>, yet bearing signs of mixture from one or more sources, we can imagine the Version as of a form of text which, diverging from the main stream, retained variations belonging to the earliest

<summary>This page discusses the historical evidence and scholarly theories regarding when the Bible was first translated into the Sahidic dialect of Coptic, suggesting an origin as early as the late 2nd or early 3rd century AD.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the historical and linguistic investigation into the origins of the Coptic Bible. While the previous page discussed the early patriarchs and the lack of firm records before 188 AD, this page examines the "DNA" of the manuscript text—specifically its "Western" readings—to argue for a date as early as the 2nd century.</meta>

<page-num>399</page-num>

# THE DATE OF THE VERSION

times, such as are known by the name of <term>Western readings</term><note>A specific group of early variations in New Testament manuscripts often found in Old Latin and Old Syriac texts, characterized by more descriptive or paraphrased wording compared to later standards.</note>. These it preserved, and adopted afterwards some of the readings which are usually regarded as due to a later <term>Syrian revision</term><note>Also known as the Byzantine text-type, this was a major editorial effort in the 4th century to harmonize and polish Greek biblical manuscripts.</note>.

This theory does not preclude the translation of the Greek having taken place as late as the third century, but the traces of early mixture shown by the definite tinge of Western influence can hardly be explained except by reference to a date as early as possible. If Christianity did not exist at all in <term>Upper Egypt</term><note>The southern region of Egypt, further up the Nile from the Mediterranean coast.</note> before 150 AD, then we must come down to the date of <term>Demetrius</term><note>Bishop of Alexandria from 188–232 AD, who oversaw the first major expansion of the organized church into the Egyptian countryside.</note> as the earliest possible date of the Version; but if, as is more likely, the Christian religion had spread by means of the Nile immediately after it began to be preached in <term>Alexandria</term><note>The great coastal metropolis of Egypt where Christianity first arrived, likely from Judea.</note>, and had already become infected by heretical and semi-pagan superstitions in the second century, we may provisionally conclude from the character of the <term>Sahidic Version</term><note>The dialect of Coptic spoken in southern Egypt; the Sahidic Bible is one of the oldest and most important witnesses to the early Christian text.</note> that it was made at that time.

**Vocabulary**

*   **Western readings:** Early textual variants associated with the Latin West and Syria.
*   **Syrian revision:** A later standardization of the Greek New Testament.
*   **Upper Egypt:** The southern part of the country, where Sahidic Coptic was spoken.
*   **Demetrius:** The 12th Bishop of Alexandria (late 2nd century).
*   **Alexandria:** The intellectual center of Egypt and the seat of the Church.
*   **Sahidic Version:** The southern Coptic translation of the scriptures.

<summary>This page argues that the Sahidic Coptic translation of the Bible likely dates to the 2nd century because it contains "Western" textual variants that predated later standardizations. It suggests Christianity spread south along the Nile much earlier than official church records indicate.</summary>

<keywords>Sahidic Version, textual criticism, Western readings, Upper Egypt, Demetrius of Alexandria, early Christianity, Coptic language, manuscript dating</keywords>

-># MONETARY SYSTEM OF THE PHILIPPINE ISLANDS<-

<note>The text on this page is extremely faint, appearing as a very light impression or heavily faded print, but remains legible upon close inspection.</note>

Since the functions of silver coins have already been demonstrated, it is unnecessary—and perhaps even ill-advised—to revisit the debates surrounding the <term>overvaluation</term><note>A situation where the government sets the legal value of a currency higher than its actual market value or the value of the metal it contains.</note> of currency, which often stem from a misunderstanding of the term itself.

This theory does not prevent <term>subsidiary silver coins</term><note>Smaller denomination coins (like change) that are used for daily transactions; their value is usually maintained by the government rather than the raw metal value.</note> from circulating alongside paper notes. However, it is difficult to determine in advance, with any degree of certainty, the exact volume of such circulation required above a basic minimum. If the <term>circulating medium</term><note>The total supply of money, including coins and bills, moving through an economy.</note> did not include silver but consisted entirely of notes, it is obvious that the volume of silver coins would be much larger than it is today. Nevertheless, it would be difficult, if not impossible, to calculate what that volume ought to be based on the <term>requirements of trade</term><note>The actual amount of physical money needed by the public to conduct daily business and purchases.</note>. For that reason, it has been decided to limit this comparison to the volume of silver coins as it is actually dictated by the <term>market for currency</term><note>the economic forces of supply and demand that naturally determine how much money is needed in a specific region.</note>—a concept that will be more precisely defined in a later chapter.

**Vocabulary and Concepts**
*   **Gresham's Law**<note>The economic principle that "bad money drives out good"—if two forms of money have the same face value but different intrinsic values, the more valuable metal will be hoarded and disappear from circulation.</note>
*   **Overvaluation**
*   **Subsidiary silver coins**
*   **Circulating medium**
*   **Requirements of trade**
*   **Market for currency**
*   **Philippine Islands**

<summary>This page discusses the challenges of balancing silver coinage and paper notes within the Philippine monetary system, emphasizing that market forces rather than central predictions should determine the volume of coins in circulation.</summary>
<keywords>Philippine Islands, monetary policy, silver coinage, overvaluation, currency circulation, trade requirements, Gresham's law, economic history</keywords>

<summary>This manuscript fragment from Akhmim contains the Coptic translation of John 11:53-56, detailing the decision of the authorities to kill Jesus and His subsequent retreat to the city of Ephraim before the Passover.</summary>
